Hard Materials
Structural materials are typically hard, because they must withstand strong
deforming forces. They include cement, concrete, and steel and are chosen fO r their
strength and endurance. Some structural materials have been known smce prehis-
toric times, but new materials have allowed architects tO design ever taller, Often
more graceful buildings and tO ensure that they are economical tO inhabit and easy
tO maintain. Some structural materials are based on those found in organlsms,
where their task is tO form a rigid framework or tO act as weapons. NOt all hard
materials, though, are used fO r construction. Many form the ObJ ects that we use
every day, some are IT11nerals that we use fO r constructing artistic artifacts, and
some are gemstones that use fO r decoration.
7 ． 5 Diamond and Graphite
Carbon is an example Of a material that lies on the borderline between hard and
soft, for its various allotropes include the very hard diamond and the softer, fran-
gible (easily broken) graphite. The differences in the properties of its allotropes can
be traced tO their structures. As described in Section 6 · 11 ， graphite consists Of
planar sheets 0f sp hybridized carbon atoms in a hexagonal network (FIG. 7 · 10 ） ·
Electrons spread through the delocalized q-network that extends across the plane.
This delocalization accounts for graphite being a black, lustrous, electrically con-
ducting solid; indeed, graphite is used as an electrical conductor in industry and as
electrodes in electrochemical cells and batteries. Electrons can move within the
sheets of graphite but much less readily from one sheet to another. Hence, graphite
conducts electricity better parallel to the sheets than perpendicular to them. Graph-
ite is actually a moderately hard material, but in its commercially available forms
many lmpurity atoms, such as nitrogen and oxygen from the air, are trapped
between the sheets; these atoms weaken the already weak intersheet bonds and let
the sheets of atoms slide over one another. Thus ， impure graphite is slippery. ln
pencil "lead," the graphite is mixed with clay. When we write with a pencil, the
mark left on the paper consists of rubbed-off layers of graphite.

ln diamond, each carbon atom is sp hybridized and linked tetrahedrally to its
four neighbors, with all electrons in C— C o-bonds (FIG. 7 · 1 1 ） · Diamond is a rigid,
transparent, electrically insulating solid. lt is the hardest substance known and the
best conductor Of heat, being about five times better than copper. These last tWO
properties make it an ideal abrasive, because it can scratch all Other substances, yet
the heat generated by friction is quickly conducted away. Diamond is also used as
a protective coating for drill bits and Other cutting tOOls. lts high heat conductivity
makes thin films Of diamond ideal for use as a base fO r some integrated circuits SO
that they dO not overheat. The vigorous vibration Of an atom in a hOt part Of the
crystal is rapidly transmitted tO distant, cooler partS through the covalent bonds,
rather like the effect of slammmg a door in a steel-framed building.
ln nature, diamond is found embedded in a soft rock called 庞乜 This
rock rises in columns from deep in the Earth, where the diamonds are formed
under intense pressure. One method used tO make synthetic industrial diamonds
re-creates the geological conditions that produce natural diamonds by compress-
ing graphite at pressures greater than 80 kbar and temperatures above 1500 OC
(FIG. 7 · 1 2 ） · Small amounts 0f metals such as chromium and iron are added to the
graphite. The molten metals are thought to dissolve the graphite and then, as they

molten metal. Another, more common, method fO r producing synthetic diamonds
is by thermal decomposition Of methane. ln this technique, the carbon atoms settle
on a COOI surface as bOth graphite and diamond. However, because hydrogen atoms
produced in the decomposition react more quickly with graphite, forming volatile
hydrocarbons, more diamond than graphite survives. This is the method most com-
monly used t0 apply diamond coatings t0 cutting t001s.

7 ． 10 Glasses
A glass is an ionic solid with an amorphous structure resembling that Of a liquid,
generally created by freezing a melt quickly so that crystals cannot form. Glass has
a network structure based on a nonmetal oxide, usually silica, Si02, that has been
melted together with metal oxides acting as "network modifiers," which alter the
arrangement Of bonds in the solid. Glass was first used in anuent tlmes and has
played an important role in the development Of modern architecture. TOday, inter-
est in glass is growing due tO the use Of optical fibers tO provide wideband telecom-
munications networks. Glasses commonly shatter intO fragments when struck with
sufficient force because their atoms form an intricate network and bonds dO not
lie in orderly arrays.
To make glass, silica in the form of sand is heated to about 1600 OC. Metal
oxides, such as MO (where M is a metal cation, such as Na Pb2+, or Zn ）， are
2 +
added to the silica. As the mixture melts, many of the Si—O bonds break and the
orderly structure of the individual crystals is lost. 、 When the melt cools, the Si—O
bonds re-form but are prevented from forming a crystalline lattice because some Of
the silicon atoms bond with the 02- ions of the metal oxide to give —Si—O—Mn+
groups in place of some of the —Si—O—Si— links present in pure silica. Because of
the strong covalent character Of the Si—O bonds, a short-range order is preserved
in the glass; however, long-range order is lost. Silicate glasses are generally trans-
parent and durable and can be formed into flat sheets, blown into bottles, or
molded into desired shapes.

7 ． 11 Ceramics
Many Of the materials used in the most advanced technologies are based on a
material characteristic Of one Of the oldest technologies: common clay. Most clays
used commercially are oxides Of silicon, aluminum, and magnesium. 乃 C /
contains primarily 0 方 e ， a form Of aluminum aluminosilicate that can be
obtained reasonably free of the iron impurities that make many clays look reddish

===== 第 383 页 =====
241
brown, and SO it is white. However, Other clays contain the iron oxides that cause
the orange color Of terra cotta tiles and flower potS.
The appearance Of a flake Of clay reflects its internal structure, which is some-
thing like an untidy stack of papers (FIG. 7 · 24 ） · Sheets of tetrahedral silicate units
or octahedral units Of aluminum or magnesium oxides are separated by layers Of
water molecules that serve to bind the layers of the flake together. Each flake of
clay is surrounded by a double layer of ions that separates the flakes by repelling
the like charges on the other flakes. This repulsion allows the flakes to slide past
one another and gives the clay the ability tO flow in response tO stress. As a result,
clays can be easily molded.
When clay is baked in a kiln, it forms the hard, tough “ materials used
in firebricks, tiles, and potS. As the water is driven out during the firing process,
strong chemical bonds form between the flakes. Large amounts of china clay, which
IS used tO make ceranmcs such as porcelain and china, are applied in the coating Of
paper (such as this page) t0 give a smooth, nonabsorbent surface. Clay was the first
substance tO be made intO a ceram1C, an inorganic material that has been hardened
by heating t0 a high temperature. Today a wide variety of compounds, often oxides,
are used tO create ceranmcs With specific properties.
Typically, a ceram1C material is very hard, insoluble in water, and stable tO cor-
roslon and high temperatures. These characteristlcs are the key tO their technologi-
cal value. Although many ceranmcs are brittle, they can be used at high tempera-
tures without failing, and they resist deformation. Cerarmcs are Often the oxides Of
elements that are on the border between metals and nonmetals, but d-metal oxides
and some compounds Of boron and silicon With carbon and nitrogen are alSO
ceram1C materials. Most ceramlcs are electrical insulators; however, some d-metal
oxides, such as barium titanate, BaTi03, and zinc OXide, are semiconductors.
ln addition, some Of the most promising high-temperature superconductors are
ceramics (see Section 7 · 14 ） ·
Many aluminosilicate ceranucs are created by heating aluminosilicate clays tO
drive the water out from between the sheets Of tetrahedra. This procedure leaves a
rigid heterogeneous mass 0f tiny interlocking crystals bound together by glassy
silica. Bone china, which is strong enough to be used fo r thin, lightweight dishes, is
made from china clay with bone ash as a binder that strengthens the ceramic.
Aluminum oxide, A1203, is a ceramic oxide found in different solid forms, each
Of which is an important material. As a-alumina, it is the very hard, stable, crystal-

Granules that form in the disperslon are compressed in a mold and sintered. Single-

matrix that has few Of the tiny cracks that can initiate breakage in brittle ceranucs.

Materials fo r N ew Technologies
Solid-state chemistry is an exciting area Of research, not only because Of the
lmportance Of the applications, but because Of what scientists are learning about
the nature Of matter. ln these sections we shall see hOW an understanding Of the
nature Of solids allows us tO design materials that are magnetic, glow in the
dark, make miniature electromcs possible, and conduct electricity with little or
no reslstance.
7 ． 12 Bonding in the Solid State
Many of the interesting and desirable properties of solids stem from their ability
tO conduct an electric current, the flow Of electric charge. ln electromc conduction,
the charge is carried by electrons. Electronic conduction is the mechanism Of con-
duction in metals and graphite. ln iomc conduction, the charge is carried by ions.
This is the mechanism Of electrical conduction a molten salt or an electrolyte
solution. Because ions are tOO bulky tO travel easily through most solids, the flow
Of charge through solids is ln most cases a result Of electromc conduction. How-
ever, solid electrolytes that allow ions tO move through their lattices are important
10111C conductors used in rechargeable batteries.
Substances are classified according tO their electrical resistance and hOW it var-
ies with temperature (FIG. 7 · 26 ）：
An insulator is a substance that has such a high resistance that it does not
conduct electricity.
A metallic conductor iS an electronic conductor With a resistance that increases
as the temperature iS raised.
A semiconductor iS an electronic conductor With a resistance that decreases
as the temperature IS raised.
A superconductor is an electronlc conductor that conducts electricity with
zero resistance, usually at very IOW temperatures.
A solid electrolyte is an conductor.
ln most cases, a metallic conductor has a much lower resistance than a semlcon-
ductor, but it is the temperature dependence Of the reslstance that distinguishes the
tWO types Of conductors.

7 · 1 2 Bonding in the Solid State
Molecular orbital theory explains the electrical properties of metallic conduc-
tors, semiconductors, and insulators by treating them as one huge molecule and
supposing that their valence electrons occupy delocalized orbitals that spread
throughout the solid. We have already seen ()n Section 4 · 9 ） that, when N atomic
orbitals merge together in a molecule, they form N molecular orbitals. The same
true of a metal; but, fo r a metal, N is enormous (about 1023 fo r 10 g of copper, for
example). lnstead of the few molecular orbitals with widely spaced energies typical
Of small molecules, the huge number Of molecular orbitals in a metal are SO close
together in energy that they form a nearly continuous band (FIG. 7 · 27 ） · As a guide
tO the type Of energy separation tO expect, we saw in Section 1 · 7 that the separation

NOW consider a molecular orbital treatment. Consider, for instance, sodium.
Each atom contributes one valence orbital (the 3s-orbital in this case) and one
valence electron. If there are N atoms in the sample, then the N 3s-orbitals merge
to form a band of N molecular orbitals, of which half are net bonding and half are
net antibonding. We say ' net ” bonding or antibonding because, in general and as
we saw in connection with benzene (Section 4 · 12L a molecular orbital is bonding
between some neighbors and antibonding between others, depending on where its
internuclear nodes lie; only the molecular orbital Of lowest energy, with no inter-
nuclear nodes, is bonding between all neighboring atoms. The N electrons contrib-
uted by the N atoms OCCUPY the orbitals according to the building-up principle.
Because tWO electrons can occupy each orbital, the N electrons occupy the lower N
bonding orbitals.
An emptY or incompletely filled band of molecular orbitals is called a conduc-
tion band. Because neighboring orbitals in metals lie SO close together in energy, it
takes very little additional energy t0 excite the electrons from the topmost filled
molecular orbitals tO the empty orbitals Of the conduction band. Electrons in the
conduction band can move freely through the solid, and so they can carry an elec-
triC current. resistance Of the metal increases With temperature because, When
it is heated, the atoms vibrate more vigorously. The passing electrons collide with
the vibrating atoms and do not pass through the solid so easily.

7 ． 13 Semiconductors
Semiconductors have revolutionized the electronics industry because very tiny
semiconducting devices can be used tO control the flow Of an electrical current. As
its name implies, an electrical current does not flow as well through a semiconduc-
tor as it does through a metal. ln an lntrmslc semiconductor, an empty conduction
band lies close in energy to a full valence band. As a result, as the solid is warmed,
electrons can be excited from the valence band intO the conduction band, where
they can travel throughout the solid. Hence, the resistance Of a semiconductor
decreases as 1tS temperature IS raised.
The ability Of a semiconductor tO carry an electric current can also be enhanced
by adding electrons tO the conduction band or by removing some from the valence
band. This modification is carried out chemically by doping the solid, or spreading
small amounts Of impurities throughout it, and results in an extri11SIC semiconduc-
tor. ln one example, a mmute amount Of a Group 15 element such as arsemc IS
added tO very pure silicon. The arsenic increases the number Of electrons in the
solid: each Si atom (Group 14 ） has four valence electrons, whereas each As atom
(Group 15 ） has five. The additional electrons enter the upper, normally emptY con-
duction band of silicon and allow the solid to conduct (FIG. 7 · 29 ） · This tYP e of
material iS called an n-type semiconductor because it contains excess negatively
charged electrons. When silicon (Group 14 ） is doped with indium (Group 13 ）
instead Of arsenic, the SOlid has fewer valence electrons than does pure silicon; SO
the valence band is no longer completely full (FIG. 7 · 30 ） · The valence band is now
said tO contain "holes. ” Because the valence band is no longer full, it has been
turned intO a conduction band, and an electric current can flow. This type Of seml-
conductor is called a p-type semiconductor, because the absence Of negatively
charged electrons is equivalent to the presence of positively charged holes. The
doped solids are overall electrically neutral, because the nuclei of the doping atoms
have a charge that matches the number Of their electrons.
S01id-state electronic devices such as diodes, transistors, and integrated circults
contain p —n Junctions in which a p-type semiconductor is contact with an n-type
semiconductor (FIG. 7 · 31 ） · The structure 0f a p—n Junction allows an electric cur-
rent tO flow in only one direction. 、 When the electrode attached tO the p-type semi-
conductor has a negative charge, the hOles in the p-type semiconductor are attracted
tO it, the electrons in the n-type semiconductor are attracted tO the Other (positive)
electrode, and current does not flow. When the polarity is reversed, with the nega-
tive electrode attached tO the n-type semiconductor, electrons flow from the n-type
semiconductor through the p-type semiconductor toward the positive electrode.

Superconductivity is the loss Of electrical resistance when a substance IS cooled
below a characteristic transition temperature (Tc). Conventional superconductivity
arises from the ability Of electrons tO pair by making use Of lattice vibrations. The
electron pairs, which are called Cooper pairs after the scientist whO first proposed
the mechanism, can travel almost freely through the lattice, rather like the way
oxen yoked together are less deflected by obstacles than individual oxen. A Cooper
pair forms when the presence Of one electron distorts the cations Of the lattice in its
vicinity, and that reglon Of distorted lattice attracts a second electron intO 1tS vicm-
ity (FIG. 7 · 33 ） · The two electrons are attracted together weakly in this way; the
palr—and the resulting superconductivity—survlves only if the temperature IS SO
IOW that the palr is not shaken apart by lattice vibrations. Superconductivity was
first observed in 1911 in mercury, fo r which Tc = 4 K. Over the years, many other
metallic superconductors were identified, some having transltion temperatures as
high as 23 K. However, low-temperature superconductors need to be cooled with
liquid helium, which is very expensive.
ln 1986 a record-high transition temperature of 35 K was observed, not fo r a
metal but fO r a ceram1C material, a lanthanum—copper oxide doped with barium.
Then, early in 1987 ， a new record of 93 K was set with a yttrium—barium—copper
oxide and a senes Of related compounds. ln 1988 ， tw 0 more oxide series Of
bismuth—strontium—calcium—copper and thallium—barium—calcium—copper exhib-
ited transition temperatures of 110 K and 125 K, respectively. By 2012 ， the highest
attained at 1 atm was 13 8 K. These temperatures can be reached by cooling the
materials with liquid nitrogen, at only 0 · 2 ％ of the cost of liquid helium.
Almost all these high-temperature superconductors (HTSCs) are hard, brit-
tle ceramic oxides that have sheets Of copper and oxygen atoms sandwiched
between layers Of either cations or a combination Of cations and oxide ions, and
all are derived from their respective parent insulators by doping (FIG. 7 · 34 ） ·

7 ． 15 Luminescent Materials
lncandescence is light emitted by a hot body, such as the filament in a lamp or the
particles Of hOt soot in a candle flame. Luminescence is the emission Of light by a
process Other than incandescence. For example, when hydrogen peroxide reacts
with chlorine, the 02 formed by the oxidation of H202 may be produced in an
energetically excited state and emit light as it discards its excess energy. This pro-
cess IS an example Of chemiluminescence, the em1SS10n Of light by products formed
in energetically excited states in a chemical reaction (FIG. 7 · 37 ） · The light sticks
used for emergency lighting glow with light from a chemiluminescent process.
BioIuminescence iS a form Of chemiluminescence generated by a living organism.
For example, the enzyme 厂陋 se catalyzes the oxidation Of 厂 in fireflies
and some bacteria, producing oxyluciferin and emitting light.
Fluorescence and phosphorescence are the em1SS10n Of light from molecules
excited by radiation of higher frequency, such as visible light being emitted when a
substance iS illuminated With ultraviolet radiation. ln fluorescence, em1SS1011 Of
light persists f0 r only a few nanoseconds after the illumination ceases. ln phospho-
rescence, the em1SS1011 persists, sometimes for seconds, as in the element phospho-
rus, from which the phenomenon gets its name (see Section 16 · 15 ） · The crucial

FIuorescent materials are very lmportant in the electromcs industry, as narrow

Triboluminescence iS luminescence that results from mechanical shock tO a
crystal. lt is observed in many crystalline substances and can be seen, fO r example,
by striking or grinding sugar crystals in a dark room. The grinding creates crystal
defects that trap electrons. When the electrons fall back intO their usual locations,
light is emitted.
The cathode-ray tubes that were once widely used fO r television and computer
displays, and the plasma screens that (together with liquid-crystal displays) have
replaced them, all make use of phosphors, phosphorescent materials that glow
when they are excited by the impact Of electrons or ultraviolet radiation. ln a cath-
ode-ray color monitor or television tube, clusters Of three phosphors consisting Of
a sulfide doped by a d-block metal are used for each dot in the screen. The red
phosphor is often yttrium oxysulfide, Y202S, activated by euromum. Silver-
activated ZnS is often used for the blue phosphor and copper-activated ZnS fo r the
green phosphor. Solid zinc sulfide is an insulator, with a large energy difference
between the conductance and the valence bands, and the activating metal has an
energy level between those tw 0 bands. When the zinc sulfide is struck by electrons
Of sufficient energy, one Of its electrons IS excited tO the conduction band, leaving a
positively charged hole in the lattice. The hole travels t0 an atom of the activating
metal ()n Other words, electrons move intO the hOle, leaving a hOle elsewhere, and
so the hole effectively travels through the solid). The excited electron then drops
back from the conduction band into that hole, emitting light of a wavelength cor-
responding tO the energy separation between the activatmg metal and the excited
state. The phosphors must Stop glowing as soon as the excitation beam passes on,
SO that the picture can change rapidly. ln a plasma screen the excitation is caused
by the ultraviolet radiation emitted by an electric discharge through a low-pressure
mixture of noble gases in a cell behind each dot of phosphor.
Light-emitting diode （ LED ） displays also use luminescent materials. ln an LED
a luminescent material generates light when an electric current is applied tO a p—n
junction. Compounds used t0 make different colors of light vary, but commonly
aluminum gallium arsenide is used to make red LEDs, indium gallium nitride green
LEDs, and zinc selenide blue LEDs. When tiny LEDs of these three colors are clus-
tered tightly together on a display screen, a ny color can be generated depending on
which of the three colors are activated.
Organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) use a film consisting of an organic
polymer that conducts electricity to generate light of different colors. Although
LCD screens (Section 6 · 15 ） are more common, LED displays do not require back-
lighting, and so can be made much thinner. LED lights are now being introduced
fO r many applications, as they use much less power than incandescent lights and
last many times longer.

7 ． 16 Magnetic MateriaIs
As remarked in Box 4 · 2 ， paramagnetism is the tendency Of a substance tO move
intO a magnetic field. lt arises when an atom or molecule has at least one unpaired
electron, which aligns with the applied field. However, because the spins on neigh-
boring atoms or molecules are aligned almost randomly, paramagnetism IS very
weak and the alignment Of electron SP1ns is lost when the magnetic field is
removed. ln some d-metals, however, when the unpaired electrons Of many neigh-
boring atoms align with one another in an applied magnetic field, the much stron-
ger effect of ferromagnetism arises. The regions of aligned spins, which are called
domains (FIG. 7 · 38 ）， survive even after the applied field is turned off.
Ferromagnetism IS much stronger than paramagnetism, and ferromagnetIC
materials are used tO make permanent magnets. They are also used in the coatings
of computer hard drives. The electromagnetic recording heads align large numbers
Of spins as the platter rotates underneath, and the spin alignment in the domains
remains for years. ln an antiferromagnetic material, neighboring spins are locked
intO an p / / e / arrangement; SO the magnetic moments cancel. Manganese IS
antiferromagnetic. ln a ferrimagnetic material, the spins on neighboring atoms are
different, and although they are locked together in an antiparallel arrangement, the
tw O magnetic moments dO not completely cancel.
Ferromagnetism also occurs in alloys such as alnico (Section 7 · 4 ） and some
compounds Of the d-metals, such as the oxides Of iron and chromium. Ceram1c
magnets, which are used in refrigerator magnets, are made Of barium ferrite
(BaO•nFe203) or strontium ferrite (SrO•nFe203). They are made by compressing
the powdered ferrite in a magnetic field and heating it until it hardens. Because
these magnets are ceramic, they are hard and brittle, with IOW densities. However,
they are the most widely used magnets because Of their IOW cost.
Ferrofluids are ferromagnetic liquids. They are suspensions of finely powdered
magnetite, Fe304, in a VISCOLIS, Oily liquid (such as IT11neral Oil) that contains a
detergent （ such as oleic acid, a long-chain carboxylic acid). The iron oxide particles
dO not settle out, because they are attracted tO the polar ends Of the detergent mol-
ecules, which form compact clusters (a type of 记 e / Section 10 · 9 ） around the
particles. The nonpolar ends of the detergent molecules point outward, allowing
the micelles to form a colloidal suspenslon in the oil. When a magnet is brought
near a ferrofluid, the particles in the liquid try to align themselves with the mag-
netic field, but they are kept in place by the oil (FIG. 7 · 39 ） · As a result, it is possible
to control the flow and position of the ferrofluid by means of an applied magnetic
field. One application of ferrofluids is in the braking systems of exercise machines.
The stronger the magnetic field, the greater is the resistance tO motion.
Recently, interest in single-molecule magnets has grown. lndividual molecular
magnets contain several d-block metal atoms bonded tO groups Of nonmetal atoms
such as carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. They can respond to a magnetic field as if
they were nano-S1ze compass needles and thus have great potential fO r nmniatunz-
ing electronic storage media such as computer disks. Typically the d-block metal
atoms are imbedded in cagelike structures, and some Of the nano-S1ze molecular
magnets have interesting shapes, such as rings, tubes, or spheres (FIG. 7 · 40 ） ·

7 ． 17 Composite MateriaIs
Some Of the most advanced materials, such as composite materials, are modeled
after materials found in nature. A composlte material conslsts Of tWO or more
substances that have been combined intO a heterogeneous material while retaining
their individual characteristics. Natural composites include seashells and bone.
Seashells owe their strength tO a tough organic matrix and their hardness tO the
calcium carbonate crystals imbedded in the matrix (FIG. 7 · 41 ） · Bones have low
density, but they are strong because Of their composite nature. ln bone tissue,
crystals of phosphate salts are embedded in fibers of a natural polymer (an
organic compound with long chains) called co llagen that hold them in place but
allow a small amount of flexibility. Artificial bone and cartilage are now becom-
ing realities through the preparation Of synthetic composite materials such as
fiberglass. These materials mimic bone in that they have inorganic solids mixed
intO a crack-resistant polymer matrix. The result is a material that has great
strength yet remains flexible. Some lightweight composites, such as the graphite
composite used fO r tennis rackets, in which graphite fibers are imbedded in a
polymer matrix, and the fibrous refractory composite insulation tiles used on the
body of the space shuttle, in which alumina-borosilicate fibers are added to a
silica ceram1C matrix, can have three times the strength-to-density ratiO Of steel
(FIG. 7 · 42 ） ·
Ceramic materials are hard but tend to be brittle. Flakes of very strong, tough
materials such as titanium diboride, TiB2, can be distributed throughout ceranucs
to strengthen them. Even if a crack did form, it would be unable to propagate past
the first flake that it encountered. A composite material containing ceramic flakes
in a polylactic acid polymer is being used t0 provide instant mends fo r broken
bones. The material is i11J ected as a paste intO the cracked bone, where it setS at
bOdy temperature intO a scaffold that actS like bone tissue and promotes healing as
new bone cellS form around it.

Nanomaterials
A new area Of research with the potential, among Other things, tO revolutionize
medical diagnosis and treatment and improve our quality Of life is nanosclence, the
study Of the properties Of nanomaterials, and its application, nanotechnology, the
procedures used tO manipulate matter on this scale. These procedures include new
lmaging technologies such as the scanning tunneling microscope and atomic force
mlcroscope (see BOX 6 · 1 ） · Nanomaterials are materials with particle sizes in the
range 1 to 100 nm; they are larger than individual molecules but too small to
exhibit most bulk properties. Nanotechnology has the promise t0 provide new
materials such as biosensors that monitor and even repair bOdily processes, nmcro-
scop1C computers, artificial bone, and lightweight, remarkably strong materials.
7 ． 18 The Nature and Uses of NanomateriaIs
ln these sections summarlze What nanomaterials are, hOW they are prepared,
some Of the ways the properties Of nanomaterials differ from atomic properties or
those Of bulk matter, and why they have raised such interest in the scientific and
business communities. discovery Of hOW some nonmetals and metalloids can
be manipulated intO assembling themselves intO regular, extended structures IS
creating entirely new areas of research (Box 16 · 2 ） ·
ln a block of metal the separation of neighboring energy levels is infinitesimal.
However, the separatlon iS significant in a cluster Of atoms With dimenslons Of up
to 100 nm or SO. A cluster Of atoms a medium can act as a trap fO r electrons, and
tO a good approximation we can treat the cluster as a potential well and use what
we already know about electrons trapped in wells to estimate the allowed energy
levels. The fact that the well is not empty does not matter; it is a region in which an
electron has lower potential energy than when in its surroundings. The difference
between the one-dimensional well treated in Section 1 · 7 (where we saw that the
energy levels are 07 = ” 乃 / 8 。 L2 ） and the present case is that the well we now
consider is three-dimensional and best regarded as spherical. Therefore, we need tO
consider the energies Of electrons trapped in a region rather like a hydrogen atom
without the central nucleus but with a surrounding wall. A spherical well is more
difficult to deal with than a rectangular well, but the results are very similar. For

7 ． 19 Nanotubes
ln 1991 scientists identified a previously unknown form of carbon when they
sealed tWO graphite rods inside a container Of helium gas and passed an electric
discharge between them. Much Of one rod evaporated, but some surprising struc-
tures resulted (FIG. 7 · 44 ） · As well as the tiny 60-atom carbon spheres known as
buckminsterfullerene, which had been known since 1985 ， hollow, perfectly straight
carbon nanotubes were detected. A nanotube can be thought Of as a graphene sheet
of millions of carbon atoms rolled into a cylinder only 1 一 3 nm in diameter.
Carbon nanotubes conduct electricity because Of the extended network of
delocalized q-bonds that runs from one end of the tube to the other. The conductiv-
ity of nanotubes depends on the way the tubes are rolled (FIG. 7 · 45 ） · If the points
are aligned perpendicular tO the long axis (the “ armchair ” configuration) ， the con-
ductivity of the nanotubes is high enough to be considered metallic. If the points of
the hexagons are aligned along the long axis of the tube (the “ zigzag" and "chiral ”
orientations), the nanotubes may be either metallic conductors or semiconductors,
depending on the angle of wrap and the diameter of the tube. Like diamonds, car-
bon nanotubes are good conductors Of heat. Their interesting electrical conductiv-
ity and high thermal conductivity make carbon nanotubes good candidates fo r the
development Of miniature integrated circuits.
Carbon nanotubes are very strong, and their tensile strength parallel tO the ax1S
Of the tube is the greatest Of any material that has been measured. Because they

may seem surpnsmg at first, because we dO not assouate graphite with great

At least 50 different types of nanotubes and nanospheres have been synthe-
sized from substances Other than carbon. For example, MOS2 and WS2 nanotubes
and nanospheres serve as SOlid lubricants, nanotubes ShOW pronuse as a
means Of storing hydrogen gas, and nanospheres Of ruthenium coated with plati-
num serve as a catalyst fo r the purification of hydrogen fuel (FIG. 7 · 46 ） · Nano-
tubes formed from boron nitride are also Of great interest. Unlike carbon nano-
tubes, boron nitride nanotubes have electrical characteristics that dO not depend
on the diameter of the tube or the way the sheets are rolled. They have a moder-
ately large band gap, and so they are considered to be only weakly semiconduct-
ing. Carbon nanotubes grow until they are capped by bonds to another element or
by five-membered rings. The five-membered rings pucker the structure, forming
bends along the length of tubes and domes at their ends. ln the case of BN nano-
tubes, however, five-membered rings cannot form, because they would reqmre
boron—boron or nitrogen—nitrogen bonds, which would be tOO weak tO maintain
the structure. lnstead, BN nanotubes are capped by the atom Of a metal such as
tungsten.
The rigidity 0f nanotubes may also allow them t0 be used as minute molds or
templates for nanostructures Of Other elements. For example, they can be filled with
molten lead tO create lead wires one atom in diameter. They can also serve as tiny
"test tubes ” that hold individual molecules in place. Nanotubes that are filled with
biomolecules such as cytochrome C hOld the promise Of acting as sensors fO r medi-
cal applications.
The very large surface area provided by the highly porous nanotubes means
that atoms Of gases are readily adsorbed on the inner surfaces Of the tubes.
Nanotubes carrying hydrogen molecules could therefore become a high-energy-
density storage medium for hydrogen-powered vehicles (see Box 14 · 1 ） · Such a
material would solve a major obstacle to the use of hydrogen fuel cells—the
problem of a safe, compact storage medium for hydrogen. Hydrogen absorbed
intO nanotubes can be stored in a volume much smaller than that required tO
store the gas.

7 ． 20 Preparation of Nanomaterials
Nanomaterials can be manufactured by one Of tw O groups Of methods. ln "top-
down ” approaches, nanoscale materials are carved intO shape by the use Of physi-
cal nanotechnology methods such as lithography (FIG. 7 · 47 ） · ln “ bottom-up
approaches, molecules are encouraged tO assemble themselves intO desired patterns
by making use 0f specific intermolecular interactions (FIG. 7 · 48 ） · ln solution-based
bottom-up methods, tiny crystals are formed in solution and prevented from grow-
ing larger by the addition of stabilizers in the form of surfactant molecules. ln
vapor-phase synthesis, a substance is vaporized and then condensed or mixed with
a reactant and the product condensed tO form the desired tiny crystals. ln bOth
methods, one-molecule-thick layers of different materials in which the molecules
are oriented in a particular direction can be formed, giving the nanomaterial inter-
esting electrical and optical properties.
One type of bottom-up approach used fo r creating very regular arrays of nano-
tubes is template synthesis. ln this approach, porous membranes 0f polymers such
as polycarbonates or ceranucs such as alumina are prepared, then placed intO a

Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? The laws of thermodynamics govern

its nutritional value. The material i n this chapter provides a foundation fo r the following
chapters, in particular Chapter 9 ， which deals with the driving f0 rce of chemical
reactions.
What Are the Key ldeas? Heat and work are tw 0 ways of transferring energy between
a system and its surroundings. The total energy Of a n isolated system is constant. The
enthalpy change fO r a process is equal tO the heat released at constant pressure.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? This chapter assumes that you a re familiar
with the concept 0f energy (Fundamentals, Section A) ， stoichiometry (Fundamentals,
Sections L and M), and the ideal gas law (Chapter 5 ） · Some of the explanations refe r to
intermolecular forces (Sections 5 · 1 2 and 6 · 1 一 6 · 6 ） · lonic bonding (Sections 3 · 3 一 3 · 4 ） and
bond strengths (Sections 3 · 1 4 一 3 · 1 5 ） are developed further in this chapter.
nergy iS the basis Of civilization. Every day we use energy in itS vanous forms
tO maintain life, tO Stay sufficiently COOI or warm, tO move about, and tO
think. All these processes involve the release, absorption, transfer, or conver-
sion 0f energy. A huge global effort is under way to find new sources 0f energy, t0
use what energy IS available more efficiently, and tO conserve currently known
energy reserves. Access tO energy is one Of the maJ or problems facing humanity, fO r
SO much depends on it.

Systemsl Statesl and Energy
Two of the fundamental concepts of thermodynamics are 乃 e and 彬 0 · People
once thought that heat was a material fluid called “ / 0 0 which flowed from a
hot substance t0 a cooler one. The French engineer Sadi Carnot (FIG. 8 · 1 ）， who
helped to lay the foundations of thermodynamics, believed that work resulted
from the flow of caloric, just as the flow of water does work by turning a water
wheel. Some Of Carnot's conclusions survive, but we now know that there iS no
such substance as caloric. About 25 years after Carnot proposed his ideas in the
early nineteenth century, the English physicist James Joule (FIG. 8 · 2 ） showed
that heat and work are simply two ways in which energy can be transferred. ln
this chapter we first exanune work, then heat, and see that in fact heat is not a
substance that flows.
8 ． 1 Systems
ln thermodynamlcs we study hOW energy is transformed from one form intO
another and transferred from one place tO another. For instance, electricity may be
generated in a power station but used a great distance away; fOOd may be digested
in your stomach but the energy released may be used in your head. To keep track
of changes in energy, we divide the world into two parts. The region in which we
are interested, such as a flask Of gas, a beaker Of acid, a reaction mixture, or a
muscle fiber, is called a system (FIG. 8 · 3 ） · Everything else, such as the water bath
in which a reaction mixture may be immersed, iS called the surroundings. The sur-
roundings are where we make observations Of the energy transferred intO or out
of the system. The system and the surroundings j ointly make up the umverse.
However, often the only part of the universe significantly affected by a process
consists Of the sample, a flask, and a water bath; in such cases, which include most
Of the processes in this bOOk, we need tO measure changes only in the sample and
itS immediate surroundings.
A system can be open, closed, or isolated (FIG. 8 · 4 ） · An open system can
exchange both matter and energy with the surroundings. Examples 0f open systems
are automobile engines and the human body. A closed system has a fixed amount
Of matter, but it can exchange energy with the surroundings. An example Of a
closed system is a cold pack used fO r treating athletic i11J uries. An isolated system
has no contact with its surroundings. We can think Of an isolated system as sealed
inside rigid, thermally insulating walls. A good approximation t0 an isolated sys-
tem is a hOt liquid inside a thermos bottle or sealed vacuum flask.

8 ． 2 Work and Energy
The most fundamental property in thermodynanmcs—in the sense that it provides
a basis fO r defining the principal concepts—is work, the process Of achieving
motion against an opposing force ” e ” / s ， Section A). AII forms of work
can be thought of as equivalent to the work of raising a weight against the pull of
gravity. The chemical reaction in a battery does work when it pushes an electric
current through a circuit. Gas in a cylinder—such as the hOt gas m1Xture in the
cylinder of an automobile engine—does work when it expands and pushes back a
piston. We can identify whether a process can dO work by noting whether, in prin-
ciple at least, it can be harnessed tO raise a weight in the surroundings. The expan-
S10n Of a gas, for example, can be used tO ralse a weight because the piston can be
connected tO the weight. An electric current produced by a battery can be used tO
ralse a weight if it is used tO power an electric motor that pulls up the weight.
The work required tO move an Object a certain distance against an opposmg
force is calculated by multiplying the opposing force by the distance moved
agamst lt:
Work = opposing force × distance moved
AS pointed out in 尹 d e / s ， Section A, the unit in which work is reported is
the 加司 e ， J, with 1 J =
1 kg•m •s¯ 。 This unit is consistent with Eq. 1 ， because force
is measured in newtons （ 1 N = 1 kg•m•s¯ ）， SO the units Of force × distance are
1 kg•m•s-2 × 1 m = 1 kg•m2•s 2 ， or 1 J.
Energy is the capacity of a system to do work (and, ultimately, to lift a weight) ·
If a system can d0 a lot of work, we say that it possesses a lot 0f energy. A hot com-
pressed gas can do more work than the same gas after it has expanded and cooled,
SO we say that it possesses more energy initially. A wound spring can dO more work
than an unwound spring, SO we say that it possesses more energy. When a system
does work on the surroundings, its capacity tO dO work is reduced, SO we say that
its energy has decreased. If we do work on a system, such as by winding a spring,
then we increase its capacity tO dO work and therefore can say that its energy has
lncreased.
ln thermodynamics, the tOtal store Of energy in a system is called its internal
energy, U. We cannot measure the absolute value Of the internal energy Of a system,
because that value includes the energies Of all the atoms, their electrons, and the
components Of their nuclei. The best we can dO iS tO measure changes in internal
energy. For instance, if a system does 15 J of work (and no other changes take
place), then it has used up some Of its store Of energy, and we say that its internal
energy has fallen by 15 J and write AU = 一 15 J. Throughout thermodynamics, the

To calculate the work done by a gas that expands against a ” g 沅 g external
pressure, we need tO specify exactly how that pressure changes in the course Of the
expansion. ln particular, consider the very important case Of "reversible ” expan-
S10n Of an ideal gas.
ln everyday language, a reversible process IS one that can take place in either
direction. ThiS common usage iS refined in sclence: in thermodynam1CS, a reversible
process is one that can be reversed by an / ely s / / change in a variable (an
“ infinitesimal ” change) · For example, if the external pressure exactly matches the
pressure Of the gas in the system, then the piston moves ln neither direction. If the
external pressure is increased infinitesimally, then the piston moves in. I f, instead,
the external pressure is reduced infinitesimally, the piston moves out. Expansion
against an external pressure that differs by a finite (measurable) amount from the
pressure Of the system iS an lrreversible process in the sense that an infinitesimal
change in the external pressure does not reverse the direction Of travel Of the piston.
For instance, if the pressure Of the system is 2 · 0 atm at some Stage Of the expansion
and the external pressure is 1 · 0 atm, then a tiny increase in the latter does not con-
vert expansion intO compresslon. Reversible processes are Of considerable impor-
tance in thermodynamics because, as we Shall see, the work a system can dO iS
greatest 111 a reversible process.
TH 《 N ℃ N G POINT How could you ensure that a n electric battery produced a n electric
current reversibly?
The simplest kind Of reversible change tO consider is the reversible, isothermal
(constant-temperature) expansion Of an ideal gas. The same temperature can be
maintained by ensuring that the system is in thermal contact with a constant-
temperature water bath at all stages Of the expansion. ln an isothermal expanslon,
the pressure of the gas falls as it expands ()y Boyle's law); so, to achieve reversible
expansion, the external pressure must be reduced in Step with the change in VOI-
ume SO that at every Stage the external pressure is the same as the pressure Of the
gas (FIG. 8 · 6 ） · To calculate the work, we must take into account the gradual reduc-
tion in external pressure and therefore the changing opposing force.

8 ． 4 Heat
The internal energy 0f a system, its capacity t0 do work, can also be changed by
transferring energy tO or from the surroundings as heat. "Heat ” is a familiar term,
but in thermodynamlcs it has a special meaning. ln thermodynamics, heat is the
energy transferred as a result Of a temperature difference. Energy flows as heat
from a high-temperature region tO a low-temperature region. Therefore, provided
that the walls of the system are not thermally insulating, if the system is cooler than
1tS surroundings, energy flows intO the system from the surroundings.
ln the introduction tO this chapter we remarked that heat is not a substance
and that heat does not flow. What, then, is heat, and what is it that is transferred
during heating? As described in 尹 ” e ” / s ， Section A, what is often called the
"thermal energy" Of a system is the sum Of the ever-changing potential and kinetic
energies arising from the chaotic thermal motion Of atoms, IOIIS, and molecules.
Molecules in a high-temperature region move more vigorously than molecules in
a lower-temperature region. 、 When the tWO regions are brought intO contact, the
energetic molecules in the higher-temperature region collide with the molecules in
the lower-temperature reglons and stimulate them tO move faster. As a result, the
internal energy Of the cooler system increases as that Of the hotter system
decreases. The “ flowing " 0f energy due t0 a temperature difference is simply the

We write the energy transferred tO a system as heat as q. Therefore, when the
internal energy 0f the system is changed by transferring energy as heat （ and no other
processes, including expansion or contraction, take place), A U = q. If energy enters
a system as heat, the internal energy Of the system increases and q is positive; if
energy leaves the system as heat, the internal energy Of the system decreases and q is
negative. Thus, if 10 J enters the system as heat, we write q = + 10 J and (provided
no other processes take place) AU = + 10 J. Likewise, if 10 J leaves the system as
heat, we write q
一 10 J and ()f no other processes take place) AU = 一 10 J.
As these examples show, energy transferred as heat (like any energy) is mea-
sured in joules, J. However, a unit still widely used in biochemistry and related
fields is the / 0 了讵， cal. Originally, 1 cal was the energy needed to raise the tem-

1 cal = 4 · 184 J (exactly)
This exact relation defines the calorie in terms Of th e joule; the j oule is th e fundamen-

tant tO note which unit is being used when assessing the energy content Of fOOd.

are endothermic. For instance, vaporizatlon IS endothermic, because heat must be
supplied to drive molecules of a liquid apart from one another. The dissolution of

The fundamental molecular difference between work and heat is related to the

changes in internal energy may be achieved in a closed system Of constant compo-
sition: the only way tO change the internal energy Of such a system is tO transfer
energy intO it as heat or as work. If the system is isolated, then even that ability is
eliminated, and the internal energy cannot change at all. This conclusion is known
as the first law Of thermodynamlcs, which states:
The internal energy Of an isolated system is constant.
According tO the first law, if an isolated system has a certain internal energy at
one instant and we inspect it again later, then we shall find that it still has exactly
the same internal energy, no matter hOW much time has passed. Alternatively, if
we allow the system tO go through a serles Of changes but ensure that it is
restored tO its original state, then we shall find that in its final state it has the
same internal energy as it had originally. We summarize these statements by say-
ing that the internal energy is a state function, a property that depends only on
the current state Of the system and is independent Of hOW that state was pre-
pared. The pressure, volume, temperature, and density Of a system are also state
functions.

8 ． 7 A MoIecular lnterlude: The Origin of lnternal Energy
lnternal energy is energy stored in a system as kinetic energy and potential energy. lt
includes all the energies Of interaction Of the fundamental particles that make up atoms:
． the interactions between electrons and nuclei in the atoms that make up molecules
． the translational, rotational, and vibrational energies Of the molecules
． the interactions between different molecules
Most Of these interactions are independent Of the temperature, but others decrease
with temperature.
Consider, fO r instance, a perfect gas. We saw in 尹 d e / s ， Section A, that
kinetic energy is energy due tO motion, and that the faster a molecule travels, the
greater is its translational kinetic energy. When we heat a gas, the average speed Of
the molecules increases. When we dO work on a gas in an insulated container (that
is, transfer energy by dOing work), the molecules are also stimulated tO move faster.
increase in the average speed Of the gas molecules corresponds tO an increase
in the tOtal kinetic energy Of the molecules and therefore tO an mcrease in the inter-
nal energy of the gas. We have already seen ()n Section 5 · 10 ） that the temperature
IS an indication Of the average speed Of gas molecules, and SO this increase ln inter-
nal energy also corresponds tO an lncrease in temperature. lt is always the case that
provided no chemical reaction occurs, s ， s 把乃乃把 pe 陋忉了 e 乃 s grea 了
/ / energy 乃 the same s ， s lower pe 忉 r 巳
Molecules in a gas can move in a variety Of different ways, and each mode Of
motion can act as a store 0f energy (FIG. 8 · 1 7 ） · The energy 0f an atom or molecule
due tO its motion through space is called its translational energy (this energy is
kinetic energy). Molecules ()n contrast tO atoms) can also store energy as rotational
energy, the energy due tO their rotational motion (this energy is also kinetic) · A
third store Of energy fO r molecules is in the oscillation Of their atoms relative tO one
another; this contribution is called vibrational energy and is the sum Of kinetic and
potential contributions. The kinetic contribution tO vibration is due tO the relative
motion Of the atoms in the molecule; the potential contribution reflects the fact that

the energy of tw 0 atoms bonded by a springlike bond depends on their relative
separation (how fa r the bond is compressed or stretched) · Most molecules are not
vibrationally excited at room temperature, and SO we ignore that mode fO r now.
The contribution Of translational and rotational motion tO the internal energy can
be estimated from the temperature.
How Do We Do That?
First, we need tO know that a ' quadratic contribution ” tO the energy is an expresslon
that depends on the square Of a velocity or a displacement, as ln 2 for transla-
tional kinetic energy. The equipartition theorem (which we shall not derive here) then
states that:
The average value Of each quadratic contribution tO the energy Of a molecule
a sample at a temperature T is equal tO 〗 T ·
The name “ equipartition" simply means that the available energy is shared
(partitioned) equally over all the available modes. ln this expression, is Boltzmann's
constant, a fundamental constant with the value 1 · 3 81 × 10 23 J•K- · Boltzmann's
constant is related to the gas constant （ 8 · 314 J•K-l•mol- ） by R = NAk, where NA
is Avogadro's constant. The equipartition theorem IS a result from classical mechan-
ICS, SO we can use it fO r translational and rotational motlon Of molecules at room
temperature and above, where quantlzation IS ummportant. cannot use it reli-
ably fO r vibrational motion, except at very high temperatures, because at ordinary
temperatures only the lowest vibrational quantum state is occupied and the effects
0f quantlzation are very important. The following remarks therefore apply only to
translational and rotational motlon.
A molecule can move through space along any Of three dimenslons, SO it has
乃了 ee translational modes Of motlon, each one givmg a quadratic contribution tO the
energy. lt follows from the equipartition theorem that the average translational kinetic
energy of a molecule in a sample at a temperature T is 3 × -kT = -kT. The contribu
tion t0 the molar internal energy (the energy per mole of molecules, Um ） is therefore
NA times this value, or
Um(translation) = NAkT = iRT
Because RT = 2 · 48 kJ•mol-l at 25 OC, the translational motion of gas molecules
contributes 3 · 72 kJ•mol
(iRT) to the internal energy of the sample at 25 OC.
Apart from the energy arising from the internal structures Of the atoms themselves,
this is the only motional contribution tO the internal energy Of a monatomic gas,
such as argon or any Other noble gas.
A 方 e 了 molecule, such as any diatomic molecule, carbon dioxide, or ethyne
(acetylene, H—C=C—H ）， can rotate about two axes perpendicular to the line of
atoms, and SO it has tWO rotational modes Of motion. lts average rotational energy
is therefore 2 × -kT = kT, and the contribution to the molar internal energy is NA
times this value:
Um(rotation, linear) = NAkT = RT
or about 2 · 48 kJ•mol-1 at 25 OC. The total motional contribution to the internal
energy Of a gas Of linear molecules is the sum Of the translational and rotational
contributions, or jRT, which corresponds to 6 · 20 kJ•mol-l at 25 OC.
A 0 方 e 7 0 / ec / e ， such as water, methane, or benzene, can rotate about any Of
three perpendicular axes, and SO it has three rotational modes Of motion. Th e average
rotational energy of such a molecule is therefore 3 × 1 T = -kT. The contribution of
rotation tO the molar internal energy Of a gas Of nonlinear molecules is therefore
Um(rotation, nonlinear) = iR T
At 25 OC, the contribution of rotation to the energy is 3 · 72 kJ•mol- (the same as
fO r the translational motion), and the tOtal motional contribution for nonlinear
molecules is therefore 3RT, or about 7 · 44 kJ•mol- at 25 OC.

Th e constant-volume and constant-pressure heat capacities Of a solid substance
are similar; the same is true Of a liquid but not Of a gas. Th e difference IS a reflection
of the fact that gases expand much more than solids and liquids when they are
heated, SO more energy is lost as work when a gas is heated at constant pressure than

8 ． 11 The EnthaIpy of Physical Change
The molecules in a solid or liquid are held together by intermolecular attractions.
A phase change in which the molecules become further separated, such as melting
or vaporization, reqmres energy tO overcome these intermolecular attractions and
is therefore endothermic. Phase changes that increase molecular contact, such as
condensation or freezing, are exothermic because energy iS released When mole-
cules come closer together and can interact with one another more strongly. When
a phase transition takes place at constant pressure, as IS most common, the heat
transfer accompanying the phase change is equal to the change ln enthalpy of the
substance.
At a given temperature, the vapor phase of a substance has a higher energy and
therefore a higher enthalpy than the liquid phase. The difference in molar enthalpy
between the vapor and the liquid states is called the enthalpy of vaporizatlon,
AHvap
AHvap = Hm(vapor) 一 Hm(liquid)
（ 14 ）
The enthalpy Of vaporization Of most substances changes little with temperature.
For water at its boiling point, 100 OC, AH

corresponding to 18 · 02 g of water, at 25 OC and constant pressure, we have to
supply 44 · 0 kJ of energy as heat.

8 ． 12 Heating Curves
The enthalpies of fusion and vaporization affect the appearance of the 乃 e 酊沅 g
C 了 e Of a substance. A heating curve is a graph showing the variation in the tem-
perature Of a sample as lt is heated at a constant rate at constant pressure and
therefore at a constant rate 0f increase ln enthalpy (BOX 8 · 1 ） ·
Consider what happens when we heat a sample of very cold ice. As we see in
at first its temperature rises steadily. Although the molecules are still
FIG. 8 · 26
locked in a solid mass, they are oscillating more and more vigorously around their
mean positions. However, once the temperature has reached the melting point, the
molecules have enough energy tO move past one another. At this temperature, all
the added energy is used tO overcome the attractive forces between molecules. Thus
although heating contmues, the temperature remams constant at the melting point
until all the ice has melted. Only then does the temperature rise again, and the rise
continues right up tO the boiling point. At the boiling point, the temperature nse
agaln comes tO a halt. NOW the water molecules have enough energy tO escape intO
the vapor state, and all the heat supplied is used to form the vapor. After the sample
has evaporated and heating continues, the temperature Of the vapor rises again.

The Enthalpy of ChemicaI Change
We have seen that enthalpy changes accompany physical changes, such as vapor-
ization. The same principles apply to the energy and enthalpy changes that accom-
pany chemical changes. Enthalpies Of chemical change are important in many areas
of chemistry, such as the selection of materials that make good fuels, the design 0f
chemical plants, and the study of biochemical processes.
8 ． 13 Reaction EnthaIpies
Every chemical reaction is accompanied by a change in energy, and commonly that
energy is released or absorbed as heat. For example, complete reaction with OXY-
gen is called combustion, and the combustion Of methane, the major component
Of natural gas, is the following reaction:
CH4(g) + 2 02(g) 一 C02(g) + 2 H20(l)
Calorimetry shows that burning 1 · 00 mol CH4(g) at 298 K and 1 bar releases
890 · kJ of energy as heat. To report this value, we write
CH4(g) + 2 02(g) 一 C02(g) + 2 H20(l) AH = 一 890 · kJ
(A)
ThiS entire expresslon iS called a thermochemical equation, and consists Of a
chemical equation together with a statement Of the reactlon enthalpy, the corre-
sponding enthalpy change. The stoichiometric coefficients indicate the number Of

2 mol 02(g). If the same reaction is written with the coefficients all multiplied by

We saw in Section 8 · 11 that the first law of thermodynamics implies that
because enthalpy is a state function, the enthalpy change for the reverse Of a process
is the negative of the enthalpy change of the forward process. The same relation

8 ． 14 The ReIation Between AH and AU
We have seen that a constant-pressure calorimeter and a constant-volume bomb
calorimeter measure changes in different state functlons: at constant volume, the
heat transfer is interpreted as A U; at constant pressure, it is interpreted as AH. How-
ever, it iS sometlmes necessary tO convert the measured value Of A [_J intO AH. For
example, it is easy tO measure the heat released by the combustion Of glucose in a
bomb calorimeter, but tO use that information in assessmg energy changes in metab-
Olism, which take place at constant pressure, we need the enthalpy Of reaction.
For reactions in which no gas IS generated or consumed, little expanslon work
is done as the reaction proceeds and the difference between AH and A U is negligi-
ble; SO we can set AH = A U. However, if a gas is formed in the reaction, SO much
expansion work is done tO make room for the gaseous products that the difference
can be significant. We can use the ideal gas law to relate the values of AH and AU
fo r gases that behave ideally.

8 · 1 5 Standard Reaction Enthalpies
8 ． 15 Standard Reaction Enthalpies
Because the heat released or absorbed by a reaction depends on the physical states
of the reactants and products, when calculating the reaction enthalpy we need tO
specify the state Of each substance. For example, when describing the combustion
Of methane, we can write tw O different thermochemical equations fO r tWO different
setS Of products:
CH4(g) + 2 02(g) 一 C02(g) + 2 H20(g) AH = 一 802 kJ
CH4(g) + 2 02(g) 一 C02(g) + 2 H20(l) AH = 一 890 · kJ
(B)
ln the first reaction, the water is produced as a vapor; in the second, it is produced
as a liquid. The heat generated is different in each case. We have already seen that
the enthalpy of water vapor is 44 kJ•mol-l higher than that of liquid water at
25 OC (see TabIe 8 · 3 ） · As a result, an additional 8 8 kJ (for 2 mol H20) remains
stored in the system if water vapor is formed (FIG. 8 · 28 ） · If the 2 mol H20(g) sub-
sequently condenses, that 8 8 kJ is given off as heat.
An enthalpy 0f reaction also depends on the conditions (such as the pressure).
AII the tables in this book list data fo r reactions in which each reactant and product
is in its standard state, its pure form at exactly 1 bar. The standard state Of liquid
water is pure water at 1 bar. The standard state Of ice is pure ice at 1 bar. A solute
in a liquid solution is in its standard state when its concentration is 1 mol•L¯1. The
standard value of a property X (that is, the value of X fo r the standard state of the
substance) is denoted XO ·
The standard reactlon enthalpy, AHO, is the reaction enthalpy when reactants
in their standard states change intO products in their standard states. For example,
fo r reaction C, the value AHO
一 890 · kJ signifies that the heat output is 890 · kJ
when 1 mol CH4(g) as pure methane gas at 1 bar is allowed to react with pure
oxygen gas at 1 bar, givmg pure carbon dioxide gas and pure liquid water, both at
1 bar (FIG. 8 · 29 ） · Reaction enthalpies do not change very much with pressure over
the small ranges normally encountered, SO the standard value alSO gives a good
indication Of the change in enthalpy fO r pressures near 1 bar, such as 1 atm.
A special type Of reaction that plays an important role in thermodynamics, as
well as in the everyday world, is combustion. The standard enthalpy of combustion,
AHc0, is the change in enthalpy per mole of a substance that is burned in a combus-
tion reaction under standard conditions. The products Of the combustion Of an
organic compound are carbon dioxide gas and liquid water; a ny nitrogen present iS
released as N2 ， unless other products are specified (such as NO(g) and N02(g)).
Most thermochemical data are reported fo r 25 OC (more precisely, for
298 · 15 K). Temperature is not part of the definition of standard states: we can have
a standard state at any temperature; 298 · 15 K is simply the most common tem-
perature used in tables Of data. All reaction enthalpies used in this text are for
298 · 15 K unless another temperature is indicated.

8 ． 16 Combining Reaction EnthaIpies: Hessls Law
Enthalpy is a state function; therefore, the value of AH is independent of the path
between glven initial and final states. We saw an application Of this approach in
Section 8 · 11 ， when we calculated the enthalpy change fo r an overall physical pro-
cess as the sum of the enthalpy changes f0 r a series of two individual steps. The
same rule applied tO chemical reactions iS known as Hess's law:
The overall reactlon enthalpy is the sum of the reaction enthalpies of the
Steps 1ntO which the reaction can be divided.
Hess's law applies even if the intermediate reactions or the overall reaction cannot
actually be carried out. Provided that the equation for each step balances and the
individual equations add up tO the equation for the reaction Of interest, a reaction
enthalpy can be calculated from a ny convenient sequence 0f reactions (FIG. 8 · 30 ） ·
As an example Of Hess's law, let's consider the oxidation Of carbon as graphite,
denoted C(gr), to carbon dioxide:
c(gr) + 02(g) 一 C02(g)
(D)
This reaction can be thought Of as the outcome Of tWO Steps. One Step is the oxida-
tion Of carbon tO carbon monoxide,
c(gr) + 02(g) 一 co(g) AH ：一 110 · 5kJ
The second Step is the oxidation Of carbon monoxide tO carbon dioxide,
co(g) + 02(g) 一 C02(g) AH = 一 283 · 0 kJ
ThiS two-step process IS an example Of a reaction sequence, a series Of reactions lll
which the products Of one reaction take part as reactants in another reaction. The
equation for the overall reaction, the net outcome Of the sequence, is the sum Of
the equations fO r the intermediate Steps:
c(gr) + 02(g) 一 co(g)
co(g) + 02(g) 一 C02(g)
c(gr) + 02(g) 一 C02(g)
AH = 一 393 · 5 kJ D = E + F
The same procedure is used tO predict the enthalpies Of reactions that we cannot
measure directly in the laboratory. The procedure is described in TooIbox 8 · 1 ·
T00 《 box 8 ． 1 H OW TO USE HESS'S LAW
CONCEPTUAL BASIS
Because enthalpy is a state function, the enthalpy change 0f
a system depends only on its initial and final states. There-
fore, we can carry out a reactlon lll one Step or, if that iS not
convement, visualize it as the sum Of several steps; the reac-
tion enthalpy is the same in each case.
PROCEDURE
To use Hess's law to find the enthalpy 0f a given reaction, we
find a sequence Of reactions with known reaction enthalpies
that adds up tO the reactlon Of interest. Different strategies
may be used. Here is one that works in many situations.
Step 1 Select one Of the reactants in the overall reaction
and write down a chemical equation in which it also
appears as a reactant.
Step 2 Select one of the products in the overall reaction
and write down a chemical equation in which it also
appears as a product. Add this equation tO the equatlon
written in Step 1 and cancel species that appear on bOth
sides Of the equation.
Step 3 Cancel unwanted species in the sum obtained in
step 2 by adding an equation that has the same substance
or substances on the opposlte side Of the arrow.
Step 4 Once the sequence is complete, combine the standard
reactlon enthalpies.
ln each Step, it might be necessary tO reverse the equation or
multiply it by a factor. Recall from Eq. 16 that, if we want
tO reverse a chemical equation, we have tO change the sign
of the reaction enthalpy. If we multiply the stoichiometric
coefficients by a factor, we must multiply the reaction enthalpy
by the same factor.

8 ． 17 Standard EnthaIpies of Formation
There are millions Of possible reactions, and it is impractical tO list every one with
its standard reaction enthalpy. However, chemists have devised an ingemous alter-
native. First, they report the "standard enthalpies Of formation ” Of substances.
Then they combine these quantities to obtain the standard enthalpy of any reac-
tion. Let's lOOk at these tWO stages in turn.
The standard enthalpy of formation, AHf0, of a substance is the standard reac-
tion enthalpy per mole Of formula units fO r the formation Of a substance from its
elements in their OS stable 厂 0 了， as in the reaction fO r the formation Of ethanol:
2 C(gr) + 3 H2(g) + 02(g) 一 C2H50H(l) AHO = 一 277 · 69 kJ
where C(gr) denotes graphite, th e most stable form Of carbon at normal temperatures.
The chemical equation that corresponds to the standard enthalpy of formation of a
substance has the substance as th e sole product with a stoichiometric coefficient Of 1
（ implying the formation of 1 mol of the substance) · Sometimes, as here, fractional
coefficients are required for the reactants. Because standard enthalpies Of formation
are expressed in kilOj oules per mole Of the substance Of interest, we report that
AHf0 （ C2H50H, l) = 一 277 · 69 kJ•mol-l. Note also how the substance and its state
are used to label the enthalpy change so that we know which species and which form
of that species (liquid, in this case) we are talking about.
You should always be alert to the difference
A Note 0 n Good Practice:
between a quantity per mole Of molecules and the same quantity 厂 0 了 or 0 厂 a
mole of molecules. Standard enthalpies of formation are expressed per mole of
molecules, as in 一 277 · 69 kJ•mol
· the standard enthalpy of forming 1 mol
C2H50H(l) = 一 277 · 69 kJ. The point might seem picky, but it will help you to
keep units straight.
0

an element in its most stable form is zero. For instance, the standard enthalpy Of forma-
tion of C(gr) is zero because C(gr) 艹 C(gr) is a "null reaction ” (that is, nothing changes ） ·
We write, for instance AHf0(), gr ） = 0 · However, the enthalpy of formation of an ele-
ment in a form Other than itS most stable one IS nonzero. For example, the converslon

C(gr) 一 C(diamond) A HO = + 1 · 9 kJ

8 ． 18 The Born—Haber Cycle
We saw in Section 3 · 4 that the energy changes accompanying the formation of a
solid could be estimated on the basis of a model—the ionic model—in which the
principal contribution tO the lattice energy was the Coulomb interaction between
10ns. However, a model can g1Ve only an estimate, and the model might be wrong:
we need a value Of the lattice energy based on measurements. If the measured and
calculated lattice energies are similar, we can conclude that the ionic model is reli-
able for the particular substance. If the two energles are markedly different, then
we know that the ionic model must be improved or even discarded. This procedure
iS yet another example Of hOW models are used in sclence.
For a given ionic solid, the difference in molar enthalpy between the solid and
a gas of widely separated ions is called the lattice enthalpy of the solid, AHL'
A HL = Hm(ions, g) 一 Hm(solid)
〈 21 ）
FIGURE 8 · 32 丨 n a Born-Haber cycle,
we select a sequence Of steps that
sta rts and ends at the S a m e point (the
solid compound, f0 r instance). The
lattice enthalpy is the enthalpy change
accompanying the reverse Of the step
in which the solid is formed fro m a gas
of ions. The sum 0f enthalpy changes
around the complete cycle is 0 because
enthalpy is a state function.
The lattice enthalpy can be identified with the heat required to vaporize the solid
tO gaseous lons at constant pressure. The greater the lattice enthalpy, the greater is
the heat required. Heat equal to the lattice enthalpy is released when the solid
forms from gaseous lons. ln Section 3 · 4 we calculated the lattice energy and dis-
cussed hOW it depended on the attractions between the ions. The lattice enthalpy
differs from the lattice energy by only a few kilojoules per mole and can be inter-
preted in a similar way.
The lattice enthalpy of a solid cannot normally be measured directly. However,
we can obtain it indirectly by combining Other measurements in an application Of
Hess's law. This approach takes advantage of the first law of thermodynamics and,
particular, the fact that enthalpy is a state function. The procedure uses a B orn—
Haber cycle, a closed path of steps, one of which is the formation of a solid lattice
from the gaseous ions. The enthalpy change fo r this step is the negative of the lat-
tice enthalpy. TABLE 8 · 5 lists some lattice enthalpies found in this way.
ln a Born—Haber cycle, we imagine that we break apart the bulk elements into
atoms, lonize the atoms, combine the gaseous lons tO form the ionic solid, then form
th e elements again from the ionic solid (FIG. 8 · 32 ） · OnIy the lattice enthalpy, the nega-
tive of the enthalpy of the step in which the ionic solid is formed from the gaseous
ions, is unknown. The sum of the enthalpy changes for a complete Born—Haber cycl e
IS zero, because the enthalpy Of the system must be the same at th e start and finish.

8 ． 20 The Variation of Reaction EnthaIpy with Temperature
Suppose we know the reaction enthalpy fO r one temperature but require it for
another temperature. For instance, the temperature Of the human bOdy is about
37 OC, but the data in Appendix 2A are for 25 OC. How can we find out whether
an mcrease of 12 0C makes much difference t0 the reaction enthalpy 0f a metabolic
process?
The enthalpies Of bOth reactants and products increase with temperature. If the
tOtal enthalpy Of the reactants increases more than that Of the products when the
temperature IS raised, then the reactlon enthalpy Of an exothermic reaction will
become more negative (FIG. 8 · 35 ） · On the other hand, if the enthalpy of the prod-
uctS increases more than that Of the reactants, then the reaction enthalpy will
become less negative. The increase ln enthalpy Of a substance when the temperature
is raised depends on its heat capacity at constant pressure (Eq. 12b ）， and it is easy
to deduce Kirchhoff ， s law (see Exercise 8 · 83L that
AH0(T2) = AHO(TI) + ()2 _ Tl)ACp

The individual values can be found in Appendix 2A. Because the difference

ALTERNATIVE FUELS
· THE ENVIRONMENT?
O ur complex modern life style was made possible by the
discovery and refining of fossil fuels, fuels that are the result
of the decay 0f orgamc matter laid down millions 0f years
ago. The natural gas that heats our homes, the gasoline that
powers our automobiles, and the coal, gas, and Oil that pro-
vide much Of our electrical power are fossil fuels. Vast
reserves 0f petroleum, the source of liquid hydrocarbon
fuels such as gasoline and coal, exist in many areas Of the
world. However, although they are large, these reserves are
limited and essentially irreplaceable. Yet we are using them
up rapidly. We need to develop renewable fuels, fuels that
are replenished every year by the Sun.
Alternat1ve and sustainable power-generation meth-
ods, such as hydroelectric power, wind power, geothermal
power, solar power, and alternative fuels are being sought
to reduce the demand for fossil fuels. Four of the most
promising alternative fuels are hydrogen, ethanol, methane,
and biodiesel. Hydrogen is extracted from ocean water by
electrolysis or produced through steam reforming of hydro-
carbons, as in thiS serles Of reactlons:
CH4(g) + H20(g) 一 co(g) + 3H2(g)
co(g) + H20(g) 一 C02(g) + H2(g)
The bulk of industrial hydrogen production relies on
hydrocarbons in petroleum and coal, but those fuels are not
renewable. Ethanol is a renewable fuel obtained by ferment-
ing biomass, the name given tO plant materials that can be
burned or reacted tO produce fuels. Methane is a renewable
fuel generated by bacterial digestion Of wastes such as sew-
age and agricultural wastes. The use of hydrogen as a fuel is
discussed in Section 16 · 3 · Here we look at ethanol, methane,
and biodiesel.
EthanoI, CH3CH20H, is produced from the biological
fermentation Of the starches in grams, mainly corn. lt is used
as an additive in gasoline or as “ E85 ， " which is 85 ％ etha-
nol and 15 ％ gasoline by volume. Ethanol currently makes
up about 10 ％ by volume of gasoline in the United States,
thereby reducing pollution as well as the use of petroleum.
The 2005 U.S. Energy Policy Act required that, by 2012 ，
7 · 5 billion gallons （ 2 · 8 × 1010 L) of renewable fuel be used
per year. The 2007 Energy lndependence and Security Act
requires that by 2022 the annual usage of renewable fuels
increase to 36 billion gallons （ 1 · 4 × 1011 L, about 23 ％ of
the total annual volume of liquid fuels used in the United
States). ln 2010 ， nearly 11 billion gallons （ 4 · 1 × 1010 L) of
ethanol were produced.

sions of carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons by helping t0
ensure complete combustion. However, because ethanol iS

The lmpact o n Technology
Most of our energy comes from the Sun, either directly or indirectly. The energy
of all the solar radiation absorbed by the vegetation on Earth is enough tO create
about 6 × 1014 kg of glucose a year. Most of this glucose is converted to starches
and cellulose. As long as these compounds do not decay completely back to car-
bon dioxide and water, dead vegetation remams a store Of energy. If losses
through forest fires are ignored, this store, called the biomass, increases by about
1019 kJ each year, which is about 20 times the current annual global industrial
demand fo r energy. However, because biomass is bulky and widely dispersed,
most Of our fuels are fossil fuels, energy-rich decomposition products Of ancient
vegetation that have been kept from oxidizing by favorable geological formations.

For practical applications it is necessary tO take intO account the mass Of fuel
that a mobile vehicle needs tO carry or the volume it occupies. TO take intO
account the burden Of the mass Of fuel, it is common tO use the specific
enthalpy, the enthalpy of combustion of a sample of the fuel divided by the
mass of the sample. lt is normally reported in kilojoules per gram. The specific
enthalpy (usually its standard value) is calculated by dividing the standard
enthalpy of combustion by the molar mass of the fuel. Fuels with a high
specific enthalpy release a lot of heat per gram when they burn. Hence,
specific enthalpy iS an lmportant criterion when mass IS important, as lt iS in
airplanes and spacecraft. Notice that fuels that have already been partially
oxygenated, such as glucose and ethanol, have lower specific enthalpies than
the hydrocarbons.
When the volume occupied by the fuel is important, we note its enthalpy
density, the enthalpy of combustion of a sample divided by the volume of the
sample. lt is calculated by dividing the (standard) enthalpy of combustion by
the molar volume of the fuel and is commonly reported in kilojoules per liter. A
great advantage 0f hydrogen over hydrocarbon fuels is that it produces no car-
bon dioxide when it burns. Carbon dioxide is potentially harmful, because it
contributes to the greenhouse effect (see Box 16 · 1 ） · However, although hydro-
gen forms only water when it burns, its use is limited by the high volume
required for a gas. Chemists are working tO synthesize solid compounds that
concentrate hydrogen and release it as needed. Candidates include the hydrides
formed when titanium, copper, and other metals are heated in hydrogen. These
compounds occupy a much smaller volume than the equivalent amount Of
hydrogen gas and release hydrogen when heated or treated with acid. One
example is an lron titanium hydride 0f approximate formula FeTiH2. Another
promising low-density storage medium for hydrogen is offered by carbon nano-
tubes (see Section 7 · 19 ） ·

What h ave you learned in this chapter?
You have learned that energy can be transferred tO or from a
system as either work, heat, or a combination Of both, and that
the net change is measured by the internal energy. You have
also learned that the first law Of thermodynanucs states that
the internal energy Of an isolated system IS constant. When
the system IS at constant pressure, it IS convement tO focus on
the changes in the enthalpy, which takes expanslon work into
account. Changes of enthalpy are equal to the heat released or
absorbed at constant pressure. You have met the concept Of
a state function, which enables you tO calculate the change
internal energy or enthalpy by selecting any convenient route
between initial and final states. You have also seen hOW tO
calculate the standard enthalpy changes accompanymg physical
changes and chemical reactlons and hOW tO relate them tO
properties of the changes taking places at a molecular level.
