Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? The second law of thermodynamics
is the key tO understanding why O n e chemical reaction has a natural tendency tO
occur but another o n e does not. We apply the second law by using the very important
concepts of entropy and Gibbs free energy. The third law of thermodynamics is the
basis Of the numerical values Of these tw O quantities. The second and third laws jointly
provide a way tO predict the effects Of changes in temperature and pressure O n physical
and chemical processes. They also lay the thermodynamic foundations fo r discussing
chemical equilibrium, which the following chapters explore in detail.
What Are the Key ldeas? The direction of natural change corresponds t0 increasing
disorder i n the way that energy and matter a re distributed. Disorder is measured by the
thermodynamic quantity called entropy. A related quantity—the Gibbs fre e energy—
links thermodynamics tO the description Of chemical equilibrium.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? The discussion d raws 0 n concepts related
to the fi rst law of thermodynamics, particularly enthalpy (Section 8 · 8 ） and work (Sections
8 · 2 and 8 · 3 ） · You need to be aware that molecules can OCCUPY only a series of discrete
energy levels and so possess only certain allowed energies (Section 1 · 7 ） ·
ome things happen naturally; some don't. Decay is natural; construction
reqmres work. Water flows downhill naturally; we have to pump it uphill. A
spark is enough tO inltiate a forest fire; the ceaseless input Of energy from the
Sun is required tO rebuild the forest from carbon dioxide and water. Anyone whO
thinks about the world may wonder what determines the / direction Of
change. What drives events forward ？ What drives a reaction toward products, and,
on a larger scale, what drives the great and intncate network Of reactlons in biO-
logical systems forward in the extraordinary phenomenon we call life ？ As this
chapter unfolds, we shall see that we can use a single quantity, "entropy," t0 pro-
Vide an elegant and quantitative answer tO all these questions: an lncrease lll
entropy accounts bOth fO r physical change and fO r the more intricate changes that
accompany chemical reactions. 、 We shall also see that, although entropy is a ther-
modynamlc concept in the sense that it is a property Of bulk samples Of matter, it
has a very straightforward molecular interpretation.

9 ． 1 Spontaneous Change
A spontaneous change is a change that has a tendency tO occur without needing tO
be driven by an external influence. A simple example is the cooling of a block of
h0t metal to the temperature 0f its surroundings (FIG. 9 · 1 ） · The reverse change, a
block Of metal spontaneously growing hotter than its surroundings, has never been
observed. The expansion 0f a gas int0 a vacuum is spontaneous (FIG. 9 · 2 ）； a gas
has no tendency tO contract spontaneously intO one part Of a container.
A spontaneous change need not be fast and in some cases must be initiated.
Molasses has a spontaneous tendency tO flow out Of an overturned can; but, at IOW
temperatures, that flow may be very slow. Hydrogen and oxygen have a tendency
tO react tO form water—the reaction iS spontaneous in the thermodynam1C sense—
but a mixture Of the tWO gases can be kept safely fO r centuries, provided it is not
ignited with a spark. Diamonds have a natural tendency tO turn intO graphite, but
diamonds last unchanged for countless years—on the human scale, diamonds are,
III practice, forever. A spontaneous process has a natural e de 乙， tO occur; it does
not necessarily take place rapidly or even occur at all. Throughout this chapter, and
whenever we consider the thermodynamics Of change, it is important tO remember
that we are exploring only the e c Of a process tO occur. Whether that ten-
dency is actually realized in practice depends on 1tS rate: rates are outside the reach
of thermodynamics and are considered in Chapter 15 ·
Changes can be made tO happen in their “ unnatural ” direction. For example,
we can force an electric current through a block Of metal tO heat it tO a temperature
higher than that Of its surroundings. We can drive a gas intO a smaller volume by
pushing in a p1Ston. ln every case, though, tO bring about a nonspontaneous change
in a system, we have to contrive a way of 和 g it t0 happen by applying an influ-
ence from outside the system. ln short, 0 spo eo s c 乃 & e ca be b 了 0 & 方

9 ． 2 Entropy and Disorder
ln science, we lOOk for patterns tO discover nature's laws. What is the pattern com-
mon tO all spontaneous changes? TO find a pattern, it is Often best tO start with
very simple examples, because then the pattern is likely tO be more obvious. SO,
let's think about tW O simple spontaneous changes—the cooling Of a hOt metal and
the expansion Of a gas—at a molecular level and search fO r their common feature.
A hot block of metal in a cold room cools as the energy 0f its vigorously vibrat-
ing atoms spreads intO the surroundings (the air and apparatus around (t). Th e vigor-
ously moving atoms Of the metal collide with the slower atoms and molecules Of the
surroundings, transferring some Of their energy in the collisions. e reverse change
IS very improbable, because it would require energy tO migrate from the cooler sur-
roundings and concentrate in a small hot block of metal. Such a process would

The entropy Of an isolated system lncreases in the course Of any spontaneous

9 ． 3 Changes in Entropy
Disorder is expected tO increase when a system is heated because the supply Of
energy increases the thermal motion Of the molecules. Heating increases the thermal
disorder, the disorder arising from the thermal motion of the molecules. The
entropy is also expected tO increase when a glven amount Of matter spreads intO a
greater volume or IS mixed with another substance. These processes disperse the
molecules Of the substance over a greater volume and increase the posltional disorder,
the disorder related tO the locations Of the molecules.

9 ． 4 Entropy Changes Accompanying Changes
in Physical State
When a solid melts, its molecules become more disordered as they form a liquid;
thus, its entropy is expected tO increase. Similarly, we expect an even greater
lncrease ln entropy When a liquid vaporizes, because itS molecules then occupy a
much greater volume and their motion is highly chaotic. As we saw in Section 5 · 8 ，
a liquid vaporizes until its partial pressure has reached a certain value, called its
p or Pressure. As the liquid is heated, its vapor pressure increases until it is equal
tO the external pressure. At that temperature, which is called the boiling tempera-
ture, the liquid boils.
ln this section, we develop expressions fO r the change in entropy at the transl-
tion temperature for the prevailing pressure. For instance, if the pressure is 1 atm,
then these expressions are applicable only at the normal melting point, Tf (the f
stands for fusion, another term fO r melting) ， the temperature at which a solid melts
when the pressure is 1 atm, or the normal boiling point, Tb, the temperature at

===== 第 469 页 =====
9 · 4 Entropy Changes Accompanying Changes i n Physical State
which a liquid boils when the pressure is 1 atm. ln most cases, the boiling tempera-
ture at 1 bar is negligibly different from the normal boiling point.
To use Eq. 1 to calculate the entropy change f0 r a substance undergoing a tran-
sition from one phase tO another at its transition temperature, we need tO note
three facts:
1 ． At the transition temperature （ such as the boiling point for vaporization), the
temperature Of the substance remams constant as heat is supplied.
All the energy supplied is used tO drive the phase transition, such as the converslon
Of liquid intO vapor, rather than tO raise the temperature. The T in the denominator
of Eq. 1 is therefore a constant and may be set equal tO the transition temperature
()n kelvins).
2 ． At the temperature Of a phase transition, the transfer Of heat is reversible.
Provided the external pressure is fixed （ at 1 atm, for instance), raising the tempera-
ture Of the surroundings an infinitesimal amount results in complete vaporizatlon,
and lowering the temperature causes complete condensation.
3 · Because the transition takes place at constant pressure (for instance, 1 atm), the
heat supplied is equal to the change in enthalpy of the substance (Section 8 · 8 ） ·
lt follows that we can replace qrev in the expression for the entropy change with
AH fo r the phase change.
The entropy of vaporization, AS is the change in entropy per mole of mole-
cules when a substance changes from a liquid intO a vapor. The heat required per
mole tO vaporize the liquid at constant pressure is equal tO the enthalpy Of vaporiza-

9 ． 5 A MoIecuIar lnterpretation of Entropy
So far, we have calculated only c 方 ” & in the entropy 0f a substance. However,
entropy is a measure Of disorder, and it is possible tO imagine a perfectly orderly
state Of matter with neither positional nor, at T = 0 ， thermal disorder. Such a
state represents a natural zero Of entropy, a state Of perfect order; therefore,
we should be able tO set up an absolute scale Of entropy JLISt as we can set up
an absolute scale of temperature. This idea is summarized by the third 1 aw of
thermodynamlcs ：
The entropies Of all perfect crystals approach zero as the absolute temperature
approaches zero.
That is, S 0 as T 艹 0 · The "perfect crystal" part of this statement of the third
law refers tO a substance in which all the atoms are in a perfectly orderly array,
and SO there is no positional disorder. The T 艹 0 part Of the statement implies
the absence Of thermal motion—thermal disorder vanishes as the temperature
approaches zero. AS the temperature Of a substance IS raised from zero, more
orientations become available tO the molecules and their thermal disorder increases.
Thus we can expect the entropy Of any substance tO be greater than zero above
ln 1877 the Austrian physicist Ludwig Boltzmann proposed a molecular defini-
tion Of entropy that enables us tO calculate the bso / entropy at a ny temperature
(FIG. 9 · 6 ） · His formula provided a way of calculating the entropy when measure-
ments could not be made and deepened our insight intO the meaning Of entropy at
the molecular level. The B oltzmann formula fo r the entropy is
S = ln W

energy. Each arrangement Of the molecules in a sample is a different state
called a mlcrostate, SO W is equal tO the number Of different mlcrostates that
correspond tO the same energy. A microstate lasts only for an instant; SO, when
measure the bulk properties Of a system, are measuring a time average

surement. The entropy calculated from the Boltzmann formula is called the

To understand Eq. 6 ， imagine that we have a large number of replicas of the
system that we are lnvestigating, with each replica having the same tOtal energy.
Although the energy of each replica is the same, the molecules may be distributed
differently over the available energy levels. Now imagine that all the replicas are
placed in a box, and we select them blindly, one by one. If there is only one way of
achieving the energy (for instance, all the molecules are in exactly the same energy
level), then W = 1 · ln this case, every replica that we select will have exactly the
same distribution Of molecules and will be in exactly the same microstate. Such a
system has zero entropy ()n 1 = 0 ） and zero disorder, because each time we make a
selection we find the system in that single microstate. We can be absolutely certain
that the selection will be the same ln each case. However, if there is more than one
way Of arranging the molecules in the sample tO achieve the same energy, then not
every replica that we draw will be the same. For instance, if a certain energy can be
achieved with 1000 different microstates （ W = 1000 ）， then there is only 1 chance
in 1000 of drawing a “ c one of those microstates. Because the disorder of the
system is higher fo r this state than for that with W ： 1 ， the entropy f0 r this state is
greater than zero.

9 ． 6 The EquivaIence of StatisticaI and
Thermodynamic Entropies
The expressions in Eq. 1 ()S = qrev/T) and Eq. 6 (S = ln W) are two apparently
very different definitions of entropy. The first was established by considerations of
the behavior of bulk matter and the second by statistical analysis of molecular
behavior. TO verify that the tWO definitions are in fact essentially the same, we need
to show that the entropy changes predicted on the basis of Eq. 6 are the same as
those deduced from Eq. 1 · do so, we will show that the Boltzmann formula
predicts the correct form of the volume dependence of the entropy of an ideal gas
(Eq. (a). More detailed calculations show that the tW O definitions are consistent
with each other in every respect. ln the process of developing these ideas, we shall
also deepen our understanding Of what we mean by "disorder. ”
An ideal gas consists Of a large number Of molecules that can be viewed as
occupying the energy levels characteristic Of a particle in a box. For simplicity, we
consider a one-dimensional box (FIG. 9.9a), but the same considerations apply t0 a
real three-dimensional container of any shape. At T = 0 (not shown), only the low-
est energy level is occupied; SO W ： 1 and the entropy is zero. There is no "disor-
because we know which state each molecule occupies.
At any temperature above T = 0 ， the molecules OCCUPY large numbers of differ-
ent energy levels, as shown in Fig. 9 · 9 · Because the molecules can now be found in a
larger number of microstates, W is greater than 1 · Therefore, the entropy (which is
proportional tO ln W) is greater than zero. NOW the disorder has increased; conse-
quently we are less confident about precisely which state a given molecule occumes.
For instance, in a tiny system with only tW O molecules, A and B, at T = 0 we can be
confident that both molecules OCCUPY the lowest energy level. However, if at a higher
temperature a second state becomes available, we don't know whether it is molecule
A that occupies the higher level, with B still in the ground State, or V1ce versa.

BO)( 9 ． 1 FRONTIERS OF CHEMISTRY: THE QUEST FOR ABSOLUTE ZERO
Th e possibility of achieving absolute zero (T = 0 ） has
intrigued scientists for many years. At absolute zero lt would
be possible tO study the properties Of materials in their lowest
allowed energy state. For instance, at very IOW temperatures
an interference pattern Of laser beams can be used tO create
an "optical lattice," a set Of spatially symmetric potential
energy wells in which atoms can be trapped to form perfect
crystals. These arrays could be used t0 create tiny building
blocks for very-low temperature nanoscale computers.
The third law of thermodynamics tells us that it is not
possible tO reach absolute zero in a cyclical thermodynanmc
process with a finite number Of Steps. However, it may still
be possible to reach absolute zero by usmg a noncyclic
process, and record IOW temperatures have recently been
reached by a variety Of means.
One method tO approach T = 0 is tO alternate isother-
mal magnetization with adiabatic demagnetlzation. This
approach takes advantage Of the fact that, in a magnetic
field, electrons with down spins （ have slightly lower ener-
gies than electrons with up spins （们 · If the up spins can be
converted tO down splns, the sample will have lower energy
overall and therefore a lower temperature. If all the up spins
could be converted tO down spins, the temperature would
reach absolute zero.
A COOI paramagnet1C sample that is not in a magnetic
field has equal numbers of up and down electrons because
the two spin states have the same energy (see Box 4 · 2 ） ·
This is true whatever the temperature. SO the first Step is
tO COOI the sample by conventional means (for instance, by
putting it in contact with liquid helium) · Then a magnetic
field is turned on. The down spin states now have lower
energy than the up spin states, and so they are slightly more
numerous. We shall call this state A. Th e sample in this state
has a characteristic entropy that reflects the slightly greater
number Of down spins than up spins and the temperature Of
the sample. If there were even more down spins, we would
report that the temperature Of the sample was lower. The
task, therefore, IS tO turn some up spms intO down spms.
TWO steps are used tO achieve thiS converslon, and are sum-
marized in the first figure.
ln the first step, the field is increased. As a result, the
energies Of the tWO states diverge and the populations adJLISt.
This adjustment of populations takes place while the sample
IS lll contact With itS surroundings and occurs without
change Of temperature: lt is the 这 0 乃 e 了 / g e 彘 0
叩 · The entropy decreases in this step because, although
the temperature remalns the same, the spins have become
more ordered. We shall call this state B.
ln the second Step, thermal contact with the surroundings
is broken, so any subsequent change will be adiabatic—that
IS, not involve a transfer Of energy as heat between the system
and the surroundings. ln any reversible adiabatic process the
entropy does not change (because AS = qrev/T and qrev
Under these adiabatic conditions, the magnetic field is reduced
tO the value it had in state A. However, although the magnet1C
field has been reduced, th e entropy is th e same as in state B
when a high magnetic field was present. As we saw, this lower
entropy corresponds tO a lower temperature than the sample
had initially: the sample has been cooled. The two steps are
repeated until the temperature has been lowered as much as
possible. However, because the tWO curves in the illustration
converge at T = 0 ， this cyclic process cannot achieve absolute
zero itself. Sophisticated procedures of this kind have achieved
temperatures as low as about 100 pK （ 1 × 10 一 0 K).

We can use the molecular interpretation Of entropy tO understand why some
substances have high molar entropies and others have IOW molar entropies. For

and the fact that the greater the mass Of the molecules, the closer together are the
energy levels (FIG. 9 · 1 3 ） · 、 We also see that large, complex species have higher molar
entropies than smaller, simpler ones (compare CaC03 with CaO or C2H50H with
H20). Liquids have higher molar entropies than solids because the greater freedom
Of movement Of the molecules in a liquid results in a less ordered state Of matter.
The molar entropies 0f gases, in which molecules OCCUPY much larger volumes and
undergo almost completely disordered motion, are substantially higher than those
of the corresponding liquids.

9 ． 8 Standard Reaction Entropies
Entropy is an lmportant concept in chemistry because lt is the basis for predicting
the natural direction Of a reaction. However, we have tO remember that the entropy
of the surroundings, not only that of the system, changes as the heat produced or
absorbed by the reaction enters or leaves them. Both the entropy change of the
system and that Of the surroundings affect the direction Of a reaction, because bOth
contribute tO the entropy Of the unlverse.
lt is easy t0 predict the sign of the entropy change of the surroundings if the
sign Of the reaction enthalpy is known. If the reaction is exothermic, heat is released
intO the surroundings and their entropy increases （ ASsurr > 0 ） · If the reaction is
endothermic, heat leaves the surroundings, SO their entropy decreases （ ASsur < 0 ） ·
We shall develop this point quantitatively in the following section, but it will be
very helpful to keep this qualitative conclusion ln mind.
ln some cases, the sign of the entropy change of the system can be predicted
without dOing any calculation. For instance, because the molar entropy Of a gas is
so much greater than that of solids and liquids, a change in the amount of gas mol-
ecules normally dominates any Other entropy change in a reaction. A net increase
in the amount Of gas usually results in a positive change in entropy. Conversely, a
net consumption Of gas usually results in a negative change. Reactions that produce
a large number of small molecules and the dissolving of a substance typically have
positive entropies. However, entropy changes are much more finely balanced for
reactions in which there is no net change in the amount Of gas or in which gases dO
not take part, and fO r these reactions numerical data must be used tO predict the
sign 0f the entropy change 0f the system.

TO calculate the change in entropy that accompanies a reaction, we need tO
know the molar entropies Of all the substances taking part; then we calculate the
difference between the entropies Of the products and those Of the reactants.
More specifically, the standard reaction entropy, ASO, is the difference between
the standard molar entropies Of the products and those Of the reactants, taking
intO account their stoichiometric coefficients. For example, the entropy change
for the reaction N2(g) + 3 H2(g) 艹 2 NH3(g) is twice the molar entropy of
NH3(g) minus the molar entropy of N2(g) and three times the molar entropy of
H2(g). The definition of standard reaction entropy can be expressed for any
reactlon as

second term is that Of the reactants. ln each case the standard molar entropy Of a
substance IS multiplied by its amount ()n moles) as it appears in the chemical equa-

GIobal Changes in Entropy
Some processes seem tO defy the second law. For example, water freezes tO ice spon-
taneously at IOW temperatures, and cold packs fO r athletic inJuries become ice cold
spontaneously, even on warm days, when the ammomum nitrate inside the pack
dissolves in the water that it contains. Life itself appears tO go against the second
law. Every cell Of a living being is organized tO an extraordinary extent. Thousands
of different compounds, each one having a specific function tO perform, move in the
intricately organized dance we call life. HOW can the molecules in our bodies form
such highly organized, complex structures from slime, mud, and gas? Our existence
seems at first sight tO be a contradiction Of the second law.

===== 第 483 页 =====
The dilemma is resolved when we realize that the second law refers tO an 0 一
磊 system. TO interpret the second law correctly, we must consider a ny system tO
be part of a larger isolated system that includes the surroundings of the system of
interest. The process is spontaneous only if the 0 / change in entropy, the sum
Of the changes in the system and the surroundings, is positive. Our task, there-
fore, is first tO see hOW tO calculate the change in entropy Of the surroundings and
then to combine that change with the change in entropy of the system. We have
already mentioned what we should expect qualitatively: exothermic processes
lead tO an mcrease in the entropy Of the surroundings and endothermic processes
reduce it. NOW we have tO make this qualitative conclusion quantitative. Then,
once we know the total entropy change, we shall be able to predict whether a
reaction iS spontaneous, whether itS reverse IS spontaneous, or whether the SYS-
tem is at equilibrium.

Spontaneous endothermic reactions were a puzzle fO r nineteenth-century
chemists, whO believed that reactions ran only in the direction Of decreasing energy
Of the system. lt seemed tO them that, in endothermic reactlons, reactants were r1S-
ing spontaneously to higher energies, like a weight suddenly leaping up from the
floor onto a table. However, the criterion for spontaneity is an 乙了 e se 乃 e 0 /
e op ， 0 厂乃 e s ， s d its s 0 / gs ， not a decrease in the energy Of a system.
ln an endothermic reaction, the entropy Of the surroundings certainly decreases as
heat flows from them intO the system. Nevertheless, there can still be an overall
lncrease entropy if the disorder Of the system increases enough. Every endother-
m1C reaction must be accompanied by increased disorder Of the system if it is tO be
spontaneous (FIG. 9 · 19 ）： spontaneous endothermic reactions are driven by the
dominating increase in disorder Of the system.

9 ． 11 Equilibrium
Although this section provides only a brief introduction t0 equilibrium, the prin-
ciples presented here are critically important, because the tendency Of reactions tO
proceed toward equilibrium is the basis Of much Of chemistry. The material in this
section lays the foundation for the next five chapters, including phase changes, the
reactions Of acids and bases, and redox reactions.
A system at equilibrium has no tendency tO change in either direction （ for-
ward or reverse). Such a system remams in 1tS current state until it is disturbed

===== 第 489 页 =====
by changing the conditions, such as raising the temperature, decreasing the VOI-
ume, or adding more reactants. The equilibrium state important in chemistry is
a dynamIC equilibrium, in which forward and reverse processes still continue but
at matching rates. For example, when a block Of metal is at the same tempera-
ture as itS surroundings, lt iS in thermal equilibrium With itS surroundings.
Energy continues tO flow as heat in bOth directions, but at the same rate; there
is no ” flow (FIG. 9 · 22 ） · When a gas confined to a cylinder by a piston has the
same pressure as that Of the surroundings, the system is ln mechanical equilib-
rlum with the surroundings and the gas has no tendency tO expand or contract.
The pressure inside is causing the piston tO move outward, but the pressure OUt-
side is causing the piston tO move lnward tO the same extent, and there is no net
change.
When a solid, such as ice, IS in contact with its liquid form, such as water, at
certain conditions Of temperature and pressure （ at 0 OC and 1 atm fO r water) ， the
tw O states Of matter are in dynanuc equilibrium with each other, and there is no
tendency fO r one form Of matter tO change intO the Other form. When solid and
liquid water are at equilibrium, water molecules continually leave solid ice tO form
liquid water, and water molecules continually leave the liquid phase t0 form ice.
However, there iS no e change, because these processes occur at the same rate and
SO balance each other.
a chemical reaction mixture reaches a certalll composition, the reaction
seems tO come tO a halt. A mixture Of substances at chemical equilibrium has no
tendency either tO produce more products or tO revert tO reactants. At equilibrium,
reactants are still forming products, but products are decaying at a matching rate
intO reactants and there is no e change Of composltion.
The common characteristic Of any kind Of dynanuc equilibrium is the continu-
ation Of processes at the microscopic level but no e tendency fO r the system tO
change in either the forward or the reverse direction. That is, neither the forward

One of the problems with using the second law t0 judge whether a reaction is
spontaneous is that tO get the tOtal entropy change we must calculate three quan-
tities: the entropy change of the system, the entropy change of the surroundings,
and the sum of the two changes. We could avoid some of this work if a single
property combined the entropy calculations fO r the system and the surroundings.
We could then carry out the calculation in one step by using a single table of
data. This simplification IS achieved by introducing a new state function, the
"Gibbs free energy." Not only does the Gibbs free energy allow us to assess

The Gibbs free energy Of a substance decreases (that is, it becomes less positive
or more negative) as itS temperature iS raised at constant pressure. ThiS conclusion
follows from the definition G = H 一 TS and the fact that the entropy of a pure
substance IS lnvariably positive; increases, increases, tOO, and a larger quan-
tity is subtracted from H. Another important conclusion is that, because the molar
entropy of the gas phase of a substance is greater than that of its liquid phase, the
Gibbs free energy decreases more sharply with temperature fo r the gas phase of a
substance than fo r the liquid phase. Similarly, the Gibbs free energy of the liquid
phase 0f a substance decreases more sharply than that of its solid phase (FIG. 9 · 25 ） ·
We can now see the thermodynanuc origin Of phase transitions. At IOW tem-
peratures, the molar Gibbs free energy of the solid phase lies lowest, so there is a
spontaneous tendency fo r a liquid to freeze and thereby reduce its Gibbs free
energy. Above a certain temperature, the molar Gibbs free energy of the liquid has
fallen below that of the solid, and the substance has a spontaneous tendency t0
melt. At an even higher temperature, the molar Gibbs free energy of the gas phase

===== 第 493 页 =====
9 · 1 3 Gibbs Free Energy 0f Reaction
has fallen to below the liquid line, and the substance has a spontaneous tendency
tO vaporize. The temperature Of each phase change corresponds tO the point Of
intersection Of the lines fO r the tWO phases, as can be seen in Fig. 9 · 25 ·
The relative positions of the three lines shown in Fig. 9 · 25 are different fo r each
substance. One possibility—which depends on the strength Of intermolecular inter-
actions in the condensed phases—is fO r the liquid line tO lie in the position shown
ln FIG. 9 · 26 ln this case, the liquid line is never the lowest line, at any temperature.
As soon as the temperature has been raised above the point corresponding tO the
intersectlon Of the solid and gas lines, the direct transition Of the solid tO the vapor
becomes spontaneous. This plot is the type expected fo r carbon dioxide, which
sublimes at atmospheric pressure.

The decrease in Gibbs free energy as a slgnpost 0f spontaneous change and

reactlons are our prmcipal interest in chemistry, now concentrate on them and

The thermodynamic function used as the criterion Of spontaneity fO r a chemi-
cal reaction is the Gibbs free energy 0f reaction, AG (which is commonly referred
tO as the "reaction free energy" ） · This quantity is defined as the difference in molar

The molar Gibbs free energy 0f a substance in a mixture depends on what
molecules it has as neighbors, so the molar Gibbs free energies of NH3, N2 ， and H2
change as the reaction proceeds. For example, at an early Stage Of the reaction, an
NH3 molecule has mostly N2 and H2 molecules around it, but at a later stage of the
reaction, most Of its neighbors may be NH3 molecules. Because the individual
Gibbs free energies change as the reaction proceeds, the Gibbs free energy of reac-
tion also changes. If AG < 0 at a certaln composition Of the reaction mixture, then
the reaction is spontaneous. If AG > 0 at a certaln composition, then the reverse
reaction (the decomposltion Of ammoma ln our example), iS spontaneous.
The standard Gibbs free energy of reaction, AGO, is defined like the Gibbs free
energy Of reaction but in terms Of the s 了 molar Gibbs energies Of the reac-
tants and products:
AGO = 〗 nGm0(products) _ 〗 nGm0(reactants)
（ 19 ）
That is, the standard Gibbs free energy of reaction is the difference in Gibbs free
energy between products in their standard states and reactants in their standard states
()t the specified temperature ） · Because the standard state Of a substance is its pure
form at 1 bar, the s ” Gibbs free energy of reaction is the difference in Gibbs
free energy between the pure products and the pure reactants: it is a fixed quantity
for a given reaction and does not vary as the reaction proceeds. We shall unfold the
enormous lmportance Of this quantity shortly. The points tO remember are these:
AGO is fixed fO r a given reaction and temperature and SO does not change as
the reaction proceeds.

reporting thermodynamic data. If AGf0 < 0 at a certain temperature, the pure com-
pound has a lower Gibbs free energy than that of its pure elements and the elements
are poised tO change spontaneously intO the compound at that temperature
(FIG. 9 · 27 ） · We say that the compound is "more stable ” under standard conditions
than the elements. If AGf0 > 0 ， the Gibbs free energy of the compound is higher
than that Of its elements and the compound is poised tO change spontaneously intO
the pure elements. ln this case, we say that the pure elements are "more stable ” than
the pure compound. For example, the standard Gibbs free energy of formation of
benzene is + 124 kJ•mol-l at 25 OC, and benzene is unstable with respect to its
elements under standard conditions at 25 OC.
A thermodynamically stable compound is a compound with a negative stan-
dard Gibbs free energy of formation (water is an example). A thermodynamically
unstable compound is a compound with a positive standard Gibbs free energy 0f
formation (benzene is an example ） · Such a compound is poised tO decompose spon-
taneously intO its elements. However, that tendency may not be realized in practice,
because the decomposition may be very slow. Benzene can, in fact, be kept indefi-
nitely without decomposing at all. Substances that are thermodynamically unstable
but survive fO r long periods are called nonlabile or even inert. For example, ben-
zene is thermodynamically unstable but nonlabile. Substances that do decompose
or react rapidly are called labile. Most radicals are labile. lt is important to keep in
mind the distinction between stability and lability:
Stable and unstable are terms that refer tO the thermodynamic tendency Of a
substance tO decompose intO its elements.

9 ． 14 The Gibbs Free Energy and Nonexpansion Work
We are now ready to see why the Gibbs free energy is called the 彦 “ energy. We
shall see that the change in Gibbs free energy that accompanies a process allows
us tO predict the maxlmum 0 e 无 p 0 彬 or that the process can dO at constant
temperature and pressure. That is, the Gibbs free energy is a measure Of the energy
that is free tO dO nonexpanslon work. As explained in Section 8 · 3 ， nonexpansion
work, We ， is any kind Of work Other than that due tO expanslon against an oppos-
lng pressure, SO it includes electrical work and mechanical work (like stretching a
spring or carrying a weight up a slope). The fact that nonexpansion work includes
electrical work—the work Of pushing electrons through an electrical circuit—is the
basis Of the chemical generation Of electrical power; we pursue that connection in
Chapter 14 · Nonexpansion work also includes the work of muscular activity, the
work Of linking amino acids together tO form protein molecules, and the work Of
sending nerve signals through neurons, so a knowledge of changes in Gibbs free
energy is central tO an understanding Of bioenergetics, the deployment and utiliza-
tion of energy in living cells.
The challenge that we now face is tO derive a q e relation between the
Gibbs free energy and the maximum nonexpansion work that a system can dO.

9 ． 15 The Effect of Temperature
The enthalpies Of reactants and products are bOth affected by a temperature rise,
and the difference between their values changes only a little with temperature
(recall Section 8 · 21 ） · The same is true of the entropies. As a result, the values of
AHO and ASO do not change much with temperature. However, AGO does depend
on temperature (remember the T in AGO = AHO 一 TASO) and might change sign as
the temperature is changed. There are four cases tO consider:
1 · For an exothermic reaction (AHO < 0 ） with a negative reaction entropy (ASO < 0 ），
一 TASO contributes a positive term tO AGO. For such a reaction, AGO is negative
(and the formation Of products spontaneous) at IOW temperatures because AHO
dominates 一 TASO but it may become positive (and the reverse reaction, the
decomposition Of pure products, spontaneous) at higher temperatures when
_ TASO dominates AHO (FIG. 9 · 28a ） · As the temperature is lowered, the reaction
becomes spontaneous when AGO = 0 ， at which point T = AHO/ASO.
ln this case, the increase ln entropy Of the surroundings drives the reaction forward,
but it is opposed by the decrease ln entropy 0f the system.

lmpact 0 n Biology
The existence Of living things seems at first thought tO be a contradiction Of the
second law of thermodynamics. Every cell of a living being is organized t0 an
extraordinary extent. Thousands Of different compounds, each one having a specific
function t0 perform, move in the intricately choreographed dance we call life. We
are examples of systems with very low entropy ()n the sense that we are highly
ordered). By considering the surroundings we can explain why the molecules in our
body form a highly organized, complex structure, rather than slime, ooze, or gas.
9 ． 16 Gibbs Free Energy Changes in Bi010gical Systems
Many biological reactions, such as the construction Of a protein from ammo acids
or the construction Of a DNA molecule, are not spontaneous and therefore must

===== 第 501 页 =====
9 · 1 6 Gibbs Free Energy Changes in Bi010gical Systems
be driven by an external source 0f energy. That energy comes from sunlight and
the chemicals in food that have stored solar energy (FIG 9 · 29 ） · When food is
metabolized, the resulting exothermic reaction generates a lOt Of entropy, and if the
reaction IS coupled tO a biochemical reaction that is nonspontaneous, the 0 e / /
change in entropy may be positive, and the 0 e / / process spontaneous. ln Other
words, 了 e C 0 乃 produces / 0 0 厂 e 了 OP ， ca drive 0 SPO eo S reac-
0 ” 和了彬 r 法 ln terms of Gibbs free energy, one biochemical process may be driven
uphill in Gibbs free energy by another reaction that rolls downhill. Staying alive is
very much like the effect of a heavy weight tied to another weight by a string that
passes over a pulley (FIG. 9 · 30 ） · The lighter weight could never fly up into the air
on its OWn. However, when it is connected tO a heavier weight falling downward
on the other side of a pulley, the light weight can soar upward.
The hydrolysis of adenosine triphosphate, ATP （ 2 ）， to adenosine diphosphate,
ADP (3), is the reaction used most frequently by biological organisms to couple
with and drive nonspontaneous reactions. This hydrolysis is the key metabolic
reaction by which Gibbs free energy is stored and used in living systems. The value
of AGO fo r the hydrolysis of 1 mol ATP is about 一 30 kJ. To restore ADP back to
ATP, which is accompanied by a Gibbs free-energy change of + 30 kJ, an ADP mol-
ecule and a phosphate group must be linked by coupling them to another reaction
fo r which the Gibbs free energy 0f reaction is more negative than 一 30 kJ. That is
one reason Why have tO eat. eat fOOd containing glucose, consume
a fuel. Like all fuels, it has a spontaneous tendency tO form combustion products.
If we were simply tO burn glucose an open contalner, it would dO no work Other
than pushing back the atmosphere, and it would give off a lot of heat. However, in
our bodies, the "combustion ” is a highly controlled and sophisticated verslon of
burning. ln such a controlled reaction, the nonexpansion work that the process can
d0 approaches 2500 kJ per mole of glucose molecules, which is enough to "recharge "
about 80 mol ADP molecules.
When living organisms die, they no longer ingest the second-hand sunlight
stored in molecules Of carbohydrate, protein, and fat. Then the natural direction Of
change becomes dominant, and the intricate molecules that support life start tO
decompose. Living orgamsms are engaged in a constant battle tO generate enough
entropy in their surroundings tO go on building and maintaming their intricate
interiors. As soon as they Stop the battle, they Stop generating that external entropy,
and their bodies decay intO the slime, ooze, and gas that in our lifetime we avoid
becoming.

PHYS ℃ AL EQUILIBRIA
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? This chapter introduces the concept
Of equilibrium between different phases Of a substance, a concept that will prove tO
be Of the greatest importance fO r chemical and biochemical transformations. Many
of the materials encountered in the everyday world, in medicine, in organisms, and
in the laboratory a re solutions, SO it is essential tO understand hOW a solute affects
the properties Of a solvent. One economically and commercially important mixture
is petroleum, and the concepts presented here will help you tO understand hOW it is
refined.
What Are the Key ldeas? Dynamic equilibrium between two phases is reached when
the rate Of conversion between them is the sa m e i n each direction. The rates a re equal
when the molar Gibbs free energy 0f the substance is the sa m e in each phase and
therefore there is n O tendency tO change in either direction. The sa m e concepts apply
tO the dissolving Of a solute. The presence Of a solute alters the entropy Of a solvent
and consequently affe cts its thermodynamic properties.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? This chapter develops the concepts of
physical equilibria introduced i n the context of thermodynamics (Chapters 8 and 9 ） and
assumes a knowledge of intermolecular forces (Sections 6 · 1 一 6 · 5 ） · The compositions of
S O m e Of the solutions discussed a re expressed in terms Of mole fraction (Section 5 · 8 ） ·
early all the gases, liquids, and solids we encounter in our daily life are
m1Xtures or solutions. ln Section 5 · 8 considered gaseous mixtures. ln
this chapter we lnvestigate liquid solutions and see hOW the solutes dis-
solved in them affect their physical properties. The largest solutions on Earth are
the oceans, which account fo r 1 · 4 × 102 kg of the Earth's surface water. That mass
amounts to nearly 2 × 108 t （ 1 t _ 103 (g) of water fo r each inhabitant, more than
enough to supply all the drinking water needed fo r a thirsty world. However,
drinking seawater itself can be fatal, because Of the high concentrations Of dis-
solved salts, in particular Na and CI- ions (TABLE 10 · 1 ） · The transformation of
seawater into potable (drinkable) water is a major challenge around the world.
This chapter describes one way that this purification can be achieved.
Another solution Of great importance tO our lives is the plasma that carries the
erythrocytes (red blood cells) through our bodies. These cells can cease to function
if the concentrations Of solutes in the plasma drift from their optimal values. This
chapter explains why such changes occur and guides us through building a model
that accounts fo r the behavior of solutions. We begin by examining phase changes
ln pure substances, then we see hOW the presence Of a solute affects the properties
Of the substance.

Phases and Phase Transitions
As we saw in Section 6 · 1 ， a single substance can exist in different phases, or
physical forms. The phases of a substance include its solid, liquid, and gaseous
forms. They also include its different solid forms, such as the diamond and graph-
ite phases Of carbon. ln one case—helium—two liquid phases are known tO exist.
The converslon Of a substance from one phase intO another, such as the melting Of
ice, the vaporization Of water, and the converslon Of graphite intO diamond, is
called a phase transltlon.
The unifying concept Of this chapter is eq / 左 b · For a given pressure, a
substance undergoes a phase transition at a specific temperature, such as the change
from solid tO liquid at the melting temperature. More precisely, at this characteristic
temperature, the solid and liquid phases Of a substance are in equilibrium, at which
point there is no change in Gibbs free energy, AG = 0 ， when one phase changes into
the other. Thus, even though the entropy of the system would increase if some of it
melted （ or if it vaporized), there is a compensating reduction in entropy Of the sur-
roundings as heat is drawn in from them, and there is no change in the 0 / entropy
Of the system and its surroundings. ln short, there is no thermodynamic driving
force in either directlon When tWO phases are III equilibrium.
10 ． 1 Vapor Pressure
A simple experiment can be used to show that, in a closed vessel, the liquid and
vapor phases Of a substance reach equilibrium with each other. First, we set up a
mercury barometer. As we saw in Section 5 · 2 ， the mercury inside the tube falls to
a height proportional tO the external atmospheric pressure, leaving it about 76 cm
high at sea level. The space above the mercury is almost a vacuum (the trace Of
mercury vapor present is SO small that it can be ignored). NOW suppose we i11J ect
a tiny drop of water into the space above the mercury. AII the water added imme-
diately evaporates and fills the space with vapor. The molecules in this vapor push
the surface Of the mercury down a few millimeters. The pressure exerted by the
vapor—as measured by the change in the height of mercury—depends on the
amount Of water added. However, suppose we add SO much water that a little
liquid water remams on the surface Of the mercury. The pressure Of the vapor now
reaches and remains at a constant value, no matter hOW much liquid water iS present
(FIG. 10 · 1 ） · We conclude that, 酊无 e pe 忉， as / 0 ” g 然 some liquid
present, 方 e p 0 exerts 乙乃 cte 万记 pressure regardless 0 厂方 e 0 0 厂
liquid 彬 present. For example, at 20 OC, the mercury falls 18 mm, and so the
pressure exerted by the water vapor is 18 Torr. The pressure Of the water vapor is
the same whether there is 0 · 1 mL or 1 mL of liquid water still present. This char-
acteristic pressure is the p 0 了 pressure Of the liquid at the temperature Of the
experiment (TABLE 10 · 2 ） ·
Liquids with high vapor pressures at ordinary temperatures are said tO be volatile.
Methanol (vapor pressure 98 Torr at 20 。 0 is volatile; mercury （ 1 · 4 mTorr) is not.
S01ids also exert a vapor pressure, but their vapor pressures are usually very much
lower than those of liquids because the molecules are held together more tightly in
a solid than they are in a liquid. For instance, even at 1000 K the vapor pressure of
lron IS only 7 × 10 一 1 Torr, which iS tOO IOW tO sustain a mercury column even one
atom high ！ Nevertheless, some solids vaporize in the process called s b 方 0
(Section 8 · (1), which we can observe at room temperature in the presence Of pun-
gent solids such as menthol and mothballs (naphthalene). The vapor pressure of
naphthalene, fo r instance, is 0 · 09 Torr at 25 OC.
To build a molecular model of the equilibrium between a liquid and its vapor,
we first suppose that the liquid is introduced intO an evacuated closed container.
Vapor forms as molecules leave the surface Of the liquid. Most evaporation takes
place from the surface of the liquid because the molecules there are least strongly
bound tO their neighbors and can escape more easily than those in the bulk. However,

as the number Of molecules in the vapor increases, more Of them become avail-

matches the number escaping (FIG. 10 · 2 ） · The vapor is now condensing as fast as
the liquid is vaporinng, and SO the equilibrium is d ，记 in the sense introduced

H20(l) 冖 H20(g)

the liquid phase), the products are changing back intO reactants at a matching rate.
With this picture in mind, we can now define the vapor pressure Of a liquid ()r a
solid) as the pressure exerted by its vapor when the vapor and the liquid ()r the

10 ． 2 Volatility and lntermolecular Forces
We can expect high vapor pressure when the molecules of a liquid are held together
by weak intermolecular forces in the liquid and IOW vapor pressure when the inter-
molecular forces are strong. We therefore expect compounds capable of formmg
hydrogen bonds (which are stronger than other typ e s of intermolecular interac-
tions) tO be less volatile than Other molecular compounds Of similar molar mass
but that are not able to form hydrogen bonds. The effect of hydrogen bonding can
be seen by comparing dimethyl ether （ 1 ） and ethanol （ 2 ）， which have the same
molecular formula, C2H60. Because the tWO compounds have the same numbers
Of electrons, we can expect them tO have similar London interactions and therefore
similar vapor pressures. However, an ethanol molecule has an —OH group and can
form a hydrogen bond to another ethanol molecule. Ether molecules cannot form
hydrogen bonds t0 one another, because all their hydrogen atoms are attached to
carbon atoms and the C—H bond is not very polar. As a result of this difference,
ethanol is a liquid at room temperature, whereas dimethyl ether is a gas.

10 ． 5 Freezing and MeIting
A liquid solidifies (freezes) when its molecules have such low energies that they are
unable to wriggle past their neighbors. ln the solid, the molecules vibrate about
their average positions but rarely move from place tO place. The freezing tempera-
ture, the temperature at which the solid and liquid phases are in dynamic equilib-
num, varies slightly as the pressure is changed, and the normal freezing point, Tf,
Of a liquid is the temperature at which it freezes at 1 atm. ln practice, a liquid
sometimes does not freeze until the temperature is a few degrees below its freezing
point. A liquid that survives below its freezing point is said to be supercooled. As
described in Section 9 · 4 ， the normal melting point Of a solid is the temperature at
which it melts at 1 atm. The melting temperature Of a solid is the same as the freez-
ing temperature of the liquid.
For most substances, the density Of the solid phase Of a substance is greater
than that of the liquid phase, because the molecules pack together more closely in
the solid phase. Applied pressure helps to hold the molecules together, and so a high
temperature must be reached before the molecules Of a solid at high pressure can

===== 第 517 页 =====
break apart. As a result, most solids melt at higher temperatures when subjected tO
pressure. However, except at very high pressures, the effect Of pressure IS usually
quite small. lron at 1 atm, for example, melts at 1800 K, but it melts at only a few
degrees higher when the pressure is a thousand times as great. At the center Of the
Earth, however, the pressure is high enough for iron to be solid despite the high
temperatures there, SO the Earth's inner core is believed tO be solid.
The common observation that ice floats on water is highly unusual; it results
from the fact that at 0 OC the density of liquid water is greater than that of ice.
Therefore, at the melting point, the molar volume of liquid water is less than that
of ice. This anomalous behavior is due to the hydrogen bonds in ice, which result
1n a very open structure (FIG. 10 · 6 · also see Section 6 · 10 ） · When ice melts, many of
the hydrogen bonds collapse, thereby allowing the water molecules to pack together
more closely. As a result, high pressure encourages the formation Of the denser liq-
uid and the melting point Of ice decreases as the pressure IS lncreased.

bonds e 0 / 0 s ：犭 e / g po 犭 decreases 彬犭 pressure.

The lines separating the reglons in a phase diagram are called phase boundaries.
At any point on a boundary between tWO regions, the tWO neighboring phases
coexist in dynamic equilibrium. If one Of the phases IS a vapor, the pressure corre-
sponding tO this equilibrium is just the vapor pressure Of the substance. Therefore,
the liquid—vapor phase boundary shows how the vapor pressure of the liquid varies
with temperature. For example, the point at 80 OC and 0 · 47 atm in the phase dia-
gram fo r water lies on the phase boundary between liquid and vapor (FIG. 10 · 1 1 ），
which indicates that the vapor pressure of water at 80 OC is 0 · 47 atm. Similarly, the
solid—vapor phase boundary shows how the vapor pressure of the solid varies with
temperature (see Fig. 10 · 7 ） ·
The solid—liquid boundary, the almost vertical line in Figs. 10 · 7 and 10 · 11 ，
shows the pressures and temperatures at which solid and liquid water coexist in
equilibrium. ln Other words, it shows hOW the melting temperature Of ice ()r the
freezing temperature Of water) varles with pressure. The steepness Of the lines indi-
cates that even large changes pressure result in only small variations ln melting
temperature. The slope of the solid—liquid boundary reveals the relative densities of
solid and liquid. A negative slope, such as that in the phase diagram fo r water (Fig.
10 · 7), implies that the liquid is the denser phase. Notice that as we increase the
pressure Of ice, it will eventually be converted tO liquid. If the slope is positive, as it
is fo r carbon dioxide (Fig. 10 · 8 ）， then the solid is the denser phase; if we increase
the pressure on liquid carbon dioxide, it will solidify.

A triple point is a point where three phase boundaries meet on a phase dia-
gram. For water, the triple point fo r the solid, liquid, and vapor phases lies at 4 · 6
Torr and 0 · 01 OC (see Fig. 10 · 7 ） · At this triple point, all three phases (ice, liquid, and
vapor) coexist in mutual dynamic equilibrium: solid is in equilibrium with liquid,
liquid with vapor, and vapor with solid. The location of a triple point of a sub-
stance is a fixed property of that substance and cannot be changed by changing the
conditions. The triple point Of water is currently used tO define the size Of the kel-
vin: by definition, there are exactly 273 · 16 kelvins between absolute zero and the
triple point Of water. Because the normal freezing point Of water is found tO lie
0 · 01 K below the triple point, 0 OC (strictly, 0 · 00 (C) corresponds to 273 · 15 K.
ln Fig. 10 · 9 ， we see that sulfur can exist in any of four phases: tw 0 solid phases
(rhombic and monoclinic sulfur) ， one liquid phase, and one vapor phase. There are
three triple points in the diagram, where various combinations Of these phases,
such as monoclinic solid, liquid, and vapor or monoclinic solid, rhombic solid, and
liquid, coexist. However, four phases in mutual equilibrium （ such as the vapor,
liquid, and rhombic and monoclinic solid forms of sulfur, all in mutual equilibrium)
111 a one-component system has never been observed, and thermodynamICS can be
used tO prove that such a “ quadruple point" cannot exist.
A phase diagram can be used to explain the changes that take place when the
pressure or temperature Of a substance is changed. lmagine that we have a sample Of
water in a cylinder fitted with a piston at IOW pressure. Suppose that the temperature
is held constant at 50 OC, and that weights are placed on the piston tO exert a pressure
of 1 · 0 atm (FIG. 10 · 12 ） · Th e piston presses on the surface of the liquid, as in Fig.
10 · 12a · Now we gradually reduce the pressure by removing some of the weights (Fig.
10 · 12b ） · At first, nothing seems to happen. Th e high pressure is keeping all th e water
molecules in the liquid state, and the volume of a liquid changes very little with pres-
sure. However, when SO many weights have been removed that the pressure has fallen
to 0 · 12 a tm （ 93 Torr, the vapor pressure of water at that temperature), vapor begins
t0 appear (Fig. 10 · 120 · The sample is now at the vapor—liquid boundary on the
phase diagram. Th e pressure remams constant SO long as the liquid and vapor phases
are bOth present at equilibrium and the temperature remains constant. We are free tO
pull the piston up by an arbitrary extent (Fig. 10 · 12d), b ut enough water will evapo-
rate tO maintain the pressure at 0 · 12 atm. When we pull the piston out far enough,
the liquid phase disappears (Fig. 10 · 12e ）； we are now free to modify the pressure of
the vapor at will without changing the temperature (Fig. 10 · 12f ） ·

a phase diagram Of a simple, familiar substance can be revealing.

A feature of the phase diagram in
is that the liquid—vapor boundary
FIG. 10 · 13
comes tO an end at point C. TO see what happens at that point, suppose that a vessel
like the one shown in FIG. 10 · 14

24 Torr (the vapor pressure of water at 25 (C). Th e tw o phases are in equilibrium,
FIGURE 10 · 14 (a) At low temperatures the liquid and vapor phases 0f a substance i n a sealed,
constant-volume container a re distinct. (b) As the temperature is raised, m O re Of the liquid
vaporizes; the density 0f the liquid decreases while the density 0f the vapor increases. （ c) Near the

and the system lies at point A on the liquid—vapor curve in Fig. 10 · 13 · Now let's raise
the temperature, which moves the system from left to right along the phase bound-
ary. At 100 OC, the vapor pressure is 760 · Torr; and, at 200 OC, it has reached 11 · 7 kTorr

When the temperature has been increased to 374 OC (point C), the vapor pres-

vapor is now SO great that it is equal tO that Of the remaining liquid. At this Stage,
the surface separating the liquid from 1tS vapor vanishes and a single uniform phase
fills the container. Because a substance that fills any container that it occupies is by
definition a gas, we have tO conclude that this single uniform phase is a gas, despite
its high density ()e shall see in a moment that a better term is “ supercritical fluid ” ） ·
Provided the temperature is at 374 OC or above, it is found that even if the pressure
is increased by compressing the sample, no surface appears. That is, 374 OC is the
critical temperature, Tc, Of water, the temperature at and above which there can be
no transition from vapor tO liquid. Similar considerations apply tO Other substances
(TABLE 10 · 4 ）； fo r instance, the critical temperature 0f carbon dioxide is 31 OC; at
and above this temperature, C02 gas will not condense tO a liquid whatever the
pressure. The pressure corresponding to the end of the liquid—vapor phase bound-
ary is called the critical pressure, Pc of the substance. The critical pressure Of water
is 218 atm; that Of carbon dioxide is 73 atm. The critical temperature and critical
pressure j Ointly define the critical point Of the substance.
We can now be more specific about when tO call a
A Note 0 n Good Practice:
gaseous phase a vapor. A "vapor" is the gaseous phase Of a substance that is
below its critical temperature, SO it can be condensed tO a liquid by the appli-
cation Of pressure.
0
A gas can be liquefied by applying pressure only if it is below its critical tem-
perature (FIG. 10 · 15 ） · For example, carbon dioxide can be liquefied by applying
pressure only if its temperature is lower than 31 OC. According to TabIe 10 · 4 ， the
critical temperature Of oxygen IS
一 118 OC, and SO we know that it cannot exist as
a liquid at room temperature whatever the pressure.
G The dense fluid that exists above the critical temperature and pressure Of a
substance is called a supercritical fluid. lt may be so dense that, although it
is formally a gas, it is as dense as a liquid phase and can act as a solvent for
liquids and solids. There is currently considerable interest in supercritical fluids as
solvents for chemical reactions, as they are an important aspect Of green chemistry.
The use Of supercritical carbon dioxide avoids contammatlon with potentially
harmful solvents and allows rapid extraction on account of the high mobility of the
molecules through the fluid. For example, because supercritical carbon dioxide can
dissolve orgamc compounds, it iS used tO remove caffeine from coffee beans, tO
separate drugs from biological fluids for later analysis, and to extract perfumes
from flowers and phytochemicals from herbs. Supercritical hydrocarbons are used
tO extract useful compounds from coal and fly ash, and a variety Of supercritical
fluids are being mvestigated fO r recovering petroleum from oil-rich tar sands.

solvent extraction?

The presence Of a solute affects the physical properties Of a solvent. For instance,
when salt is spread on icy sidewalks, a mixture is created that has a lower freezing
point than pure water and the ice melts tO form a salt solution. ln this part Of the
chapter we explore the molecular nature Of these effects and see hOW tO treat them

10 ． 8 The Limits of SolubiIity
Let's imagine that we could see at the molecular level what happens when we
add a crystal Of glucose tO some water. The water molecules next tO the surface
of the crystal form hydrogen bonds to the glucose molecules. As a result, the
surface glucose molecules are pulled toward the solution by water molecules but
are held back by other glucose molecules. When the interactions with water
molecules are comparable tO the interactions with the Other glucose molecules,
the glucose molecules can drift O ff intO the solvent, surrounded by water mol-
ecules. A similar process takes place when an iomc solid dissolves. The polar
water molecules hydrate the ions (surround them in a closely held "solvent
shell," Section 6 · 2 ） and pry them away from the predominately attractive forces
within the crystal lattice (FIG. 10 · 16 ） · Stirring and shaking speed the process
because they bring more free water molecules tO the surface Of the solid and
sweep the hydrated ions away.
If we add only a small amount—20 g, fo r instance—of glucose to 100 mL of
water at room temperature, it all dissolves. However, if we add 200 g, some glu-
cose remains undissolved (FIG. 10 · 1 7 ） · A solution is said to be s aturated when the
solvent has dissolved all the solute that it can and some undissolved solute
remains. At this point the concentration Of solid solute in a saturated solution has
reached its greatest value, and no more can dissolve. The molar solubility, S, Of a
substance is its molar concentration ln a saturated solution. ln Other words, the
molar solubility Of a substance represents the limit Of its ability tO dissolve in a
given quantity Of solvent.
ln a saturated solution, the solid solute still present continues tO dissolve, but
the rate at which it dissolves exactly matches the rate at which the solute returns tO
the solid, so the concentration remains at its equilibrium value (FIG. 10 · 1 8 ） · ln a
saturated solution, the dissolved and undissolved solute are in dynamic equilibrium
with each other.

10 ． 9 The Like-Dissolves-Like Rule
Understanding the interplay of forces that takes place when a solute dissolves can
help us answer some practical questions. Suppose, fO r instance, that we need tO
remove some Oil that has soiled a fabric. HOW can we select a good solvent fO r the
oil? A good guide is the rule that 方 diss 0 lves 方 · That is, a polar liquid, such as
water, is generally the best solvent fO r iomc and polar compounds. Conversely,
nonpolar liquids, including hexane and tetrachloroethene, C12C=CC12, are often
better solvents fo r nonpolar compounds such as hydrocarbon oils, which are held
together by London forces.
The "like-dissolves-like ” rule can be understood by examining the attractions
between solute and solvent molecules. 、 When a solute dissolves in a liquid solvent,
the solute—solute attractions must be replaced by solute—solvent attractions, and
dissolving can be expected tO occur if the new interactlons are similar tO the origl-
nal interactions (FIG. 10 · 1 9 ） · For example, when the main cohesive forces in a sol-
ute are hydrogen bonds, the solute is more likely to dissolve in a hydrogen-bonded
solvent than in Other solvents. The molecules can slip intO solution only if they can
replace their strong solute—solute hydrogen bonds with strong solute—solvent
hydrogen bonds. Glucose, fo r example, has hydrogen-bond-forming —OH groups
and dissolves readily in water but not in hexane.
If the principal cohesive forces between solute molecules are London forces,
then the best solvent is likely tO be one that can mlmic those forces. For example,
a good solvent for nonpolar substances is the nonpolar liquid carbon disulfide
CS2. lt is a fa r better solvent than water fO r sulfur because solid sulfur is a
molecular solid of S8 molecules held together by London forces (FIG. 1 0 · 20 ） · The
sulfur molecules cannot penetrate intO the strongly hydrogen-bonded structure
Of water, because they cannot replace those bonds with interactions Of similar
strength.

rule. Soaps are the sodium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids, including

10 ． 10 Pressure and Gas SolubiIity: Henry's Law

High charge and small ionic radius both contribute to a high enthalpy of hydra-
tion. However, the same properties also contribute tO high lattice enthalpy. lt is there-
fore very difficult tO make reliable predictions about solubilities on the basis Of ion
charge and radius. Th e best we can dO is tO use these properties tO rationalize what is
observed. With that limitatlon in mind, we can begin tO understand the behavior Of
some everyday substances and the properties Of some IT11nerals. For example, nitrates
have big, singly charged anions and hence low lattice enthalpies. Their hydration
enthalpies, though, are quite large, because water can form hydrogen bonds with the
nitrate amons. As a result, they are rarely found in mlneral deposits because they are
soluble in groundwater, the water that trickles through th e ground and washes away
soluble substances. Carbonate lons are about the same S1ze as mtrate ions, but they
are doubly charged. As a result, carbonates commonly have higher lattice enthalpies
than dO nitrates, and it is much harder tO break the ions out Of solids such as lime-
stone (calcium carbonate) · Hydrogen carbonate ions (bicarbonate ions, HC03¯)
have a single charge, and their salts are more soluble than carbonates.
The difference solubility between carbonates and hydrogen carbonates is
responsible for the behavior Of "hard water," which is water that contains dissolved
calcium and magneslum salts. Hard water originates as ramwater, which dissolves
carbon dioxide from the air and forms a very dilute solution Of carbonic acid:
C02(g) + H20(l) 一 H2C03(aq)
As the water runs over and through the ground, the carbonic acid reacts with the
calcium carbonate of limestone or chalk and forms the more soluble hydrogen
carbonate:
CaC03(s) + H2C03(aq) 一 Ca2+(aq) + 2 HC03- (aq)
These tw O reactions are reversed when water containing Ca(HC03)2 is heated in a
kettle or furnace:
Ca2+(aq) + 2 HC03-(aq) 一 CaC03(s) + H20(l) + C02(g)
The carbon dioxide is driven Off and the calcium carbonate is deposited as the
hard, insoluble deposit known as s / 巳

10 ． 13 The Gibbs Free Energy of SoIution
A negative enthalpy 0f solution tells us that energy is released as heat when a sub-
stance dissolves. However, tO judge whether dissolving is spontaneous at constant

===== 第 529 页 =====
1 0 · 1 3 The Gibbs Free Energy of Solution
temperature and pressure, we need tO consider the change in Gibbs free energy,
AG = AH _ TAS. ln other words, we have to consider changes in the entropy of
the system, not just the change in enthalpy.
The disorder of a system typically increases when a solid dissolves (FIG. 1 0 · 25 ） ·
Therefore, ln most cases, we can expect the entropy Of the system tO lncrease when
a solution forms. Because TAS iS positive, thiS increase in disorder makes a negative
contribution tO AG. If AH is negative, we can be confident that AG is negative
overall. Therefore, we can expect most substances with negative enthalpies Of solu-
tion to be soluble.
ln some cases, the entropy Of the system is lowered when the solution forms
because the solvent molecules form cagelike structures around the solute molecules.
As a result, AS is negative and the term 一 TAS makes a positive contribution tO AG.
Even if AH is negative, AG might be positive. ln other words, even if energy
released tO the surroundings, the increase in the entropy Of the surroundings may
not be enough tO overcome the decrease ln entropy Of the solution. ln such a case
AG is positive and the substance does not dissolve. For this reason, some hydrocar-
bons, such as heptane, are insoluble in water even though they have weakly nega-
tive enthalpies Of solution.
If AH is positive, AG = AH 一 TAS can be negative only if TAS is positive and
larger than AH. That is, th e solubilities of substances that dissolve endothermically
depend on the balance of entropy changes in the system and in the surroundings. A
substance with a strongly positive enthalpy 0f solution is likely to be insoluble
because the entropy Of the surroundings may decrease SO much as energy leaves them
and enters the solution that dissolving corresponds tO an overall decrease in disorder.
Understanding the contributions to the Gibbs free energy of dissolving helps
explain the temperature dependence of solubility. The Gibbs energy becomes more
negative and favorable tO dissolving as the temperature increases only when AS is
posltive. For most ion1C substances, dissolving does indeed result in an lncrease ln
the entropy Of the system, and these substances are more soluble at higher tem-
peratures (see Fig. 10 · 23 ） · However, when a gas dissolves in a liquid, its molecules
occupy much less space and there is a considerable reduction in the entropy Of the
system. ln such a case, 一 iS posltive. Consequently, an lncrease in temperature
causes AG tO rise and dissolving is less favorable.
Because AG for the dissolving Of a solute depends on the concentration Of the
solute, even if AG is negative at IOW concentrations, it may become positive at high
concentrations (FIG. 10 · 26 ） · A solute dissolves spontaneously only until AG = 0 · At
that point, dissolved and undissolved solute are in equilibrium—the solution is
saturated.

C011igative Properties
Some properties Of a solution are essential to life. For example, OS OS ， the ten-
dency Of a solvent tO flow through a membrane intO a solution, promotes the flow
of nutrients through biological cell walls. When chemists started to study the
physical properties of solutions quantitatively, they discovered that some proper-
ties, including osmosis, depend only on the relative amounts Of solute and solvent
and are independent of the chemical identity of the solute. Properties that depend
on the relative numbers Of solute and solvent molecules and not on the chemical
identity of the solute are called colligative properties. The four colligative proper-
ties we shall consider are the lowering Of the vapor pressure Of the solvent, the
raising of its boiling point, the lowering of its freezing point, and osmosis. AII four
properties involve an equilibrium between tW O phases Of a solvent or (for osmosis)
between tw O solutions with different concentratlons.

A hypothetical solution that Obeys Raoult's law exactly at all concentrations is
called an ideal solution. ln an ideal solution, the interactions between solute and
solvent molecules are the same as the interactions between solvent molecules in the
pure state and between solute molecules in the pure state. We can summarize this
statement by saying that A—A, B—B, and A—B interactions are all the same in an
ideal solution. Consequently, the solute molecules mingle freely with the solvent
molecules. Because the interactions are all the same, fO r an ideal solution, the
enthalpy Of solution is zero. Solutes that form nearly ideal solutions are Often simi-
lar in composition and structure tO the solvent molecules. For instance, methylben-
zene (toluene), C6H5CH3, forms nearly ideal solutions with benzene, C6H6. ReaI
solutions dO not Obey Raoult's law at all concentrations; however, the lower the
solute concentration, the more closely they resemble ideal solutions. Raoult's law is
another example Of a limiting law (Section 5 · 4), which in this case becomes increas-
ingly valid as the concentration Of the solute approaches zero. A solution that does
not Obey Raoult's law at a particular solute concentration is called a nonideal solu-
tion. Real solutions are approximately ideal at solute concentratlons below about
0 · 1 M fo r nonelectrolyte solutions and 0 · 01 M fo r electrolyte solutions. The greater
departure from ideality in electrolyte solutions arises from the interactions between
Electrolyte solutions, which have ionic
solutes, and nonelectrolyte solutions,
which have intact molecular solutes,

TH 《 N ℃ N G POINT Laws a re useful summaries 0f experience, but why a re limiting laws
useful?
The lowering Of the vapor pressure Of a solvent due tO the presence Of a solute
has a thermodynamic basis. We saw in Section 10 · 2 that, at equilibrium, and in the
absence of any solute, the molar Gibbs free energy of the vapor is equal to that of
the pure liquid solvent. ln an ideal solution, a solute increases the disorder and
therefore the entropy of the liquid phase: we can no longer be sure that a molecule
picked at random from the solution will be a solvent molecule. Because the entropy
of the liquid phase is raised by a solute but the enthalpy is left unchanged, overall
there is a decrease in the molar Gibbs free energy of the solvent. At equilibrium, the
molar Gibbs free energy of the vapor must equal that of the solvent. Because the
Gibbs free energy of the solvent has been lowered, fo r the two phases t0 remam in
equilibrium it follows that the Gibbs free energy of the vapor must be lower, too.
Because the Gibbs free energy 0f a gas depends on its pressure (recall Fig. 10 · 4 ）， it
follows that the vapor pressure alSO must be lower. ln other words, 乃 e p or p res 一
s 0 厂 e so e / 0 彬沅 e presence 0 厂 e so (FIG. 10 · 29 ） ·

10 ． 16 Boiling-Point Elevation and Freezing-Point Depression
Because the presence Of a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure Of the SOI-
vent, the boiling point Of the solvent rises. This increase is called boiling-point
elevation. The elevation Of the boiling point has the same origin as vapor-pressure
lowering and is also due to the effect of the solute on the entropy of the solvent.
shows how the molar Gibbs free energies of the liquid and

At low temperatures, Gm ～ Hm, and so the line representing Gm of the vapor
lies well above that fo r the liquid because the molar enthalpy of a vapor is
considerably greater than that of a liquid.
The slope of the line is 一 Sm the negative value of the molar entropy. Because
the molar entropy of the vapor is much greater than that of the liquid, the line
fo r the vapor slopes down more sharply than that of the liquid.

1 0 · 1 6 Boiling-P0int Elevation and Freezing-P0int Depression
Above the boiling point, the molar Gibbs free energy of the vapor phase is lower
than that of the liquid; therefore, the vapor is the more stable phase. We have already
seen that the presence Of a solute in the liquid phase Of the solvent increases the
entropy of the solvent and therefore （ through Gm = Hm 一 TSm again) lowers its
Gibbs free energy. As shown in Fig. 10 · 30b ， the lines representing the molar Gibbs
free energies Of the liquid solution and the vapor intersect at a higher temperature
than they do fo r the pure solvent, and so the boiling point is higher in the presence
Of the solute. The increase is usually quite small and is Of little practical importance
ln sclence. A 0 · 1 m aqueous sucrose solution, for instance, bOils at 100 · 05 OC.
Of broader practical significance is freezing-point depression, the lowering of
the freezing point Of the solvent caused by a solute. For example, seawater freezes
about 1 OC lower than fresh water. People living in regions with cold winters make
use of the depression of the freezing point when they spread salt on icy walkways
and roads. The salt lowers the freezing point Of water as it produces a salt solution.
ln the laboratory, chemists make use of the effect to judge the purity of a solid
compound: if impuritles are present, the compound's melting point is lower than
the accepted value. lt is commonly said that antifreeze added tO car engines IS an
example Of the lowenng Of freezing point; it is, but it is not a colligative effect, as
the concentration is far t00 high. lt is better to think of the ethylene glycol mole-
cules (HOCH2CH20H, the common active component) as lying between the water
molecules and preventing their linking together tO form 1Ce.
Figure 10 · 30a shows how the molar Gibbs free energies of the liquid and solid
phases 0f a pure solvent vary with temperature. The explanation of the layout of
the lines is similar tO that fO r a liquid and its vapor, but the differences in position
and slope are less pronounced:
At low temperatures, Gm ～ Hm, and so the line representing Gm of the liquid
lies above that fo r the solid (but not much above, because the enthalpies are
not as different as for a liquid and a vapor).
． Because the molar entropy of the liquid is greater than that of the solid, the line
for the liquid slopes down more sharply than that of the solid (but not much,
because the entromes are not as different as fO r a liquid and a vapor).
The solid is the more stable phase below the freezing point, where the molar
Gibbs free energy of the solid is lower than that of the liquid. The presence of a
solute in the liquid phase of the solvent raises the entropy of the solvent and hence
lowers its Gibbs free energy (FIG. 10 · 31 b). However, because the solute is insoluble
in the solid solvent, the Gibbs free energy of the solid phase of the solvent is
unchanged. The lines representing the molar Gibbs free energies of the liquid and
solid phases Of the solvent intersect at a lower temperature than they dO fO r the
pure solvent, and SO the freezing point is lower in the presence Of the solute.

acetate, fO r instance, allows water molecules tO pass through it, but not solute mol-

However, the level of the solution inside the tube begins tO nse as pure solvent
passes through the membrane intO the solution. At equilibrium, the pressure exerted
by the higher level of the column of solution is sufficiently great that the rate of flow
Of molecules through the membrane is the same in each direction, and SO the net
flow is zero. The pressure needed tO Stop the flow Of solvent is called the osmotic
pressure, II (the Greek uppercase letter (i). Th e greater the osmotic pressure, the
greater is the height Of the solution needed tO reduce the net flow tO zero.
Life depends on osmosis, which is the most important of all the colligative proper-
ties. Biological cell walls act as semipermeable membranes that allow water, small
molecules, and hydrated ions t0 pass (FIG. 10 · 33 ） · However, they block the passage 0f
the enzymes and proteins that have been synthesized within the cell. Th e higher con-
centration Of solutes within a cell compared tO th e solution outside the cell gives r1Se
tO an osmotic pressure, and water passes 1ntO the more concentrated solution in the
interior Of the cell, carrying small nutri e nt molecules with it. This influx Of water also
keeps the cell turgid (swollen) · When the water supply is cut off, th e turgidity is lost
and the cell becomes dehydrated. ln a plant, this dehydration results in wilting. Salted
meat is preserved 丘 OI 嗆 bacterial attack by osmosis. ln this case, the concentrated salt
solution dehydrates—and kills—the bacteria by causing water to flow o ut of them.
Because osmosls is a thermodynanuc property, we can expect it tO be related tO
the effect of the solute on the enthalpy and entropy of the solution: solvent flows
until the molar Gibbs free energy of the solvent is the same on each side of the
membrane. We have seen several times that a solute lowers the molar Gibbs free
energy 0f the solution below that of the pure solvent, and solvent therefore has a
tendency t0 pass into the solution (FIG. 10 · 34 ） ·

ln reverse osmosls, a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure iS applied tO
the solution side Of the semipermeable membrane. This application Of pressure
increases the rate at which solvent molecules leave the solution and thus reverses
the flow Of solvent, forcing it tO flow from the solution tO pure solvent. Reverse
osmosls IS used tO remove salts from seawater tO produce fresh water fO r drinking
and irrigation. The water is almost literally squeezed out Of the salt solution through
the membrane. The technological challenge is tO fabricate new membranes that are
strong enough to withstand high pressures and do not easily become clogged. Com-
mercial plants use cellulose acetate membranes at pressures as high as 70 atm.
