Binary Liquid Mixtures
The following thr e e sections Of this chapter examine hOW the vapor pressure varies
with composltlon when bOth components Of a mixture are volatile and how that
information can be used tO separate them by distillation. Distillation, which you first
encountered in 尹 d e / s ， Section G, is used tO separate the many compounds
that make up petroleum and tO purify alternative fuels such as ethanol and methanol.
10 ． 18 The Vapor Pressure of a Binary Liquid M ixtu re
Consider an ideal binary mixture of the volatile liquids A and B. We could think
of A as benzene, C6H6, and B as toluene (methylbenzene, C6H5CH3), fo r example,
because these tWO compounds have similar molecular structures and SO form
nearly ideal solutions. Because the mixture can be treated as ideal, each component
has a vapor pressure given by Raoult's law:
PA = XA(I)PA 、
PB = XB(I)PB"
ln these equations, XA(I) is the mole fraction of A in the liquid mixture and PA ：卜 is the
vapor pressure of pure A; similarly, XB(I) is the mole fraction of B in th e liquid and
PB* is the vapor pressure of pure B. According to Dalton's law (Section 5 · 8 ）， the total
pressure of the vapor, P, is the sum of these two partial pressures (FIG. 10 · 36 ）：
尸 = PA + PB = XA(I)PA* + XB(I)PB
Therefore, we can calculate the vapor pressure Of a mixture Of tWO volatile liquids
if we know their individual vapor pressures at the temperature Of interest and their
mole fractions in the mixture.

The normal boiling point of a binary liquid mixture is the temperature at which
the tOtal vapor pressure is equal tO 1 atm. If we were tO heat a sample Of pure
benzene at a constant pressure of 1 atm, it would boil at 80 · 1 OC. Similarly, pure
toluene bOils at 110 · 6 OC. Because, at a given temperature, the vapor pressure Of
a mixture Of benzene and toluene is intermediate between that Of toluene and
benzene, the boiling point Of the mixture will be intermediate between that Of the
tWO pure liquids. ln FIG. 10 · 38 ， which is called a temperature—composltion dia-

The process called fractional distillation uses a method Of continuous redis-
tillation tO separate mixtures Of liquids with similar boiling points, such as ben-
zene and toluene: the mixture is heated and the rising vapor passes up through a
tall column packed with material having a high surface area, such as glass beads
(FIG. 10 · 40 ） · The vapor begins t0 condense on the beads near the bottom of the
column. However, as heating contlnues, the vapor condenses and vaponzes over
and over again as it rises; the liquid drips back into the boiling mixture. The
vapor becomes richer in the component with the lower boiling pomt as it con-
tinues tO rise through the column and passes out intO the condenser. For exam-
ple, in the case Of benzene and toluene, the final distillate is nearly pure benzene,
the more volatile Of the components, whereas the liquid in the pot is nearly pure
toluene.

distillate that bOil in specific temperature ranges. Giant fractionating columns

10 ． 20 Azeotropes
Most liquid mixtures are not ideal, and SO their vapor pressures dO not follow
Raoult's law (FIG. 10 · 42 ） · ln these cases, the temperature—composition curves are
determined experimentally by analyzing the composition of the vapor (often,
after condensing it tO a liquid). Deviations from Raoult's law can be correlated
with the enthalpy of mixing, AHrmx, the enthalpy difference between the mixture
and the pure components. The enthalpy of mixing of ethanol and benzene is
posltive—the m1XIng process IS endothermic because the interactions between
ethanol and benzene molecules are less favorable than between each type 0f
molecule separately—and this mixture has a vapor pressure higher than that
predicted by Raoult's law (a positive deviation). The enthalpy of mixing of ace-
tone and chloroform IS negative—the mixmg process IS exothermic because the
interactions between acetone and chloroform molecules are stronger than those
between molecules Of chloroform or between molecules Of acetone—and this
mixture has a vapor pressure lower than that predicted by the law (a negative
deviation).
Some deviatlons from Raoult's law can make it impossible tO separate liquids
completely by distillation. The temperature—composition diagrams for mixtures
of ethanol and benzene and 0f acetone and chloroform show why. A positive

without change.'
deviation from Raoult's law means that the attractive forces between solute and
solvent are lower than those between the molecules Of the pure components. As
a result, the vapor pressure Of the mixture is higher and its boiling P01nt
is lower than that predicted by Raoult's law. For some pairs Of components,
the boiling point of the mixture is in fact lower than the boiling point of either
constituent (FIG. 10 · 43 ） · A mixture for which the lowest boiling temperature is
below that Of bOth pure components is called a mrmmum-boiling azeotrope, and
the components cannot be separated by distillation: in a fractional distillation, a
mixture with the azeotropic composition bOils over first, not the more volatile
pure liquid.
Th e opposite behavior is found for a mixture 0f acetone in chloroform (FIG. 10 · 44 ） ·
This maxrmum-boiling azeotrope bOils at a higher temperature than either constituent
and is the last fraction to be collected, not the less volatile of the pure liquids. Th e
reduction in vapor pressure results from th e fact that, although neither molecule can
form hydrogen bonds in the pure state, the partially positive hydrogen atom in the
highly polar chloroform molecule can form a hydrogen bond to th e partially negative
oxygen atom in the acetone molecule.

10 ． 21 CoIloids
A colloid is a dispersion of large particles (from 1 nm to 1 in diameter) in a
solvent. Colloidal particles are much larger than most molecules but are tOO small
tO be seen with an optical microscope. As a result, colloids have properties between
those Of a solution and those Of a heterogeneous mixture. The small particles give
the colloid a homogeneous appearance but are large enough t0 scatter light. The
light scattering explains why milk is white, not transparent, and why searchlight
and laser beams are more visible in fog, smoke, and clouds than in clear, dry air
(FIG. 10 · 45 ） · Many foods are colloids, as are clay particles, smoke, and the fluids
in living cells. Some self-assembling materials are colloids that form orderly struc-
tures spontaneously (see Box 16 · 2 ） ·
CoIIoids are classified according to th e phases of their components (TABLE 1 0 · 9 ） ·
A colloid that is a suspenslon of solids in a liquid is called a sol, and a suspension of
one liquid in another is called an emulsion. For example, muddy water is a SOI in
which tiny flakes Of clay are dispersed in water; mayonnalse IS an emulsion in which
small droplets Of water are suspended in vegetable Oil. Foam is a suspension Of a gas
ln a liquid or solid. Foam rubber, Styrofoam, soapsuds, and aerogels (insulating
ceramic foams that have densities nearly as IOW as that Of air, Section 7 · 11 ） are foams.
Zeolites (Section 15 · 15 ） are a tYP e of solid foam in which the openings in th e solid
are comparable in Size tO molecules.
A solid emulsion is a suspension of a liquid or solid phase in a solid. For
example, opals are solid emulsions formed when partly hydrated silica fills the
interstices between close-packed microspheres Of silica aggregates. Gelatin des-
serts are a type of solid emulsion called a gel, which is soft but holds its shape.
Photographic emulsions are gels that also contain solid colloidal particles of light-
sensitive materials such as silver bromide. Many liquid crystalline arrays can be
considered colloids. Cell membranes form a two-dimensional colloidal structure
(FIG. 10 · 46 ） ·
Aqueous colloids can be classified as hydrophilic or hydrophobic, depending on
the strength Of the molecular interactions between the suspended substance and
water. Suspensions Of fat in water (such as milk) and water in fat (such as mayon-
naise and hand lotions) are hydrophobic colloids, because fat molecules have little
attraction for water molecules. Gels and puddings are examples of hydrophilic col-
loids. The macromolecules of the proteins in gelatin and the starch in pudding have
many hydrophilic groups that attract water. The giant protein molecules in gelatin

===== 第 551 页 =====
10 · 22 Bio-Based and Biomimetic Materials
uncoil in hot water, and their numerous polar groups form hydrogen bonds with the
water. When the mixture COOIS, the protein chains link together again, but now they
have entwined tO form a three-dimensional web that encloses many water mole-
cules, as well as molecules of sugar, dye, and flavoring agents. The result is a gel: an
open network Of protein chains that holds the water in a flexible solid structure.
Clusters of metal atoms can form colloidal suspensions. CoIIoidal clusters of
copper, silver, and gold in glass are responsible fo r some of the vivid colors of
stained glass in medieval cathedrals (FIG. 10 · 47 ） · Even aqueous suspensions 0f
metal clusters are known (FIG. 10 · 48 ） ·
Many precipitates, such as Fe(OH)3, form initially as colloidal suspensions.
The tiny particles are kept from settling out by Brown1an motion, the motion Of
small particles resulting from constant bombardment by solvent molecules. The sol
is further stabilized by the adsorption of ions on the surfaces of the particles. The
IOIIS attract a layer Of water molecules that prevents the particles from adhering tO
one another.

10 ． 22 Bio-Based and Biomimetic Materials
Bi0-based materials are materials that are taken from or made from natural
materials in living things. Examples include packing pellets made from corn and
soybeans, polylactic acid (a polymer used to make plastic packaging), and various
kinds of pharmaceuticals.
One example of a colloidal bio-based pharmaceutical material is hyaluronic
acid （ 5 ） · This compound occurs naturally in the human body, where it is a major
component of the fluid that lubricates joints and plays an important role in the
repair Of tissues, especially in the skin. Because the molecules Of hyaluromc acid
contain many —OH groups, it can form hydrogen bonds to water and form a col-
loid. As a result, as it moves through the body, large numbers of water molecules
move with it. This property makes it useful in regions of the body that require
lubrication, such as ] omts, and in the healing Of wounds and connective tissue
(FIG. 10 · 49 ） · Hyaluronic acid is widely used in sports medicine to heal joint inj u-
ries by reducing inflammation. Because hyaluronlc acid is easily metabolized in
the stomach, it must be injected intO the region where it is needed.
Biom1met1c materials are materials that are modeled after naturally occur-
ring materials. Gels or flexible polymers (Chapter 20 ） modeled after natural
membranes and tissues are biomimetic materials With remarkable properties.
Some can be made tO crawl on their ()Nvvn like tiny nanometer worms, others
pulsate t0 an internally generated rhythm, and still others respond in seemingly
lifelike ways t0 stimuli.

layers of phospholipid molecules that line up with their hydrocarbon tails point-

face. This structure separates the contents Of the cell from the intercellular fluid.
lt is possible to coax phospholipids to form artificial membranes that close up t0

modified according t0 conditions in the body. For example,
the amount Of insulin that a nondiabetic person needs is

However, a diabetic person must take insulin at specified

above a certain concentration, the gel swells SO much that it
becomes porous, releasing insulin intO the blood.
H OW MIGHT YO U CONTRIBUTE?
Both basic and applied research are needed for effective drug
delivery systems. Basic research on the self-assembly of mol-
ecules may allOW more lnnovatlve solutions in the future.
Applied research may have more immediate benefits. For
example, the optimal drug delivery system must be designed
fo r each specific drug. Coatings for implants or nanospheres

MAJOR TECHNIQUE 4 Chromatography
ecause the scent Of a flower may be due tO hundreds
of different compounds, it is difficult for perfume
manufacturers tO duplicate floral scents. Establishing
the identities and relative amounts Of the components Of a
fragrance was actually impossible until the development of
chromatography. Related techniques are used in forensic
laboratories t0 match samples of fluids, by food manufactur-
ers tO test product quality, and tO search fO r evidence Of life
on other planets. AII these techniques depend on subtle dif-
ferences ln intermolecular forces tO separate compounds.
Solvent Extraction
If an aqueous solution Of a compound is shaken with another
liquid that is immiscible (mutually insoluble) with water,
some Of the compound may dissolve in the Other solvent. For
example, molecular iodine, 12, is very slightly soluble in
water but is highly soluble in tetrachloromethane, CC14,
which is immiscible with water. 、 When tetrachloromethane IS
added tO water containing iodine, most Of the iodine dis-
solves in the CC14. The solute is said to p 历 0 ” itself
between the tw O solvents. SO / e e 无 c 0 is used tO
obtain plant flavors and aromas from aqueous slurries Of the
plant that have been crushed in a blender.
ln some cases, the solids themselves are subjected tO
extraction by a solvent. For example, in one process used tO
decaffeinate coffee, the coffee beans are mixed with activated
charcoal and a high-pressure stream Of “ supercritical carbon
dioxide ” (carbon dioxide at high pressure and above its
critical temperature) is passed over them at approximately
90 OC. A supercritical solvent is a highly mobile fluid with a
very IOW vlscosity. The carbon dioxide removes the soluble
caffeine preferentially, without extracting the flavoring
agents, and evaporates without leaving a harmful residue.
Liquid Chromatography
ln the early part Of the twentieth century, the Russian botanist
M. S. Tsvet found a way t0 separate the many P1gments ln
flowers and leaves. He ground up the plant materials and dis-
solved the pigments, then poured the solution over th e top of
a vertical tube of ground chalk. Th e different pigments trick-
led through the chalk at different rates, producing colored
bands in the tube, inspiring the name 动酊 og p 乃（ "color
writing " ） · Th e separation occurred because the different pig-
ments were absorbed tO different extents by the chalk.
Chromatography is one of the most powerful and
Widely used means fO r separatlng mixtures, because lt iS
Often inexpensive and it can be used tO provide quantita-
tive as well as qualitative information. The simplest method
is paper chromatography. A drop of solution is placed near
the bottom edge of the s 0 ” 0 phase, an absorbent sup-
port, such as a strip of paper. The 0 历 phase, a fluid
solvent, is added below the spot and the solvent is absorbed
on the support. As the mobile phase rises up the stationary
phase by capillary action, the materials in the spot are
carried upward at a rate that depends on how strongly they
are adsorbed on (adhere (o) the stationary phase (Fig. 1 ） ·
The more strongly the solute is adsorbed on the stationary
phase, the longer it will take to travel up the support.

Gas Chromatography—Mass Spectrometry
Some detectors can give additional information about the elutes

CHEM ℃ AL EQUILIBRIA
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? The dynamic equilibrium toward which
every chemical reaction tends is such a n important aspect Of the study Of chemistry
that the next four chapters deal with it. You need tO know the composition Of a reaction
mixture at equilibrium because it tells you hOW much product tO expect. TO control the
yield Of a reaction, you need tO understand the thermodynamic basis Of equilibrium
and hOW the position Of equilibrium is affected by conditions such as temperature and
pressure. The response Of equilibria tO changes in conditions has considerable economic
and biological significance: the regulation of chemical equilibrium affects the yields of
products in industrial processes, and living cells struggle tO avoid sinking intO equilibrium.
What Are the Key ldeas? Reactions proceed until the composition Of a reaction
mixture corresponds tO minimum Gibbs free energy. This composition is described by
a n equilibrium constant that is characteristic Of the reaction. The equilibrium is dynamic
and responds tO changes in the conditions.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? The concepts of chemical equilibrium
a re related to those of physical equilibrium (Sections 10 · 1 一 10 · 3 ） · Because chemical
equilibrium depends O n the thermodynamics Of chemical reactions, you will need tO use
the Gibbs free energy 0f reaction (Section 9 · 1 3 ） and standard enthalpies of formation
(Section 8 · 1 7 ） · ChemicaI equilibrium calculations require a thorough knowledge of molar
concentration (Fundamentals, Section G), reaction stoichiometry (Fundamentals, Section
L) ， and the gas laws (Chapter 5 ） ·
arly in the twentieth century, the looming Pr0SPect of World War I created a
desperate need fO r nitrogen compounds, because mtrates normally used for
agriculture were being made intO explosives. Almost all the nitrates used for
fertilizers and explosives were quarried from deposits in Chile, and the limited
supply could not keep up with the demand. Moreover, shipping channels were
vulnerable to attack, which threatened to cut off the supply altogether. Although
nitrogen is abundant in air, the methods used at the time tO convert nitrogen intO
compounds were tOO costly tO employ on a large scale. Any nation that could
develop an economical process tO ' ' fix ” atmospheric nitrogen—that is, tO combine
it with Other elements—would have all the nitrogen compounds it needed.
Scientists on bOth sides Of the conflict were urgently seeking ways tO fix nitro-
gen. Finally, through determination, application, and—as so often happens in
research—a bit Of luck, the German chemist Fritz Haber, in collaboration with the
German chemical engineer Carl Bosch, found an economical way tO harvest the
nitrogen Of the air and tO provide an abundant source Of compounds fO r bOth agri-
culture and armaments.

And, we might add, to change th e

The metal actS as a catalyst for this

15 · 14 ） · Osmium is t00 expensive to be

One difficulty Haber faced is that the reactions used to produce compounds from
nitrogen dO not go tO completion, but appear tO Stop after only some Of the reactants
have been used up · At this point the mixture Of reactants and products has reached
chemical equilibrium, the Stage in a chemical reactlon when there is no further ten-
dency for the composition Of the reaction mixture—the concentrations or partial pres-
sures Of th e reactants and products—to change · TO achieve the greatest converslon Of
nitrogen intO its compounds, Haber had tO understand hOW a reaction approaches
and eventually reaches equilibrium and then use that knowledge—as we shall see in
Section 11 · 12—to improve th e yield by changing the conditions of the reaction.
Like physical equilibria, all chemical equilibria are dynamic, with the forward
and reverse reactions occurrmg at the same rate. ln Chapter 10 considered sev-
eral physical processes, including vaporizing and dissolving, that reach dynanmc
equilibrium. This chapter shows how to apply the same ideas to chemical changes.
lt also shows hOW tO use thermodynamics tO describe equilibria quantitatively,
which putS enormous power intO our hands—the power tO control the direction Of
a reaction and the yield of products. 、 We first show that a single quantity, the equi-
方 br / 7 CO S characterizes the composition Of a reaction mixture at equilib-
rium. Then we explore how the equilibrium constant arises from thermodynanmcs
and see hOW it is related tO the free energy Of the reaction. We then see hOW tO use
the equilibrium constant tO calculate the equilibrium composition Of a reaction
mixture. Finally, we develop thermodynamic arguments tO deduce hOW the compo-
sition Of a reactlon mixture at equilibrium responds tO changes in the conditions
under which the reaction is taking place.
Reactions at Equilibrium
TO say that chemical equilibrium is “ dynamlc " means that when a reaction has
reached equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions continue tO take place, but
with reactants being formed as fast as they are consumed. As a result, the compo-
sition Of the reactlon mixture remams constant. TO develop these ideas we first
establish that reactlons can take place in their reverse direction as soon as some
products have accumulated. Then we see hOW tO relate the equilibrium composi-
tion tO the thermodynamic properties Of the system.
11 ． 1 The ReversibiIity of Reactions
Some reactions, such as the explosive reaction Of hydrogen and oxygen, appear tO
proceed tO completion, but others seem tO Stop at an early Stage. For example,
consider the reaction that took place when Haber heated nitrogen and hydrogen
under pressure in the presence Of a small amount Of the metal osnuum:
N2(g) + 3 H2(g) 一 2 NH3(g)
The reaction does produce ammonia rapidly at first, but eventually the reaction
seems t0 stop (FIG. 1 1 · 1 ） · As the graph shows, no matter how long we wait, no
more product forms. The reaction has reached equilibrium.
Like phase changes, chemical reactions tend toward a dynanmc equilibrium ln
which, although there is no net change, the forward and reverse reactions are still
taking place, but at matching rates. What actually happens when the formation of
ammonia appears tO Stop is that the rate Of the reverse reaction,
2 NH3(g) 一 N2(g) + 3 H2(g)
(B)
lncreases as more ammoma iS formed. At equilibrium, the ammoma iS decompos-
ing as fast as it is being formed. Just as we did fO r phase transitions, we express
this state Of dynamic equilibrium by replacing the arrow in the equation with
equilibrium "harpoons"
N2(g) + 3 H2(g) 冖 2 NH3(g)

11 ． 3 The Thermodynamic Origin of Equilibrium Constants
Guldberg and Waage's description of equilibrium was entirely empirical. Now,
though, chemists know that th e law Of mass action is a consequence Of thermody-
nanucs and that the apparently mysterious form Of K arises from thermodynarmc
considerations and ultimately from the expression for the entropy Of mixing Of reac-
tants and products as the latter are formed. The Gibbs free energy Of a reaction
mixture depends on the entropies Of reactants and products and, hence, on their
partial pressures or concentrations. Therefore, the tendency Of a reaction tO go in the
forward or the reverse directlon iS determined by those pressures or concentratlons.
Every chemical reaction has a tendency tO proceed spontaneously toward equi-
librium, but the directlon Of reaction depends on the composition Of the reaction
mixture. At constant temperature and pressure:
． ln a reaction mixture that has not yet produced enough products tO reach
equilibrium, the spontaneous direction Of change is toward more products and
AG < 0 for the forward reaction.
． ln a reactlon m1Xture that has excess products, the revers e reactlon iS spontaneous
and AG > 0 fo r the forward reaction ()o that AG < 0 fo r the reverse reaction).
． For the reaction at equilibrium, there is no tendency fO r spontaneous change ln
either the forward or the reverse direction and AG = 0 ·

has become the equilibrium constant, K, Of the reaction. That is,
At equilibrium,
Thermodynamics has explained the puzzling form of K: it is a direct consequence of

and is simply th e value of Q when all the species have their equilibrium values.

11 ． 4 The Extent of Reaction
When AGro fO r a reaction is strongly negative, the reaction goes nearly tO comple-
tion before it reaches equilibrium and the equilibrium reaction mixture consists
mainly Of products. Because the concentrations or partial pressures Of products
appear in the numerator Of K and those Of reactants in the denominator, the
numerator will be large and the denominator small. Therefore, the value of K is
large. ln contrast, when AGr0 fO r a reaction is strongly positive, equilibrium is
reached after very little reaction has taken place, the numerator is small, and the
denominator is large; therefore, K is small.

11 ． 5 The Direction of Reaction
Now suppose that the system Of interest is not at equilibrium. For example, we
may be given the concentrations Of reactants and products fO r some arbitrary Stage
Of a reaction, but we want tO know whether it will produce more products or more
reactants as lt moves toward equilibrium. If we know the value Of K, we can cal-
culate the reaction quotient, Q, from the actual composition Of the reaction m1X-
ture and then compare Q with K.
If Q < K, AG is negative; the concentrations or partial pressures Of the products
are tOO IOW relative tO those Of the reactants for equilibrium. Hence, the reactlon
has a tendency tO proceed toward products.
If Q = K, AG is zero; the mixture has its equilibrium composition and has no
tendency tO change in either direction.
If Q > K, AG is positive; the reverse reaction is spontaneous and the products
tend tO decompose intO the reactants.
ThiS pattern IS summarized in
FIG. 11 · 6 ·
The same pattern is seen when we plOt the Gibbs free energy Of a reaction m1X-
ture against its changing composition, as we did in Fig. 11 · 4 · Reaction tends tO
proceed toward the composition at the lowest point Of the curve, because that is the
direction Of decreasing Gibbs free energy. The composition at the lowest point Of
the curve—the point Of mirumum Gibbs free energy—corresponds tO equilibrium.
For a system at equilibrium, any change would lead tO a reaction mixture with a
greater Gibbs free energy, and SO neither the forward nor the reverse reactlon IS
spontaneous. When the 1 嗆 illll 嗆 um value Of the Gibbs free energy lies very close tO pure
products, the equilibrium composition strongly favors products and "goes tO com-
pletion" (FIG. 1 1.7a). When the Gibbs free-energy minimum lies very close to the
pure reactants, the equilibrium composition strongly favors the reactants and the
reaction "does not go" (Fig. 11 · 7b ） ·
Whether a reaction is spontaneous depends on the

AGr0 rather than that it is spontaneous. However, fO r reactlons with very
large equilibrium constants, it is very unlikely that the mixture Of reagents
prepared in the laboratory will correspond tO Q > K, and it is common tO
refer tO such reactions as ' spontaneous.

11 ． 8 Using Equilibrium Constants
The equilibrium constant Of a reaction contains information about the equilibrium
composition at the given temperature. However, ln many cases, we know only the
initial composition Of the reaction mixture and need tO predict the equilibrium
composition. If we know the value Of K, the equilibrium composition can usually
be inferred by using the reaction stoichiometry. The easlest way tO proceed is tO
draw up an equilibrium table, a table showing the initial composition, the changes
needed tO reach equilibrium in terms Of some unknown quantity 无， and the final
equilibrium composition. The procedure is summarized in TooIbox 11 · 1 and illus-
trated in the examples that follow.

The Response of Equilibria
tO Changes in Conditions
Because chemical equilibria are dynamic, they respond tO changes in the conditions
under which a reaction is taking place. 、 When we disturb an equilibrium by adding
or removing a reactant, the value Of AG is changed and the composition shifts until
AG = 0 again. The composition also might change in response to a change in pres-
sure or temperature. ln the following sections, we shall see how Haber used this
responsiveness tO control the equilibrium between ammoma, nitrogen, and hydro-
gen tO increase the production Of ammoma.
We can predict how the composition Of a reaction mixture at equilibrium tends
to change when the conditions are changed by following the general principle iden-
tified by the French chemist Henri Le ChateIier (FIG. 1 1 · 9 ）：
Le Chatelier's prmciple: When a stress IS applied t0 a system in dynanuc eqtll-
librium, the equilibrium tends tO adjust tO minimize the effect Of the stress.
This empirical principle is no more than a rule Of thumb. lt provides neither an
explanation nor a quantitative prediction. However, we shall see that it is consls-
tent with thermodynanmcs; and, as we develop it, we shall see the powerful q ” 一
e conclusions that can be drawn from thermodynamlcs.
11 ． 9 Adding and Removing Reagents
We start by considering changes in the composition Of a system. Let's suppose that
the ammonia synthesis reaction (reaction C) has reached equilibrium. NOW sup-
pose that we pump in more hydrogen gas. According to Le Chatelier's principle,
the increase in the concentratlon Of hydrogen molecules will tend tO be minlmized
by the reaction of hydrogen with nitrogen. As a result, additional ammonia will
be formed. I f, instead Of hydrogen, we were tO add some ammonia, then the reac-
tion would tend instead tO form reactants at the expense Of the added ammonia
(FIG. 11 · 10 ） ·
TH 《 N ℃ N G POINT Suppose one of the products of a reaction at equilibrium is a pure
solid. H ow will the equilibrium be affected if s o m e of the solid is
removed? 阡 the solid is removed?
We can explain these responses thermodynamically by considering the relative
sizes Of Q and K (FIG. 1 1 · 11 ） · When reactants are added, the reaction quotient Q
falls below K, because the reactant concentrations in the denommator Of Q increase.
As we have seen, when Q < K, the reaction mixture responds by forming products
until Q is restored to K. Likewise, when products are added, Q rises above K,
because products appear in the numerator. Then, because Q > K, the reaction 1 嗆 IX 一
ture responds by forming reactants at the expense Of products until Q = K again.
lt is important tO understand that K is a constant that is not altered by changing
concentrations. Only the value Of Q changes, and always in a way that brings its
value closer tO that of K.

Le Chatelier's principle suggests a good way Of ensuring that a reaction goes
on generating a substance: simply remove products as they are formed. ln its
continuing hunt for equilibrium, the reaction generates more product. lndustrial

11 ． 12 Catalysts and Haber's Achievement
A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate Of a chemical reaction without being
consumed itself. We shall see a lOt more Of catalysts later, when we consider reaction
rates in Chapter 15 · However, it is important tO be aware at this Stage that a catalyst
has no effect on the equilibrium composition Of a reaction mixture · A catalyst can
speed up the rate at which a reaction reaches equilibrium, but it does not affect the
composition at equilibrium. lt actS by providing a faster route tO the same destination.

A catalyst speeds up bOth the forward and the reverse reactions tO the same
extent. Therefore, the dynamic equilibrium IS unaffected. The thermodynamic JI-IS-
tification Of this observation is based on the fact that the equilibrium constant
depends only on the temperature and the value of AGr0. A standard Gibbs free
energy Of reaction depends only on the identities Of the reactants and products and
is independent Of the rate Of the reaction or the presence Of any substances that dO
not appear in the overall chemical equation fO r the reaction. The fact that a catalyst
IS present tO provide a different route between reactants and products has no effect
on the value of AGr0 and therefore no effect on the value of K.
We have seen how Haber's understanding of chemical equilibrium enabled him
t0 increase the yield of ammonia (FIG. 1 1 · 16 ） · He realized that he had t0 compress
the gases and remove the ammonla as it was formed. AS have seen, compression
shifts the equilibrium composition in favor Of ammonia, which increases the yield of
product. Removing the ammonia also encourages more tO be formed. ln addition,
Haber realized that he should run the reaction at as IOW a temperature as possible:
IOW temperature favors the formation Of product, because the reaction is exothermic.
However, nitrogen and hydrogen combine tOO slowly at IOW temperatures, and SO
Haber solved this problem by developing an appropriate catalyst ()e used osmium
and later uranium) · Th e process was brought tO an industrial scale by the chemical
engmeer Carl Bosch, whO identified a cheaper catalyst (iron) and overcame the enor-
mous problems of working at high pressure, which makes even hydrogen corrosive.

accounts for almost the entire annual production Of about 1 · 6 × 1010 kg Of ammoma

11 ． 13 Homeostasis
Because a living being is not a closed system, true equilibrium in living systems can
be reached only fO r very fast reactions such as those between acids and bases. ln
general, however, our bodies maintain nearly constant values Of properties such as
temperature and levels Of certain chemicals in the blood. A beneficial environment
in the bOdy is maintained through the process Of homeostasis, the maintenance Of
constant lnternal conditions. HomeostaSIS IS not a true equilibrium, because there
are usually slight variations above and below the desired point. However, it
responds tO changes ln conditions in the same way as a system in chemical equl-
librium and so is governed by Le Chatelier's principle.
An important homeostatic biological process that involves chemical equilibria
is the transport of oxygen. Most of the oxygen in the blood is carried by hemoglo-
bin (Hb). When blood flows through lung tissues, about 98 ％ of the hemoglobin
molecules pick up oxygen molecules and a small amount of additional oxygen sim-
ply dissolves in the blood plasma (the solution in which blood cells are suspended).
However, when blood enters the small blood vessels called capillaries ln muscle tis-
sue far from the lungs, the hemoglobin molecules are surrounded by tissues that are
depleted in oxygen and the level of oxygen in blood plasma drops. The equilibrium
Hb(aq) + 02(aq) 冖
Hb02(aq)
is shifted toward reactants as some Of the hemoglobin molecules release their OXY-
gen molecules tO re-establish the equilibrium compositions. When a person IS
exercising heavily, muscles use an additional mechanism tO encourage the hemo-
glObin molecules tO release oxygen in the muscle tissue. Hydrogen ions from acids
can cause the oxygen molecules in hemoglobin tO be released; SO, when lactic acid
is produced by working muscle tissue, additional oxygen molecules are released
from the hemoglobin.
FIGURE 1 1 · 18 shows how 02 uptake by hemoglobin and myoglobin (Mb), the
oxygen storage protein, vanes with the partial pressure 0f oxygen. The shape of the
Hb saturation curve means that Hb can load 02 almost as fully in the lungs as Mb,

===== 第 597 页 =====
Exercises
455
and unload it more completely than Mb in different regions of the organism. ln the
lungs, where Po
105 Torr, 98 ％ of the Hb molecules have taken up 02, resulting
in almost complete saturation. ln resting muscular tissue, the concentration Of 02
corresponds to a partial pressure of about 40 Torr, at which value 75 ％ of the Hb
molecules are saturated with oxygen. This figure implies that sufficient oxygen is
still available should a sudden surge of activity take place. If the local partial pres-
sure falls to 20 Torr, the fraction of Hb molecules saturated falls to about 10 ％ ·
Note that the steepest part of the curve falls in the range 0f typical tissue oxygen
partial pressure. Myoglobin, on the other hand, begins to release 02 only when Po
has fallen below about 20 Torr, and SO it actS as a reserve tO be drawn on only when
the Hb oxygen has been used up.
Overloading the body's coping mechanisms can lead tO failure tO maintain
homeostasis. The result can be sudden and even fatal illness. Mountain climbers
encounter low oxygen conditions at high altitudes and, if they climb vigorously,
their lungs may not be able tO provide sufficient oxygen tO maintain homeostasls.
For this reason, mountain climbers spend some time in high-altitude base camps
before climbing, so that their bodies can adjust by producing more hemoglobin
molecules.

ACIDS AND BASES
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? Chapter 1 1 developed the concepts
Of chemical equilibria in gaseous systems; this chapter extends those ideas tO aqueous
systems, which a re important throughout chemistry and biology. EquiIibria between
acids, bases, and water i n plant and animal cells a re vital fO r the survival Of individual
organisms. TO sustain human societies and protect O u r ecosystems, you alSO need these
ideas tO understand the acidity Of rain, natural waters such as lakes and rivers, and
municipal water supplies.
What Are the Key ldeas? Brønsted acids a re proton donors; Brønsted bases a re
proton acceptors. The composition Of a solution Of a n acid O r base immediately adj usts
tO satisfy the values Of the equilibrium constants fO r all the proton transfer reactions
taking place.
What Do Yo u Need to Know Already? This chapter builds o n the introduction
tO acids and bases i n Fundamentals, Section J · lt also extends the principles Of
thermodynamics (Chapters 8 and 9 ） and chemical equilibrium (Chapter 1 1 ） to aqueous
systems. To a lesser extent, it uses the con cepts of hydrogen bonding (Section 6 · 5),
bond polarity (Section 3 · 12 ）， and bond strength (Sections 3 · 1 4 and 3 · 1 5 ） ·
WO Of the most important classes Of compounds in the whole Of chemistry
are the acids and bases. They are involved in huge numbers Of reactlons, lll
laboratory synthetic and analytical procedures, in industry, and in living
organisms. lt is not much Of an exaggeration tO say that most Of the processes that
go on inside our bodies are the reactlons Of acids and bases; one could take the
view that life is one long titration.
ln this chapter, we see what acids and bases are and why they vary in strength.
We shall use thermodynamics, particularly equilibrium constants, tO describe the
strengths 0f acids and bases quantitatively and thereby develop our insight into
their behavior. We then use our knowledge of equilibria involving acids and bases
tO examme systems in which more than one equilibrium is taking place simultane-
ously, as occurs ln many natural systems Of ecological and biological importance.
The Nature of Acids and Bases
When chemists see a pattern in the reactions Of certain substances, they formulate
a definition Of a class Of substance that captures the pattern. Then, by identifying
a substance as belonging t0 that class, they immediately know a great deal about
its behavior. Classification Of this kind opens the door tO understanding and
reduces the need tO memorize the properties Of individual substances. The reac-
tions Of the substances we call "acids ” and "bases ” are an excellent illustration Of
The Nature of Acids and Bases

12 ． 1 Brønsted—Lowry Acids and Bases
ln 1923 ， the Danish chemist J0hannes Brønsted proposed that
An acid iS a proton donor.
A base is a proton acceptor.
The term p 了 0 0 in these definitions refers tO the hydrogen ion, H+. An acid is a
species containing an acidic hydrogen atom, which is a hydrogen atom that can be
transferred as itS nucleus, a proton, tO another species acting as a base. same
definitions were proposed independently by the English chemist Thomas Lowry,
and the theory based on them is called the Brønsted—Lowry theory of acids and
bases. A proton donor IS commonly referred tO as a Brønsted acid and a proton
acceptor as a Brønsted base. Whenever we refer tO an ” or a ” in this
chapter, we shall mean a Brønsted acid or a Brønsted base.
A substance can act as an acid only if a base is present tO accept its acidic pro-
tons. An acid does not simply release its acidic proton; the proton is s 了 e 磊 tO
the base through direct contact. For example, HCI is a Brønsted acid. ln the gas
phase, an HCl molecule remams intact. However, when HCl dissolves ln water,
each HCI molecule immediately transfers an H+ ion to a neighboring H20 mole-
cule, which here is acting as a base (FIG. 12 · 1 ） · This process is a proton transfer
reactlon, a reactlon lll which a proton IS transferred from one species tO another.
We say that the HCI molecule becomes deprotonated:
HCl(aq) + H20(l) 一 H30+(aq) + cl-(aq)
Because at equilibrium virtually all the HCI molecules have donated their protons
tO water, HCI is classified as a s 0 g · The proton transfer reaction essentially
goes t0 completion. The H30+ ion called the 乃， ” 忉 ” · lt is strongly
hydrated in solution, and there is some evidence that a better representation Of the
species is H904+ ()r even larger clusters Of water molecules attached tO a proton).
A hydrogen ion ln water is sometimes represented as H (aq), but we must remem-
ber that H+ does not exist by itself in water and that H30+ is a better representa-
tion because it indicates that a Brønsted base (H20) has accepted a proton.
Another example of an acid is hydrogen cyanide, HCN, which transfers its
proton tO water when it dissolves tO form the solution known as hydrocyamc acid,
HCN(aq). However, only a small fraction of the HCN molecules donate their pro-
tons, and SO, as described in 尹 e / s ， Section J, we classify HCN as a 彬 e
C in water. The proton transfer reaction iS written as an equilibrium:
H30+(aq) + CN-(aq)
HCN(aq) + H20(l)
Like all chemical equilibria, this equilibrium is dynamic and we should think of pro-
tons as ceaselessly exchanging between HCN and H20 molecules, with a constant but
IOW concentration Of CN¯ and H30 ions. The proton transfer reaction Of a strong
acid such as HCI in water is also dynamic, but the equilibrium lies so strongly in favor
Of products that we represent it Just by its forward reaction, with a single arrow.
ln 尹 e / s ， Section J, we saw that an Arrhenius acid is a compound that
produces hydronium ions in water and an Arrhenius base iS a compound that produces
hydroxide ions ln water. The Brønsted definition is more general because it includes the
possibility th at an ion is an acid ()n option not allowed by the Arrhenius definition) ·
For instance, a hydrogen carbonate ion, HC03 ， one Of th e species present in natural
waters, can act as an acid and donate a proton t0 an H20 molecule (FIG. 12 · 2 ）：
H30+(aq) + C032-(aq)
HC03-(aq) + H20(l)

ln the Brønsted—Lowry theory, the strength of an acid depends on the extent to
which it donates protons tO the solvent. 、 We can therefore summarize the distinction
between strong and weak acids as follows:
Almost all the molecules Of a strong acid are deprotonated in solution.
Only a small fraction of the molecules or ions of a we ak acid are deprotonated
lll solution.
The strength Of an acid depends on the solvent, and an acid that is strong in
water may be weak in another solvent or V1ce versa (see Section 12 · 8 ） · However,
because almost all reactions in living tissues and most reactions in laboratories take
place in water, unless otherwise specified, the solvent in this chapter is water.
A Brønsted base possesses a lone pair Of electrons tO which a proton can bond.
For example, an oxide ion is a Brønsted base. Wh e n CaO dissolves in water, the
strong electric field of the small, highly charged 02- ion pulls a proton out of and
away from a neighboring H20 molecule (FIG. 12 · 3 ） · ln the process, a coordinate
covalent bond forms between the proton and a lone pair Of electrons on the oxide
ion. By accepting a proton, the oxide ion has become protonated. Every oxide ion
present accepts a proton from water, and SO O 一 is an example Of a s 0 g base in
water, a species that is fully protonated. That is, the following reaction goes essen-
tially to completion:
02- (aq) + H20(l) 一 2 0H-(aq)
Another example Of a Brønsted base is ammonia. When an NH3 molecule is pres-
ent in water, the lone pair Of electrons on the N atom accepts a proton from H20:
NH4+(aq) + 0H-(aq)
NH3(aq) + H20(l)
The fact that the NH3 molecule is electrically neutral means that it has much less
proton-pulling power than the oxide ion. As a result, only a very small proportion of
the NH 3 molecules are converted into NH4 + ions (FIG. 12 · 4 ） · Ammoma is therefore a
彬 e base. AII amines, organic derivatives Of ammonia, such as methylamine, CH3NH2,
are weak bases lll water. Because the proton transfer equilibrium lll an aqueous SOlu-
tlon Of ammoma is dynanmc, we should imagine the protons as ceaselessly exchanging
between NH3 and H20 molecules with a constant, very IOW concentratlon Of NH4
and OH- ions. The proton transfer to the strong base O 一 is also dynamic, but the
equilibrium lies SO strongly in favor Of products that, as fO r a strong acid, we represent
it just by its forward reactlon with a single arrow.
We can summarize the distinction between strong and weak bases as follows:
All the molecules or lons Of a strong base are protonated in solution.
Only a small fraction Of the molecules or lons Of a weak base are protonated
ln solution.
As fO r acids, the strength Of a base depends on the solvent: a base that is strong in

12 ． 2 Lewis Acids and Bases
The Brønsted—Lowry theory focuses on the transfer Of a proton from one species
tO another. However, the concepts Of acids and bases have a much wider signifi-
cance than the transfer Of protons. Even more substances can be classified as acids
or bases under the definitions developed by G. N. Lewis:
A Lewis acid iS an electron pair acceptor.
A Lewis base iS an electron pair donor.
When a Lewis base donates an electron pair tO a Lewis acid, the tWO species share
the pair and become J0ined by a coordinate covalent bond. A proton (H+) is an
electron palr acceptor. lt is therefore a Lewis acid because lt can attach tO
（ "accept" ） a lone pair Of electrons on a Lewis base. ln Other words, a Brønsted acid
IS a supp lier Of one particular Lewis acid, a proton.
The Lewis theory is more general than the Brønsted—Lowry theory. For instance,
metal atoms and ions can act as Lewis acids, as in the formation Of Ni(CO)4 from
nickel atoms (the Lewis acid) and carbon monoxide (the Lewis base), but they are
not Brønsted acids. Likewise, a Brønsted base is a special kind Of Lewis base, one
that can use a lone pair Of electrons tO form a coordinate covalent bond tO a proton.
For instance, an OXide ion iS a Lewis base. lt forms a coordinate covalent bond tO a
proton, a Lewis acid, by supplying both electrons for the bond:
The curved arrows show the direction in which a pair Of bonding electrons moves.
Similarly, when the Lewis base ammonia, NH3 ， dissolves ln water, some Of the
molecules accept protons from water molecules:
H H
The Lewis definition of a base is broader than the Brønsted definition. That is,
although every Brønsted base is a Lewis base, not every Lewis base is a Brønsted
base. For instance, carbon monoxide iS an lmportant Lewis base in 1tS reactlons
with metals, but it is not a Brønsted base because it does not accept protons.
Th e entities that are regarded as acids and bases are

12 ． 4 Proton Exchange Between Water MoIecuIes
An important implication Of the Brønsted definitions Of acids and bases is that the
same substance may be able tO function as bOth an acid and a base. For example,
we have seen that a water molecule accepts a proton from an acid molecule （ such
as HCI or HCN) to form an H30+ ion. So water is a base. However, a water mol-
ecule can donate a proton to a base (such as 02- or NH3 ） and become an OH
ion. SO water is also an acid. We describe water as amphiprotic, meaning that an
H20 molecule can act bOth as a proton donor and as a proton acceptor.

Weak Acids and Bases
Solutions Of different acids having the same concentration might not have the same
pH. For instance, the pH of 0 · 10 M CH3COOH(aq) is close to 3 ， but that of
0 · 10 M HCl(aq) is close to 1 · We have to conclude that the concentration of H30
ions in 0 · 10 M CH3COOH(aq) is / 0 彬 than that in 0 · 10 M HCl(aq). Similarly, the
concentration of OH- ions is found to be lower in 0 · 10 M NH3(aq) than in 0 · 10 M
NaOH(aq). The explanation must be that, in water, CH3COOH is not fully depro-
tonated and NH 3 is not fully protonated. That is, acetic acid and ammonia are,
respectively, a weak acid and a weak base. The incomplete deprotonation Of
CH3COOH explains why solutions of HCI and CH3COOH having the same
molarity react with a metal at different rates (FIG. 12 · 14 ） ·
Most acids and bases that exist in nature are weak. For example, the natural
acidity of river water is generally due to the presence of carbonic acid (H2C03,
from dissolved C02), hydrogen phosphate ions, HP042-, dihydrogen phosphate
ions, H2P04- (from fertilizer runoff) ， and other carboxylic acids arising from the
degradation of plant tissues, and all those acids are weak. Similarly, most naturally
occurring bases are weak. Some arise from the decomposition ()n the absence Of
air) of compounds containing nitrogen. For example, the odor of dead fish is due
tO ammes, which are weak bases.
ln this part Of the chapter, we develop a quantitative measure Of the strengths
Of weak acids and bases. We then use this information tO explore hOW acid strength
is related tO molecular structure.

12 ． 8 The Conjugate Seesaw
Hydrochloric acid is classified as a strong acid because it is fully deprotonated in
water. lt follows that its COIIJ ugate base, CI¯, must be a very, very weak proton
acceptor (weaker, in fact, than H20). Conversely, acetic acid is a weak acid. lts
conJ ugate base, the acetate ion, CH3C02 ， must be a relatively good proton accep-
tor, because it readily forms CH3COOH molecules in water. Similarly, because
methylamine, CH3NH2, is a stronger base than ammonia (see TabIe 12 · 2 ）， the
conjugate acid of methylamine—the methylammonium ion, CH3NH3 —must be a
weaker proton donor (and therefore a weaker acid) than NH4 + · ln general:
． the stronger the acid, the weaker is 1tS conJ ugate base; and
． the stronger the base, the weaker is its conjugate acid.
TO express the relative strengths Of an acid and its conJ ugate base (a "conju-
gate acid—base pair" ）， we consider the special case Of the ammonia proton transfer
equilibrium, reaction C, fO r which the basicity constant was glven earlier (Kb
[NH4+][OH-]/[NH3]). The proton transfer equilibrium of ammonia's conjugate
acid, ， in water iS
NH4+ (aq) + H20(l) H30+(aq) + NH3(aq) Ka

Equation 11—in either form—confirms the seesaw relation between the strengths
of acids and of their conJ ugate bases. Equation 11a tells us that if an acid has a
large Ka, then its conJugate base must have a small Kb. Similarly, if a base has a large
Kb, then its conjugate acid must have a small Ka · Equation 11b tells us that if the
p Ka of an acid is large, then the pKb of its conjugate base is small, and vice versa.
ThiS reclprocal relation IS summarized in
FIG. 12 · 17 and TABLE 12 · 3 · For example,
because pKb fo r ammonia in water is 4 · 75 ， the pKa of NH4 + is
pKa = pKw 一 p Kb = 14 · 00 一 4 · 75 = 9 · 25
This value shows that NH4 + is a weaker acid than boric acid (pKa = 9 · 14 ） but
stronger than hydrocyanic acid (HCN, p Ka = 9 · 31 ） · Consequently, as we shall
verify in Section 12 · 13 ， solutions Of ammonium salts such as NH4 Cl are acidic.
Although the proton transfer in a solution Of a strong acid is actually an equi-
librium, the proton-donating power Of a strong acid, HA, is SO much greater than
that of H30+ that proton transfer tO water effectively goes tO completion. As a
result, the solution contains only H30 ions and A¯ ions; there are virtually no HA
molecules left. ln other words, the only acid speues present in an aqueous solution
of a strong acid, other than the H20 molecules, is the H30 ion. Because all strong
acids in water behave as though they were solutions of the acid H30+, we say that
strong acids are leveled in water tO the strength Of the acid H30

12 ． 9 MoIecuIar Structure and Acid Strength
Chemists commonly interpret trends in the properties Of compounds by consider-
ing the structures Of their molecules. However, there are tW O reasons why the rela-
tive strengths of acids and bases are difficult to predict. First, Ka and Kb are equi-
librium constants, and so they are related to the Gibbs free energy 0f the proton
transfer reaction. Their values therefore depend on considerations Of entropy as
well as energy. Second, the solvent plays a significant role in proton transfer reac-
tions, and SO we cannot expect tO relate acid strength solely tO the acid molecule
itself. However, although absolute values are difficult to predict, we can look fo r
trends among series Of compounds With similar structures and in the same solvent
(normally water ） · Because acid strength in aqueous solutions depends on the breaking

12 ． 10 The Strengths of Oxoacids and CarboxyIic Acids
We can learn more about the effect Of structure on acidity by considering the OXO-
acids. These acids form structurally related families, and SO we can examine the
effect of different central atoms with the same number of O atoms ()s in HC103
and HBr03). Alternatively, we can look at the influence of different numbers of O
atoms attached to the same central atom ()s in HC103 and HC104).
The high polarity of the O —H bond is one reason why the proton of an —OH
group in an oxoacid molecule is acidic. For example, phosphorous acid, H3P03,
has the structure (HO)2PHO （ 1 ）： it can donate the protons from its tw o —OH
groups but not the proton attached directly to the phosphorus atom. The difference
in behavior can be traced to the much lower electronegativity of phosphorus （ 2 · 2 ）
relative to that 0f oxygen （ 3 · 4 ） · ln nearly all common inorganic oxoacids, however,
all the hydrogen atoms are attached to oxygen atoms.
Let's consider a family Of oxoacids in which the number of O atoms is con-
stant, as in the hypohalous acids HCIO, HBrO, and HIO. By referring t0
TABLE 12 · 5
we see that e grea 了 e e / ec 0 eg 忉 / 0 0 厂 e 乃 / 0 & e 仫乃 e stronger 乃 e 0 无 0 一
法 A partial explanation of this trend is that electrons are withdrawn slightly
from the O —H bond as the electronegativity of the halogen increases. As these
bonding electrons move toward the central atom, the O —H bond becomes more
polar, and so the molecule becomes a stronger acid. The high electronegativity of a
halogen atom also weakens the ugate base by making the electrons in the mol-
ecule less accessible tO an lncommg proton.

The effect of the number of O atoms on the strengths of organic acids is
similar. For example, we have seen （尹 d e / s ， Section D) that alcohols are
organic compounds in which an —OH group is attached tO a carbon atom, as
in ethanol （ 2 ） · Carboxylic acids, on the other hand, have two O atoms attached
tO the same carbon atom: one IS a doubly bonded terminal O atom and the
other is the O atom of an —OH group, a s in acetic acid （ 3 ） · Although carboxylic
acids are weak acids, they are much stronger acids than alcohols, partly as a
result Of the electron-withdrawing power Of the second O atom. ln fact, alco-
hols have such weak proton-donating power that usually they are not regarded
as oxoacids.
The strength Of a carboxylic acid is also increased relative tO that Of an alcohol
by electron delocalization in the conj ugate base. The second O atom Of the car-
boxyl group, —COOH, provides an additional electronegative atom over which the
negative charge Of the conJugate base can spread. This electron delocalization Sta-
bilizes the carboxylate anion, —C02- （ 4 ） · Moreover, because the charge is spread
over several atoms, it is less effective at attracting a proton. A carboxylate ion IS
therefore a much weaker base than the conjugate base of an alcohol (for example,
the ethoxide ion, CH3CH20-).
The formula Of a carboxylic acid is written

RCOOH, because the tw o O atoms are distinct (one is part of an OH group);
the formula Of a carboxylate ion, however, is written RC02¯ because the tWO
O atoms are equivalent.
0
The strengths 0f carboxylic acids also vary with the total electron-withdrawing
power of the atoms bonded to the carboxyl group. Because hydrogen is less electro-
negative than chlorine （ 2 · 2 and 3 · 2 ， respectively), the —CH3 group bonded to
—COOH in acetlc acid is less electron withdrawing than the —CC13 group in tri-
chloroacetic acid. Therefore, we expect CC13COOH to be a stronger acid than
CH3COOH. ln agreement with this prediction, the p Ka of acetic acid is 4 · 75 ，
whereas that Of trichloroacetic acid is 0 · 52 ·

12 ． 13 The pH of Salt Solutions
We saw in 尹 d e / s ， Section J, that a salt is produced by the neutralization Of
an acid by a base. However, if we measure the pH Of a solution Of a salt, we dO
not in general find the “ neutral ” value ()H = 7 ） · For instance, if we neutralize

acetate has pH = 9 · 0 · How can this be? The Brønsted—Lowry theory provides the
explanation. According tO this theory, an ion may be an acid or a base. The acetate
ion, fO r instance, iS a base, and the ammonlum IOII IS an acid. pH Of a solution
Of a salt depends on the relative acidity and basicity Of its ions.

weakens the O —H bonds and allows one or more hydrogen ions to be lost from
the water molecules. SmaII, highly charged cations exert the greatest pull on the

Cations of Group 1 and 2 metals, as well as those of charge + 1 from other
groups, are such weak Lewis acids that the hydrated ions dO not act as acids.
These metal cations are tOO large or have tOO IOW a charge tO have an appreciable
polarizing effect on the hydrating water molecules that surround them, and SO the
water molecules dO not readily release their protons. These cations are sometlmes
called “ neutral cations," because they have so little effect on the pH.
Notice that no cations are basic. Cations cannot readily accept protons, because
the positive charge Of the cation repels the positive charge Of the incoming protons.
Very few anlons that contain hydrogen produce acidic solutions.
lt is difficult fo r a positively charged proton to leave a negatively charged anion.
The few anions that do act as acids include H2P04- and HS04

P01yprotic Acids and Bases
A polyprotlc acid is a compound that can donate more than one proton. Many
common acids are polyprotic, including sulfuric acid, H2S04, and carbonic acid,
H2C03, each of which can donate tw o protons, and phosphoric acid, H3P04
which can donate three protons. Polyprotic acids play a critical role in biological
systems, because many enzymes can be regarded as polyprotic acids that carry out
their vital functions by donating one proton after another. A polyprotic base is a
species that can accept more than one proton. Examples include the C03 _ and
S03 一 anions, both of which can accept two protons, and the P04 一 anion, which
can accept three protons.
A polyprotic acid is viewed as donating its protons a successlon Of depro-
tonation Steps. For example, a carbonic acid molecule can lose one proton tO form
HC03 ， and then that ion can donate the remalmng proton to form C03 · We

AQUEOUS EQUILIBRIA
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? The techniques described in this
chapter provide the tOOls that you need tO analyze and control the concentrations
Of ions i n solution. Many reactions a re carried out i n solution, and SO this material iS
fundamental tO understanding chemistry. The ionic compounds released intO waterways
by individuals, industry, and agriculture ca n impair the quality 0f water supplies.
However, these hazardous ions can be identified and removed if the right reagents a re
added. Aqueous equilibria govern the stabilization of the pH in blood, seawater, and
Other solutions encountered in biology, medicine, and the environment.
What Are the Key ldeas? The concentrations of dissolved ions satisfy the equilibrium
constants fo r the reactions in which they participate.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? This chapter develops the ideas in Chapters
1 1 and 1 2 and applies them t0 equilibria involving ions in aqueous solution. TO prepare
fo r the sections 0 n titrations, review Fundamentals, Section L. For the discussion of
solubility equilibria, review Fundamentals, Section 上 The discussion of Lewis acids and
bases in Section 1 3 · 1 3 is based o n Section 12 · 2 ·
primary goal of this chapter is t0 learn how t0 manage the pH of solutions
of acids, bases, and their salts. Th e control of pH is crucial for the ability of
organlsms—including ourselves—to survive, because even mlnor drifts from
th e optimum value Of th e pH can cause enzymes tO change their shape and cease tO
function. The information in this chapter is used in industry tO control the pH of
reactlon m1Xtures and tO purify water. ln medicine and biology, th e information is
used tO control the conditions Of cultures and biological cells and tO maintain blOOd
good condition. ln agriculture it is used tO maintain th e soil at an optimal pH. ln
th e laboratory it is used tO interpret the change in pH Of a solution during a titration,
one Of the most common quantitative analytical techniques · lt also forms th e basis Of
qu alit ative analysis, the identification Of the substances and ions present in a sample.
All these applications involve equilibria between species ln solution, especially
between species that can exchange protons. The common theme throughout this
chapter is that all these equilibria can be treated in a similar way:
1 · ldentify the solute speues present in the solution.
2 · ldentify the stoichiometric relations between the concentratlons Of solute specles.
3 ． Use those relations together with equilibrium constants tO calculate the
equilibrium concentrations Of the solute species (often by setting up an
equilibrium table).

Mixed Solutions and Buffers
We have seen how to estimate the pH of a solution of a weak acid or base (Chap-
ter 12L but suPPOSe a salt of the acid or base is also present? How does that salt
affect the pH of the solution?
To set the scene, suPP0se we have some dilute hydrochloric acid and add to it
appreciable concentrations of the conjugate base of HCI, the CI- ion, as sodium
chloride. Because HCI is a strong acid, its COIIJ ugate base is a very weak proton accep-
tor and its presence has no measurable effect on pH. The pH of 0 · 10 M HCl(aq) is
about 1 · 0 ， even after 0 · 10 mol NaCl has been added to a liter of the solution.
NOW suppose instead that the solution contains acet1C acid tO which sodium
acetate has been added (the acetate ion, CH3C02-, is the ugate base of
CH3COOH). Because CH3C02- is a weak base in water, we can predict that add-
lng acetate ions ()s sodium acetate ） tO a solution Of acet1C acid will increase the pH
Of the solution. Similarly, suppose we have a solution Of ammonia and add ammo-
mum chloride tO it. The NH4 ion actS as a weak acid in water; therefore, we can
predict that adding ammonium ions ()s ammonium chloride, for instance) tO a
solution of ammonia will lower the pH of the solution. As we shall see, such "mixed
solutions
—solutions that contain a weak acid or a weak base and one Of its
salts—provide a means of stabilizing the pH of aqueous solutions such as blood
plasma, seaMJater, detergents, sap, and reaction mixtures.
13 ． 1 Buffer Action
The most important type Of mixed solution is a buffer, a solution in which the pH
resists change when small amounts Of strong acids or bases are added. Buffers are
used tO calibrate pH meters, tO culture bacteria, and tO control the pH Of solutions
in which chemical reactions are taking place. They are also administered intrave-
nously to hospital patients. Human blood plasma is buffered to pH = 7 · 4 ； the
ocean is buffered to about pH = 8 · 4 by a complex buffering process that depends
on the presence Of hydrogen carbonates and silicates. A buffer consists Of an aque-
ous solution Of a weak acid and its COIIJ ugate base supplied as a salt, or a weak
base and its conJ ugate acid supplied as a salt. Examples are a solution Of acetic acid
and sodium acetate and a solution Of ammoma and ammomum chloride.
When a drop of strong acid is added to pure water, the pH changes signifi-
cantly. However, when the same amount is added to a buffer, the pH hardly changes
at all. To understand why not, consider the dynamic equilibrium between a weak
acid and its conJ ugate base in water:
CH3COOH(aq) + H20(I) 冖 H30+(aq) + CH3C02- (aq)
TO prepare a buffer that makes use Of this equilibrium, we need a solution that
consists of similar amounts of acid (CH3COOH) and its salt (NaCH3C02). When
a few drops of a strong acid are added to such a solution, the newly arrived H30
ions transfer protons to the CH3C02- ions to form CH3COOH and H20 mole-
cules (FIG. 13 · 1 ） · Because the added H30+ ions are removed by the CH3C02- ions,
the pH remalns almost unchanged. ln effect, the acetate ions act as a "sink ” for
protons. If a small amount Of strong base is added instead, the incoming OH¯ ions
remove protons from the CH3COOH molecules to produce CH3C02- ions and
H20 molecules. ln this case, the acetic acid molecules act as a source Of protons.
Because the added OH- ions are removed by the CH3COOH molecules, the

concentration Of OH¯ ions remams nearly unchanged. Consequently, the H30
concentration (and the (H) is also left nearly unchanged.
NOW consider the equilibrium
NH4+ (aq) + OH- (aq)
NH3(aq) + H20(l)
For a buffer based on this equilibrium, we prepare a solution that contams similar
amounts of base (NH3 ） and its salt (NH4CI). When a few drops of a solution of strong
base are added tO this solution, th e incoming OH¯ ions remove protons from NH4
ions to form NH3 and H20 molecules. When instead a few drops of a strong acid are
added, the incoming protons attach tO NH3 molecules tO make NH4 ions and hence
are removed from the solution. ln each case, the pH is left almost unchanged.

13 ． 2 Designing a Buffer
Suppose we need to make up a buffer with a particular pH. For instance, we might
be culturing bacteria and need tO maintain a precise pH tO sustain their metabolism.
To choose the most appropriate buffer system, we need to know the value of th e pH
at which a given buffer stabilizes a solution. A mixture Of a weak acid and its salt
will act as a buffer at pH < 7 (the acidic side of neutrality) and is known as an acid
buffer. A mixture of a weak base and its salt will act as a buffer at pH > 7 (the basic
side of neutrality) and is known as a basic buffer. To find the precise pH at which a
mixed solution Of given composition Will act as a buffer, carry out an equilibrium
calculation very similar t0 those in Chapter 12 ， as shown in the following example.

13 ． 3 Buffer Capacity
Just as a sponge can supply or hold only so much water, a buffer can supply or
mop up only S O many protons. lts proton sources and sinks become exhausted
if tOO much strong acid or base is added tO the solution. Buffer capacity is the
maximum amount Of acid or base that can be added before the buffer loses its
ability to resist large changes in pH. A buffer with a high capacity is able to
maintain its buffering action against the addition Of strong acid or base better
than can one with only a small capacity. The buffer is exhausted when most of
the weak base has been converted intO its conjugate acid or when most Of the
weak acid has been converted intO its conjugate base. A concentrated buffer
solution has a greater capacity than the same volume Of a more dilute solution
of the same buffer.
Buffer capacity also depends on the relative concentrations Of weak acid and
base. Broadly speaking, a buffer is found experimentally to have a high capacity fo r
stabilizing against the addition Of acid when the amount Of weak base present is at
least 10 ％ of the amount of weak acid. Otherwise, the weak base is used up quickly
as strong acid is added. Similarly, a buffer has a high capacity for stabilizing against
the addition of base when the amount of weak acid present is at least 10 ％ of the
amount Of weak base, because otherwise the weak acid is used up quickly as strong
base is added.
We can use these percentages tO express the range Of buffer action in terms Of
the pH of the solution. The Henderson—Hasselbalch equation shows us that, when
the acid is 10 times as abundant as the base （ [acidl = 10[baseI), the pH of the solu-

a KH2P04/K2HP04 buffer can be expected to be most effective between about

The composition of blood plasma, in which the concentration of HC03- ions
is about 20 times that of H2C03, seems to be outside the range for optimum buffer-
ing. However, the principal waste products of living cells are carboxylic acids, such
as lactic acid. Plasma, with its relatively high concentration Of HC03¯ ions, can
absorb a significant surge of hydrogen ions from these carboxylic acids. The high
proportion of HC03- also helps us to withstand disturbances that lead to excess
acid, such as disease and shock due to burns (BOX 13 · 1 ） ·

Buffer systems are SO vital tO the existence Of living organ-
lsms that the most immediate threat tO the survival Of a
person with severe inJury or burns a change in blood pH.
One Of a paramedic's first Steps in savmg a life is tO admin-

Metab01ic processes normally maintain the pH of
human blood within a narrow range （ 7 · 35 一 7 · 45 ） · To con-
trol blood pH, the body uses primarily the carbonic acid/
hydrogen carbonate (bicarbonate) ion system. The normal
ratio of HC03- to H2C03 in the blood is 20 ： 1 ， with most
of the carbonic acid in the form of dissolved C02. When the
concentration Of HC03- increases further relative tO that Of
H2C03, blood pH rises. If the pH rises above the normal
range, the condition is called os · Conversely, blood
pH decreases when the ratio decreases; and when blood pH
falls below the normal range, the condition is called 乙记 os ·
Because these conditions are life threatening and death can
result within mmutes, lt IS critical that the cause Of the pH
imbalance be identified and treated quickly.

Patients WhO have suffered traumatic injuries must receive a n immediate
intravenous solution tO combat the symptoms Of shock and help
maintain the pH of blood.
The body maintains blood pH by tw o primary mecha-
msms: resmration and excretlon. Carbonic acid concentra-
tion is controlled by respiration: as we exhale, we deplete
our system of C02 and hence deplete it of H2C03, too.
This decrease ln acid concentration raises the blood pH.
Breathing faster and more deeply increases the amount Of
C02 exhaled and hence decreases the carbonic acid con-
centration in the blood, which in turn raises the blood pH.
Hydrogen carbonate ion concentratlon is controlled by its
rate Of excretion ln urme.
Resp 0 了， C / OS 丞 results When decreased respira-
tion ralses the concentration Of C02 in the blood. Asthma,
pneumoma, emphysema, or inhaling smoke can all cause
respiratory acidosis. SO can any condition that reduces a
person's ability to breathe. Respiratory acidosis is usually
treated with a mechanical ventilator, tO assist the victim's
breathing. The improved exhalation mcreases the excre-
tion of C02 and raises blood pH. ln many cases of asthma,
chemicals can facilitate respiration by opening constricted
bronchial passages.
入 /le bO / 记 ci OS IS caused by the release intO the
bloodstream Of excesslve amounts Of lactic acid and Other
acidic by-products of metabolism. These acids enter the
bloodstream, react with hydrogen carbonate ion tO pro-
duce H2C03, and shift the ratio HC03-/H2C03 to a lower
value. Heavy exercise, diabetes, and fasting can all produce
metabolic acidosis. The normal response of the body is t0
increase the rate Of breathing tO eliminate some Of the C02.
Thus, we pant heavily when running uphill.
Metabolic acidosis can alSO result When a person iS
severely burned. Blood plasma leaks from the circulatory
system into the inJ ured area, producing edema （ swelling)
and reducing the blood volume. If the burned area is large,
this loss of blood volume may be sufficient to reduce blood
flow and oxygen supply to all the body's tissues. Lack of
oxygen, lll turn, causes the tissues tO produce an excesslve
amount Of lactic acid and leads tO metabolic acidosis. TO
mlmmize the decrease in pH, the inj ured person breathes
harder to eliminate the excess C02. However, if blood vol-
ume drops below levels fo r which the body can compensate,
a VICIOLIS circle ensues lll which bIOOd flOW decreases still
further, blood pressure falls, C02 excretion diminishes, and
acidosis becomes more severe. People in thiS state are said tO
be in shock and will die if not treated promptly.
The dangers 0f shock are avoided or treated by intrave-
IIOUS infusion Of large volumes Of a salt-contaming solution
that is isotomc with blood (has the same osmot1C pressure
as blood), usually one known as 酊 e Ringer's so 0 ” ·
The added liquid increases blood volume and blood flow,
thereby improving oxygen delivery. The [HC03-]/[H2C03]
ratiO then increases toward normal and allows the severely
lnjured person tO survlve.
Resp / 0 ， / OS is the rise in pH associated with
excesslve respiration. Hyperventilation, which can result
from anxiety or high fever, is a common cause. The body
may control blood pH during hyperventilation by fainting,
which results in slower respiration. An intervention that may
prevent fainting is tO have a hyperventilating person breathe
into a paper bag, which allows much of the respired C02 to
be taken up again.
Metabolic os is the increase in pH resulting from
illness or chemical ingestion. Repeated vomiting or the overuse
Of diuretics can cause metabolic alkalosis. Once again the bOdy
compensates, this time by decreasing the rate Of respiration.

Titrations
As we saw in 尹 d e / s ， Section L, titration involves the addition Of a solution,
called the titrant, from a buret to a flask containing a sample called the analyte.
For example, if an envlronmental chemist iS monitoring acid mine drainage and
needs tO know the concentration Of acid in the water, a sample Of the effluent from
the mine would be the analyte and a solution Of base Of known concentration
would be the titrant. At the stoichiometric point, the amount of OH- ()r H30+)
added as titrant is equal to the amount of H30+ ()r OH-) initially present in the
analyte. The techniques in this chapter are used to identify the roles of different
speues in determining the pH Of the analyte solution at any Stage Of a titration and
tO select the appropriate indicator fO r the titration.
13 ． 4 Strong Acid—Strong Base Titrations
When a strong acid iS mixed With a strong base in water, a neutralization reaction
occurs fO r which the net iomc equation iS
H30+(aq) + 0H-(aq) 一 2 H20(l)
However, it is best tO use the full chemical equation when working with titrations
tO ensure the correct stoichiometry. For example, if hydrochloric acid is used tO
neutralize Ca(OH)2, we must take intO account the fact that each formula unit Of
Ca(OH)2 provides tw o OH- ions:
2 HCl(aq) + Ca(0H)2(aq) 一 CaC12(aq) + 2 H20(l)

point. However, if we were tO continue the titration, we would find that the pH
falls slowly toward the value of the acid itself as the dilution due to the original
analyte solution becomes less and less important.

13 ． 5 Strong Acid—Weak Base and Weak Acid—Strong
Base Titrations
ln many titrations, one solution—either the analyte or the titrant—contains a
weak acid or base and the Other solution contains a strong base or acid. For
example, if we want tO know the concentration Of formlc acid, the weak acid
found in ant venom (l), we can titrate it with sodium hydroxide, a strong base.
Alternatively, tO find the concentration Of ammoma, a weak base, a solution,
we titrate it with hydrochloric acid, a strong acid. Weak acids are not normally
titrated with weak bases, because the stoichiometric point is tOO difficult tO
locate.
FIGURES 13 · 6 and
1 3 7 show the different pH curves that are found experimen-
tally for these tWO types Of titrations. Notice that the stoichiometric point does not
occur at pH = 7 · Moreover, although the pH changes reasonably sharply near the
stoichiometric point, it does not change as abruptly as it does ln a strong acid—
strong base titration.
The pH at the stoichiometric point depends on the type of salt produced in the
neutralization reaction. ln the titration Of acetic acid, CH300H, with sodium
hydroxide, the following reaction takes place:
CH300H(aq) + NaOH(aq) 一 NaCH3C02(aq) + H20(l)
At the stoichiometric point the solution consists Of sodium acetate, NaCH3C02
and water. Because Na+ ions have virtually no effect on pH and the acetate ion,
CH3C02- (2), is a weak base, overall the solution is basic and the pH > 7 · The
same is true for the stoichiometric P01nt Of the titration Of any weak acid with
strong base. At the stoichiometric point Of the titration Of aqueous ammoma
with hydrochloric acid, the solute is ammonium chloride. Because CI¯ ions
have virtually no effect on the pH and NH4 is an acid, we expect pH < 7 · The
same is true for the stoichiometric point Of the titration Of any weak base with
strong acid.

Now consider the overall shape of the pH curve. The slow change
in pH about halfway tO the stoichiometric point indicates that the
solution acts as a buffer in that region (see Fig. 13 · 3 ） · At the halfway
point of the titration, [HA] = [A-] and pH = pKa. ln fact, one way to
prepare a buffer is tO neutralize half the amount Of weak acid present
with strong base. The flatness of the curve near pH = pKa illustrates
very clearly the ability of a buffer solution to stabilize the pH of the
solution. Moreover, we can now see hOW tO determine pKa: plOt the
pH curve during a titration, identify the pH halfway to the stoichio-
metric point, and set pKa equal to that pH (FIG. 13 · 8 ） · To obtain the
pKb of a weak base, we find pKa of its conJugate acid in the same way
but then find pKb from pKa + pKb = pKw. The values recorded in
TabIes 12 · 1 and 12 · 2 were obtained in this way.

the stoichiometric point. An acid—base indicator is a water-soluble organic dye
with a color that depends on the pH. The sudden change in pH that occurs at the
stoichiometric point Of a titration is signaled by a sharp change in color Of the dye
as it responds to the pH.
An acid—base indicator changes color with pH because it is a weak acid that
has one color in its acid form (Hln, where ln stands fO r indicator) and another
color in its conjugate base form (ln¯). The color change results because the proton
in HIn changes the structure of the molecule in such a way that the light absorption
characteristics Of Hln are different from those Of ln¯. When the concentration Of
HIn is much greater than that of ln 一 the solution has the color of the acid form of
the indicator. 、 When the concentration Of ln is much greater than that of Hln, the
solution has the color Of the base form Of the indicator.
Because it IS a weak acid, an indicator takes part in a proton transfer equilibrium:

One common indicator is phenolphthalein (FIG. 13 · 1 0 ） · The acid form of this
large molecule （ 3 ） is colorless; its conjugate base form （ 4 ） is pink. The structure of

Up tO this point, we have focused on aqueous equilibria involving proton transfer.
Now we apply the same principles to the equilibrium that exists between a solid
salt and its dissolved ions ln a saturated solution. We can use the equilibrium con-
stant fO r the dissolution Of a substance tO predict the solubility Of a salt and tO
control precipitate formation. These methods are used in the laboratory tO sepa-
rate and analyze m1Xtures Of salts. They also have important practical applications
mumcipal wastewater treatment, the extraction Of minerals from seawater, the
formation and loss of bones and teeth, and the global carbon cycle.

its dissolved ions is called the solubility product, K 、 p, of the solute. For example,
