13 ． 9 The Common-Ion Effect
Sometimes we have tO precipitate one ion Of a sparingly soluble salt. For example,
heavy metal ions such as lead and mercury can be removed from mumcipal waste-
water by precipitating them as the hydroxides. However, because the ions are
dynamic equilibrium with the solid salt, some heavy metal ions remain in solution.
HOW can remove more Of the ions?
Le Chatelier's principle provides a guide. This principle tells us that, if we add
a second salt or an acid that supplies one Of the same lons—a ' common 10n ” —tO
a saturated solution of a salt, then the equilibrium will tend to adjust by decreasing
the concentration of the added ions (FIG. 13 · 1 5 ） · That is, the solubility of the origi-
nal salt is decreased, and it precipitates. We can conclude that the addition Of excess
OH- ions to the water supply should precipitate more of the heavy metal ions as
their hydroxides. ln other words, the addition of OH- ions reduces the solubility
of the heavy metal hydroxide. The decrease in solubility caused by the addition of
a common IOII iS called the comr 嗆 on · 10n effect.
FIGURE 13 · 15 阡 the concentration of o n e of the ions of a slightly soluble salt is increased, the
concentration Of the Other decreases tO maintain a constant value Of Ksp. (a) The cations (pink) and
anions (green) in solution. (b) When m 0 re anions a re added (together with their accompanying
spectator ions, which a re not shown), the concentration Of cations decreases. 貊 Other words, the
solubility 0f the original compound is reduced by the presence 0f a CO m m 0 n ion. 貊 the insets, the
blue background represents the solvent (water).

13 ． 12 DissoIving Precipitates
When a precipitate has been formed during the qualitative analysis of the ions
present in a solution, it may be necessary tO dissolve the precipitate again tO iden-
tify the cation or anion. One strategy is tO remove one Of the ions from the solubil-
lty equilibrium SO that the precipitate will continue tO dissolve, in a fruitless chase
fo r equilibrium. SLIPP0se, fo r example, that a solid hydroxide such as iron(lll)
hydroxide is in equilibrium with its ions ln solution:
Fe(0H)3(s) Fe3+(aq) + 3 OH- (aq)
To dissolve more of the solid, we can add acid. The H30+ ions from the acid
remove the OH- ions by converting them into water, and the Fe(OH)3 dissolves.
TH 《 N ℃ N G POINT SiIver ions can be brought into solution fro m solid Ag20 by
adding HN03, but not by adding HCI. Why cannot HCI be used?
Many carbonate, sulfite, and sulfide precipitates can be dissolved by the addi-
tion Of acid, because the anions react with the acid tO form a gas that bubbles out Of
solution. For example, in a saturated solution Of 云 nc carbonate, solid ZnC03 is in
549
equilibrium with its ions:
ZnC03(s) zn2+ (aq) + C032- (aq)
The C03 一 ions react with acid to form C02.•
C032-(aq) + 2 HN03(aq) 冖
C02(g) + H20(l) + 2 N03-(aq)
The dissolution Of carbonates by acid is an undesired result Of acid rain, which has

The solubility of a salt can be increased by finding a way to hide away the ions in
solution, because then the dissolution process contmues ln a vain attempt tO reach
equilibrium. TO remove an 10n, can use the fact that many metal cations are
Lewis acids (Section 12 · 2 ） · When a Lewis acid and a Lewis base react, they form
a coordinate covalent bond and the product is called a coordination complex. ln
thiS sectlon, we consider complexes in which the Lewis acid iS a metal cation, such
as Ag · An example is the formation of Ag(NH3)2 when an aqueous solution of
the Lewis base ammoma iS added tO a solution Of silver ions:
Ag+ (aq) + 2 NH3(aq) 一 Ag(NH3)2+ (aq)
If enough ammonia is added to a precipitate of silver halide, all the precipitate dis-
solves. A similar procedure iS used tO remove the silver halide emulsion from an
exposed photographic film after it has been developed. ln this case, the reagent
used to form the complex is the thiosulfate ion, S203
Ag+(aq) + 2 S2032-(aq) 一 Ag(S203)23-(aq)
Complex formation removes some Of the Ag ions from solution. As a result, tO
preserve the value Of K 、 p, more silver chloride dissolves. Formation Of a complex
increases the solubility of a sparingly soluble compound.
TO treat complex formation quantitatively, note that complex formatlon and
the dissolving of the salt are both at equilibrium:
AgCl(s) 冖 Ag+(aq) + cl- (aq) Ksp = [Ag+l[Cl-l
Ag+(aq) + 2 NH3(aq) 冖 Ag(NH3)2+ (aq)

13 ． 14 QuaIitative Analysis
Complex formation, selective precipitation, and control Of the pH Of a solution all
play important roles in the qualitative analysis Of the ions present in aqueous solu-
tions. There are many different schemes of analysis, but they follow the same
general principles. Let's think through a simple procedure fo r the identification of
five cations by following the steps that might be used in the laboratory. We shall
see how each step makes use of solubility equilibria.
Suppose we have a solution that contains lead(ll), mercury(l), silver,
copper(ll), and zinc ions. The method is outlined in FIG. 13 · 20 which includes
additional cations, and is illustrated in FIG. 1 3 · 21 · Most chlorides are soluble•
so, when hydrochloric acid is added to a mixture of salts, only certain chlorides
precipitate (see Table 13 · 4 ） · Silver and mercury(l) chlorides have such small
values Of Ks that, even with IOW concentrations Of Cl¯ ions, the chlorides pre-
cipitate. Lead(II) chloride, which is slightly soluble, will precipitate if the chlo-
ride ion concentration is high enough. The hydronium lons provided by the acid
play no role in this step; they simply accompany the chloride ions. At this point,
the precipitate can be separated from the solution by using a centrifuge tO com-
pact the solid and then decanting (pouring off) the solution. The solution now
contains copper(ll) and zinc ions, whereas the solid consists of PbC12, Hg2C12,
and AgCl.
Because PbC12 is slightly soluble, if the precipitate is rinsed with hot water,
the lead(ll) chloride dissolves and the solution is separated from the precipitate.
If sodium chromate is then added to that solution, the presence of lead can be
verified because any lead(ll) ions present will precipitate as yellow lead(ll)
chromate:
Pb2+(aq) + Cr042-(aq) 一 PbCr04(s)

ELECTROCHEMISTRY
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This Material? The topics described in this chapter
may 0 n e day unlock a virtually inexhaustible supply 0f clean energy supplied daily
by the Sun. The key is electrochemistry, the study of the interaction of electricity and
chemical reactions. The transfer Of electrons from O n e species tO another iS O n e Of
the fundamental processes underlying life, photosynthesis, fuel cells, and the refining
Of metals. An understanding Of h OW electrons a re transferred helps us tO design ways
tO use chemical reactions tO generate electricity and tO use electricity tO bring about
chemical reactions. Electrochemical measurements alSO allOW CIS tO determine the
values Of thermodynamic quantities.
What Are the Key ldeas? The tendency of electrons to be transferred i n a chemical
reaction depends O n the species involved and their concentrations. When the process is
spontaneous and reduction and oxidation occur at different locations, the reaction ca n
dO work and drive electrons through a n external circuit.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? This chapter extends the thermodynamic
discussion presented in Chapter 9 · | n particular, it builds o n the concept of Gibbs free
energy (Section 9 · 1 2 ）， its relation t0 maximum nonexpansion work (Section 9 · 14L and
the dependence of the reaction Gibbs free energy O n the reaction quotient (Section
1 1 · 3 ） · For a review of redox reactions, see Fundamentals, Section K. To prepare fo r the
quantitative treatment Of electrolysis, review stoichiometry in Fundamentals, Section L.
he nature Of electricity was unknown until the late eighteenth century, when
the ltalian scientist Luigi Galvani discovered that by touching the muscles of
dead animals, mainly frogs, with rods bearing electric charges, he could
make their muscles twitch. He believed that electricity came from the muscles
themselves. However, at the end Of that century another ltalian, Alessandro V01ta,
suggested that the electricity came from the fact that the muscles were between tWO
different metals when touched by the rods. He proved that the electricity came
from metals by constructing a tower Of alternating discs Of different metals in lay-
ers separated by paper strips soaked in a solution of sodium chloride (FIG. 14 · 1 ） ·
This apparatus, a "voltaic pile," was the first electrical storage device, a simple
battery, but because it opened a door tO a new understanding Of the structure Of
matter, it amazed the scientists and even the rulers Of the day.
Those early observations have evolved into the branch of chemistry called elec-
trochemistry. This subj ect deals not only with the use Of spontaneous chemical

Representing Redox Reactions
An electric current is the flow Of electrons through a circuit. When the current is
generated chemically, the electrons emerge from a location where oxidation takes
place and travel tO a location where reduction occurs. Because oxidation and
reduction are involved in the generatlon Of an electric current, redox reactlons
（尹 d e / s ， Section K) are central tO the discusslon Of electrochemistry. ln this
chapter we take a closer look at them and see how they and other types 0f reac-
tions can be used tO generate electricity.
For a quantltative discusslon Of redox reactlons, lt IS necessary tO write bal-
anced chemical equations. Some redox reactions can be tricky tO balance, and spe-
cial techniques, which we describe in Sections 14 · 1 and 14 · 2 ， have been developed
to simplify the procedure.
The chapter begins with a revlew Of redox reactions, which are particularly
important for understanding the chemical production Of electricity, a topic that
occupies the major part Of this chapter. Redox reactions are also important in the
final part of the chapter, which discusses the use of electricity t0 bring about chem-
ical reactions.
14 ． 1 HaIf-Reactions
The key tO writing and balancing equations for redox reactions is tO think Of the
reduction and oxidation processes separately. We saw in 尹 e / s ， Section K,
that oxidation is the loss Of electrons and reduction the gain Of electrons.
A half-reaction is the oxidation or reduction part Of a reaction considered
alone. An oxidation half-reaction shows the removal Of electrons from a species
that is being oxidized in a redox reaction. For example, VOlta used silver and zinc
plates in one Of his voltaic piles tO carry out the reaction
zn(s) + 2 Ag+(aq) 一 Zn2+(aq) + 2 Ag(s)
TO show the oxidation Of zinc explicitly, we write
zn(s) 一 zn2+(s) + 2 一
An oxidation half-reaction is a CO cep / way Of reporting an oxidation: the elec-
trons are never actually free. ln an equation fO r an oxidation half-reactlon, the
electrons released always appear on the right Of the arrow. Their state is not given,
because they are in transit and dO not have a definite physical state. The reduced
and oxidized species in a half-reaction j ointly form a redox couple. ln this example,
the redox couple consists of Zn2+ and Zn, and is denoted Zn2+/Zn. A redox couple
has the form Ox/Red, where Ox is the oxidized form of the species and Red is the
reduced form.

ing the equations for half-reactions, we match the number Of electrons released by
oxidation With the number used in reduction, because electrons are neither created
nor destroyed in chemical reactions. The procedure outlined in Toolbox 14 · 1

Whenever we turn on a portable media player or a laptop computer, we are
completing a circuit that allows a chemical reaction tO take place ln a battery,
a direct descendant of Volta's pile of metals and paper. A battery is an example
Of an electrochemical cell. ln general, an electrochemical cell is a device ln
which an electric current—a flow Of electrons through a circuit—is either produced
by a spontaneous chemical reaction or used tO bring about a nonspontaneous
reaction. A galvanic cell is an electrochemical cell in which a spontaneous
chemical reaction IS used tO generate an electric current. Technically, a battery
is a collection Of galvanic cells jOined in serles, SO the voltage that it produces—
its ability tO push an electric current through a circuit—is the sum Of the volt-
ages of each cell.
14 ． 3 The Structure of Galvanic Cells

Galvanic cells are alSO known as
voltaic cells.

potential difference," measured in

consider the redox reaction between zinc metal and copper(ll) ions:
zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) 一 Zn2+(aq) + cu(s)
(A)
If we were to place a P1ece of zinc metal into an aqueous copper(ll) sulfate solu-
tion, we would see a layer Of metallic copper begin tO deposit on the surface Of
the zinc ()s in Fig. K.5). If we could watch the reaction at the atomic level, we
would see that, as the reaction takes place, electrons are transferred from the Zn
atoms tO adjacent Cu + lons in the solution. These electrons reduce the Cu + lons
to Cu atoms, which stick to the surface of the zinc or form a finely divided solid
deposit in the beaker. The piece of zinc slowly disappears and the blue color of
2 +
the solution is lost as the Zn atoms give up electrons and form colorless Zn
ions that drift o ff into the solution, replacing the Cu ions. The Gibbs free
energy Of the system decreases as electrons are transferred and the reaction
approaches equilibrium. However, although energy is released as heat, no electri-
cal work iS done.

NOW suppose we separate the reactants but provide a pathway fO r the elec-
trons tO travel from the zinc metal tO the copper(ll) ions. The reaction will still
occur, even though the reactants are not in direct contact. As the reaction proceeds,
the electrons can dO work—for example, drive an electric motor—as they pass
from the species being oxidized to the species being reduced. This process is what
happens in a galvanic cell. A galvanic cell consists Of tw O electrodes, or metallic
conductors, which make electrical contact with the contents Of the cell but not with
each other, and an electrolyte, an lonically conducting medium, inside the cell. ln an
IOIMC conductor, an electric current IS carried by the movement Of ions. electro-
lyte is typically an aqueous solution Of an iomc compound. Oxidation takes place
at one electrode as the species being oxidized releases electrons intO the metallic
conductor. Reduction takes place at the Other electrode, where the species that is
undergoing reduction collects electrons from the metallic conductor (FIG. 14 · 2 ） · We
can think Of the overall chemical reaction as pushing electrons on tO one electrode
from the oxidation process taking place there and pulling them off the other elec-
trode from the reduction taking place at it. This push—pull process sets up a flow of
electrons in the external circuit ] Oining the tw O electrodes, and that current can be
used tO dO electrical work.
The electrode at which oxidation takes place is called the anode. The electrode
at which reduction takes place is called the cathode. Electrons are released by the
oxidation half-reaction at the anode, travel through the external circult, and re-
enter the cell at the cathode, where they are used in the reduction half-reaction. A
commercial galvanic cell has its cathode marked with a + sign and its anode with
a 一 sign. Think Of the + sign as indicating the electrode at which the electrons enter
and "add to ” the cell and the 一
sign as indicating the electrode at which the elec-
trons leave the cell.
The Daniell “ / / is an early example of a galvanic cell that makes use of the
oxidation Of copper by zinc ions, as reaction A. The British chemist JOhn Daniell

cheap, reliable, steady source Of electric current. Daniell set up the arrangement

The electrodes in the Daniell cell are made of the metals involved in the reac-

14 · 4 Cell Potential and Reaction Gibbs Free Energy
14 ． 4 CeIl PotentiaI and Reaction Gibbs Free Energy
A reaction with a lot of pushing-and-pulling power generates a high potential dif-
ference (colloquially, a high voltage) · A reaction with little pushing-and-pulling
power generates only a small potential difference (a low voltage). An exhausted
battery is a cell in which the reaction is at equilibrium; it has lost its power tO move
electrons and has a potential difference of zero. The SI unit of potential (and poten-
tial difference) is the volt (V). A volt is defined so that a charge of one coulomb
（ 1 0 falling through a potential difference of one volt （ 1 V) releases one joule
（ 1 J) of energy:
1 C•V ： 1 J
TO express these ideas quantitatively, it is helpful tO note that electrical poten-
tial is analogous tO gravitational potential. The maxlmum work that a falling
weight can dO is equal tO its mass times the difference in gravitational potential.
Similarly, the 1 嗆 axll 嗆嗆 work that an electron can dO is equal tO its charge times
the difference in electrical potential through which it falls. EIectrical work is a type
Of nonexpanslon work because it involves movmg electrons rather than changing
the volume Of the system. ln Section 9 · 14 we established that, at constant tempera-
ture and pressure, the maxlmum nonexpanslon work that a system can dO iS equal
to the change in the Gibbs free energy. We need to bring these tw 0 concepts together
by finding the relation between the Gibbs free energy 0f a reaction (a thermody-
namic property) and the potential difference ()n electrochemical property) pro-
duced by that reaction.

CONCEPTUAL BASIS
A cell diagram corresponds tO a specific cell reaction in
which the right-hand electrode in the cell diagram is treated
as the site Of reduction and the left-hand electrode is treated
as the site of oxidation. The sign of the cell potential then
distinguishes whether the resulting reaction is spontaneous
in the direction written （ > 0 ） or whether the reverse reac-
tion is spontaneous （ < 0 ） ·
PROCEDURE
Step 1 Write the equation fo r the electrode on the right of
the cell diagram as a reduction half-reaction (remember:
Right for Reduction) ·
S 孕 2 Write the equation fo r the electrode on the left of
the cell diagram as an oxidation half-reaction.
Step 3 Multiply one or both equations by a factor if neces-
sary t0 equalize the number of electrons, and then add the
tWO equatlons.
If the cell potential is positive, then the reaction IS
spontaneous as written. If the cell potential is negative,
then the reverse reaction IS spontaneous.

A problem with compiling a list Of standard potentials is that we can measure

placed between the tW O electrodes Of a galvanic cell measures the difference Of their
potentials, not the individual values. TO provide numerical values fO r individual
standard potentials, we arbitrarily set the standard potential Of one particular elec-
trode, the hydrogen electrode, equal tO zero at all temperatures:
2 H+(g) + 2 e- 一 H2(g) EO = 0

1 mol•L- （ strictly, unit activity) ， is called a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE).
The standard hydrogen electrode is then used to define the standard potentials of
all other electrodes:
The standard potential of a couple is the standard potential of a cell
(including the sign) in which the couple forms the right-hand electrode in
the cell diagram and a hydrogen electrode forms the left-hand electrode in
the cell diagram.

14 ． 7 The ElectrochemicaI Series
When redox couples are ordered by their standard potentials, we have a list of
oxidizing and reducing agents ordered by their strengths. As we have seen, the
more negative the standard potential Of a couple, the greater is its reducing
strength. Only a couple with a negative potential can reduce hydrogen ions under
standard conditions (that is, have K > 1 fo r the reduction of hydrogen ions). A
couple with a positive potential, such as Au +/Au, cannot reduce hydrogen ions
under standard conditions in the sense that such a reaction would have K < 1 ， and
commonly K 《 1 fo r the reduction of hydrogen ions (FIG. 14 · 10 ） ·
When TabIe 14 · 1 is viewed as a table of relative strengths of oxidizing and
reducing agents, it is called the electrochemical series. The species on the left of
each equation in TabIe 14 · 1 are potentially oxidizing agents. They can themselves
be reduced. Species on the right of the equations are potentially reducing agents. An
oxidized speues in the list ()n the left of the equation) has a tendency ()n the sense
2 +
that K > 1 ） to oxidize a reduced species that lies below it. For example, Cu ions
oxidize zinc metal. A reduced species ()n the right Of the equation) has a tendency
tO reduce an oxidized species that lies above it. For example, zinc metal reduces H
ions to hydrogen gas.
The higher the position of a species on the left side of an equation in TabIe 14 · 1 ，
the greater is its oxidizing strength. For example, F2 is a strong oxidizing agent,

===== 第 725 页 =====
14 · 7 The Electrochemical Series
whereas Li is a very, very poor oxidizing agent. lt also follows that, the lower the
standard potential, the greater is the reducing strength Of the reduced species on the
right side of an equation in Table 14 · 1 · For example, lithium metal is the strongest
reducing agent in the table.

CONCEPTUAL BASIS
The logarithm Of the equilibrium constant Of a reaction is
proportional tO the standard potential Of the correspond-
ing cell. We can expect a cell reaction with a large positive
potential tO have a strong tendency tO take place, and
therefore to produce a high proportion of products at equi-
librium. Therefore, we expect K > 1 when 。 > 0 (and
often K 1 ） · The opposite is true fo r a cell reaction with
a negative standard potential.

electrochemical data is as follows.

combine tO give that equation. Reverse one Of the half-
reactlons and add them together.

the change in oxidation numbers or by examining the
half-reactions (after multiplication by appropriate factors ）
fO r the number Of electrons transferred in the balanced
equatlon.

14 ． 9 The Nernst Equation
As a reaction proceeds toward equilibrium, the concentratlons Of its reactants and
products change and AG approaches zero. Therefore, as reactants are consumed in
a working electrochemical cell, the cell potential also decreases until finally it reaches
zero. A "dead ” battery is one in which the cell reaction has reached equilibrium. At
equilibrium, a cell generates zero potential difference across its electrodes, and the
reaction can no longer dO work. TO describe this behavior quantitatively, we need tO
find how th e cell potential varies with the concentrations Of species in the cell.
How Do We Do That?

ElectroIytic Cells
Redox reactions that have a positive Gibbs free energy Of reactlon are not sponta-
neous, but an electric current can be used tO make them take place. For example,
there iS no common spontaneous chemical reaction in which fluorine iS a product,
and SO the element cannot be isolated by any common chemical reaction. lt was
not until 18 86 that the French chemist Henri Moissan found a way to force the
formation Of fluorine by passing an electric current through an anhydrous molten
mixture of potassium fluoride and hydrogen fluoride. FIuorine is still prepared
commercially by the same process.
ln the next tWO sections we study electrolysis, the process Of driving a reaction
ln a nonspontaneous direction by usmg an electric current. First, we see hOW elec-
trochemical cells are constructed for electrolysis and hOW tO predict the potential
needed tO bring electrolysis about. Then, we examine the products Of electrolysis
and see hOW tO predict the amounts Of products tO expect fO r a given flow Of elec-
tr1C current.
14 ． 11 EIectroIysis
An electrochemical cell in which electrolysis takes place is called an electrolytic
cell. The arrangement Of components in electrolytic cells is different from that in
galvanic cells. Typically, the tw O electrodes share the same compartment, there is
only one electrolyte, and concentratlons and pressures are fa r from standard. As in
all electrochemical cells, the current is carried through the electrolyte by the ions

where “ melt ” signifies the molten salt. A rechargeable battery functions as a galvanic
cell when it is doing work and as an electrolytic cell when it is being recharged.
TO drive a reaction ln a nonspontaneous direction, the external supply must
generate a potential difference greater than the potential difference that would be
produced by the reverse reaction. For example, because
2 + 02(g) 一 2 H20(l)

tO achieve the nonspontaneous reverse reaction,

ference, which varies with the type of electrode, is called the overpotential. For
platinum electrodes, the overpotential fO r the production Of water from hydrogen and
oxygen is about 0 · 6 V, so about 1 · 8 V (that is, 0 · 6 + 1 · 23 V) is actually required to
electrolyze water when platinum electrodes are used. Hydrogen is a clean-burning
energy source, and much contemporary research on electrochemical cellS involves
attempts tO reduce the overpotential and hence tO mcrease the efficiency Of electrolytic
processes such as those that produce hydrogen.
When carrying out an electrolysis in solution, we must consider the possibility
that Other species present might be oxidized or reduced by the electric current. For
example, suppose that we want tO electrolyze water tO produce hydrogen and OXY-

The lmpact o n Materials
Electrochemical cells play important roles in both the purification and the preserva-
tion Of metallic materials. Redox reactions are used throughout the chemical industry
tO extract metals from their ores. However, redox reactlons also corrode the artifacts
that industry produces. What redox reactions achieve, redox reactions can destroy.

modification Of the Downs process, the electrolyte is an aqueous solution Of sodium

Water is more highly conducting when it has dissolved ions, and the formation of
rust is then accelerated. That is one reason why the salt air Of coastal cities and salt
used fo r de-icing highways is so damaging t0 exposed metal.
Because corroslon IS an electrochemical process, should be able tO use our
knowledge Of redox reactions tO combat it. The simplest way tO prevent corro-
S10n is tO protect the surface Of the metal from exposure tO air and water by
painting. A method that achieves greater protection is tO galvanize the metal,
coating it with an unbroken film of zinc (FIG. 14 · 1 9 ） · Zinc lies below iron in the
0

===== 第 741 页 =====
599
electrochemical series; SO, if a scratch exposes the metal beneath, the more
strongly reducing zinc releases electrons tO the iron. As a result, the zinc, not the
lron, IS oxidized. zinc itself survlves exposure on the unbroken surface
because it is passlvated, protected from further reaction, by a protective oxide. ln
general, the oxide Of any metal that takes up more space than does the metal that
it replaces actS as a protective oxide, an oxide that protects the metal from further
oxidation. Zinc and chromium bOth form low-density protective oxides that can
protect iron from oxidation.
lt is not possible tO galvanize large metal structures, such as ships, under-
ground pipelines, gasoline storage tanks, and bridges, but cathodic protection,
the electrochemical protection Of a metal object by connecting it tO a more
strongly reducing metal, can still be used. For example, a block of a more strongly
reducing metal than iron, typically zinc or magnesium, can be buried in moist soil
and connected to an underground pipeline (FIG. 14 · 20 ） · The block of magnesium
IS oxidized preferentially and supplies electrons tO the iron fO r the reduction Of
oxygen. The block, which is called a sacrificial anode, protects the pipeline and is
lnexpensive tO replace. For similar reasons, automobiles generally have negative
ground systems as part Of their electrical circuitry, which means that the bOdy Of
the car is connected to the anode of the battery. The decay of the anode in the
battery is the sacrifice that helps preserve the vehicle itself.
A common means Of protecting the steel bodies Of automobiles and
trucks is through cationic electrodeposition coatings. ln this process, a
corroslon-resistant primer is deposited electrochemically on tO the auto-
mobile body, which serves as the cathode for the process. For many years,
lead(lV) oxide was used tO provide this corrosion protection. However, lead is
tOXiC, and concerns for envlronmental pollution stimulated research intO alter-
native metals for cationic electrodeposition coatings. Eventually it was discov-
ered that yttrium oxide alSO offers corroslon resistance and, in fact, iS tVV1ce as
effective as lead. ln addition, yttrium IS nontoxic and its oxide is a ceram1C.
Thus, the oxide is insoluble in water and is not spread intO the envlronment
through waterways.

A primary cell is a galvanic cell with the reactants sealed inside at manufacture.
lt cannot be recharged; when it runs down, it is discarded. A fuel cell is like a pri-
mary cell, but the reactants are continuously supplied (BOX 14 · 1 ） ·
A 0 / / is the primary cell used in most common applications, such as

cylindrical zinc container serves as the anode; in the center iS the cathode, a
carbon rod. The interior Of the container is lined with paper that serves as
the porous barrier. The electrolyte is a moist paste Of ammonium chloride,
manganese(IV) oxide, finely granulated carbon, and an inert filler, usually starch.
2 +
The ammonia provided by the ammonium ions forms the complex ion Zn(NH3)4
with the Zn lons and prevents their buildup and a consequent reduction Of the
potential.
Two primary cells that provide a more stable and longer-lasting potential than
the d ry cell are the alkaline cell and the silver cell. An 沅 e “ / / is similar to a dry
cell but uses an alkaline electrolyte, with which the zinc electrode does not readily
react when the battery is not in use. As a result, alkaline cells have longer lives than
dry cells. They are used in smoke detectors and backup power supplies. A / " “ / /
has a cathode made of solid Ag20 and Ag. The relatively high potential of a silver
cell, with its solid reactants and products, is maintained with great reliability over
long periods of time, and the cell can be manufactured in very small sizes. These
features make it desirable fO r medical implants such as pacemakers, fO r hearing
aids, and fO r cameras.
Secondary cells are galvanic cells that must be charged before they can be used;
this type of cell is normally rechargeable. The batteries used in portable computers
and automobiles are secondary cells. ln the charging process, an external source Of

electricity reverses the spontaneous cell reaction and creates a nonequilibrium m1X-
ture Of reactants. After charging, the cell can again produce electricity.

several grids that act as electrodes (FIG. 14 · 22 ） · AIthough it has a low specific
energy, because the tOtal surface area Of these grids is large, the battery can generate

BOX 14 ． 1 FRONTIERS OF CHEMISTRY: FUEL CELLS
Spacecraft need a source Of electrical power, and astronauts
need enough water fo r drinking and washing. Because the
mass of spacecraft that are built to lift o ff from planets
must be kept as IOW as possible, most battenes—which
usually provide energy from the oxidation of a metal—
would be too heavy. Electricity can be obtained from com-
bustion reactions by burning a fuel tO create heat, which
runs a generator. Hoyvever, producing electricity from
burning fuels is very inefficient, because energy IS wasted
as heat.
An answer tO the problem already existed. Franc1s
Bacon, a British scientist and engmeer, had developed an
idea proposed by Sir WiIIiam Grove in 1839 · A fuel cell
generates electricity directly from a chemical reactlon, as
a battery, but uses reactants that are supplied continu-
ously, as in an engine. A fuel cell that runs on hydrogen and
oxygen was installed on the space shuttle (see Fig. L.I). An
advantage of this fuel cell is that the only product of the cell
reaction, water, can be used for life support.
ln a simple version of a fuel cell, a fuel such as hydro-
gen gas is passed over a platinum electrode, oxygen is
passed over the Other, similar electrode, and the electrolyte
is aqueous potasslum hydroxide. A porous membrane that
is permeable tO ions separates the tw O electrode compart-
ments. Many varieties Of fuel cells are possible, and in some
the electrolyte is a solid polymer membrane or a ceram1C
(see Section 7 · 11 ） · Three of the most promising fuel cells
are the alkali fuel cell, the phosphoric acid fuel cell, and the
methanol fuel cell.
The hydrogen—oxygen cell used in the space shuttle
is called an alkali fuel cell, because it has an alkaline
electrolyte:
An acid electrolyte may also be used, as in a phosphoric
acid fuel cell:

lng plants and power sources lll colleges and universities,
hotels, and apartment buildings.
Although hydrogen gas is an attractive fuel, it has disad-

What have you learned in this chapter?
You have learned that the reaction in an electrochemical cell
can be written as the sum Of balanced reduction and oxidation
half-reactions. The cell potential Of a reaction is related tO the
Gibbs free energy through the relation AG = 一 ” 尹 E. Reactions
with positive cell potentials are spontaneous and can be used in
Galvanic cells to perform electrical work. The cell potential fo r
a system involving aqueous IOIIS depends on the concentratlon
Of specles ln solution and can be calculated using the Nernst
equation. An important application Of the Nernst equatlon is tO
use the measured cell potential tO calculate the concentration
Of an unknown species solution. You have also learned that
A proton exchange membrane is used in both hydrogen and methanol
fuel cells. lt allows protons but not electrons t0 travel through it: the
protons flow through the porous membrane t0 the cathode, where they
combine with oxygen tO form water, while the electrons flow through a n
external circuit. Severa | layers Of cells a re combined tO generate the
power required.
cell reactlons can be forced tO proceed in the nonspontaneous
direction through the application Of an external electrical
potential in a process called electrolysis. Faraday's law allows
you tO relate the time that electrolysis occurs and the current
that flows to the amount of material electrolyzed. Lastly, you
have seen that cell reactions are important in the understanding
Of corroslon and in the production Of batterles.

An exciting emerging technology is the biofuel cell. A
biofuel cell is like a conventional fuel cell; however, in place
Of a platinum catalyst, lt uses enzymes or even whole organ-
lsms. The electricity is extracted through organic molecules
that can support the transfer Of electrons. One application IS
as the power source fO r medical implants, such as pacemak-
ers, perhaps by using the glucose present in the bloodstream
as the fuel.
H OW MIGHT YO U CONTRIBUTE?
Fuel cell technologies developed fo r aerospace have the poten-
tial to change the way we live on Earth. Vehicles powered by
hydrogen fuel cells are already being manufactured (see the
illustration) · However, there are many obstacles that must be
overcome before fuel cells reach their potential tO provide us
with pollution-free energy. Th e hydrogen fuel cells are the
most attractive, because Of their use Of a renewable fuel.
Hydrogen can be obtained from th e water in the oceans. Th e
challenge is tO extract it from seawater by using solar energy
nd tO find safe means Of transportation and storage. Many
practical problems with fuel cells also need to be solved, such
as controlling corrosion by electrolytes and reducing the cell
size and operating temperature · Th e development of biofuel
cells is also potentially 0f great significance ·

CHEM ℃ AL KINET ℃ S
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? Chemical kinetics provides tools that
you can use tO study the rates Of chemical reactions O n bOth the macroscopic and the
atomic levels. At the atomic level, chemical kinetics is a source Of insight intO the nature
and mechanisms Of chemical reactions. At the macroscopic level, information from
chemical kinetics allows you tO model complex systems, such as the processes taking
place in the human body and the atmosphere. The development of catalysts, which a re
substances that speed up chemical reactions, is a branch Of chemical kinetics that is
crucial tO the chemical industry, tO the solution Of major problems such as world hunger,
and to the development of new fuels.
What Are the Key ldeas? The rates of chemical reactions ca n be described by simple
expressions that enable us tO predict the composition Of a reaction mixture at any time;
these expressions alSO suggest the Steps by which the reaction takes place.
What Do Yo u Need to Know Already? There are n 0 specific prerequisites fo r this
chapter, but it might be helpful to review the kinetic model of gases (Section 5 · 10 ） and
equilibrium constants (Section 1 1 · 2 ） ·
n the prevlous four chapters we saw hOW tO use thermodynamics tO predict the
spontaneous direction and extent Of chemical change. However, thermodynamlcs
does not tell us hOW fast the reactlon goes. Some spontaneous reactions—such
as the decomposition Of benzene intO carbon and hydrogen—do not seem tO
proceed at all, whereas Other reactions—such as proton transfer reactions—
reach equilibrium very rapidly. ln this chapter, we examine the intimate details
of hOW reactions proceed, what determlnes their rates, and hOW tO control those
rates. The study Of the rates Of chemical reactions is called chemical kinetics.
When studying thermodynamics, we consider only the initial and final states of
a chemical process (its origin and destination) and ignore what happens between
them (the journey itself, with all its obstacles). ln chemical kinetics, we focus on
the journey—the changes that take place in the course Of reactions and the
speed of each step.
This chapter begins by looking at how the rates 0f reactions are determined
experimentally and summarized by succinct expressions known as laws. ” We
then see hOW tO use these rate laws tO predict the concentrations Of reactants and
products at any Stage Of a reactlon and tO gain insight about hOW reactions occur.
Finally, we see hOW substances called catalysts accelerate reactions and control
biological processes.

The experimental technique used tO measure a rate Of reaction depends on
how rapidly the reaction takes place. Some biologically important reactions, such
as the growth Of hair, may take weeks tO show significant changes, but Other reac-
tions, such as the explosion Of nitroglycerin, are very rapid. Special techniques
have tO be used when the reaction is SO fast that it is over ln seconds. There are tWO
maln consideratlons. One iS tO initiate the reaction at a very precise time. The
Other is tO monltor the concentration at preuse lnstants after the reaction has been
initiated.
Some reactions can be initiated by a flash Of light. Because lasers can produce
very short pulses at precisely known times, they are Often used tO study the rates Of
such reactions. Spectrometry—the determination Of concentrations by measurmg
the absorption of light by species (see Major Technique 2 ， following Chapter 4 ）一
can respond very quickly tO concentration changes and iS Often used in combina-
tion with a laser flash tO study very fast reactions. For instance, suppose we are
studying the effect Of a chlorofluorocarbon on the concentration Of ozone, a blue
gas that absorbs light Of certain wavelengths. We could use a spectrometer tO mon-
itor the light absorbed by the ozone at one of those wavelengths and calculate the
molar concentration Of 03 molecules from the intensity Of absorption. By usmg
pulsed lasers, chemists can study reactions that are complete in less than a picosec-

1 5 · 2 The lnstantaneous Rate of Reaction
Box 15 ． 1 H OW DO WE KNOW · · · WHAT HAPPENS TO ATOMS DURING A REACTION?
The events that happen tO an atom ln a chemical reaction
are on a time scale 0f approximately 1 femtosecond （ 1 fs
s), the time that it takes for a bond tO stretch or bend
and, perhaps, break. If we could follow atoms on that time
scale, we could make a movie Of the changes in molecules as
they take part in a chemical reaction. The new field of 一
0 c 乃 e 丞 the study Of very fast chemical processes, is
bringing us closer tO realizing that dream. Lasers can emlt
very intense but short pulses Of electromagnetic radiation,
and SO they can be used tO study processes on very short
time scales. Recent developments have pushed the time scale
= 10 18 s),
Of observations toward the attosecond region （ 1 at
where even the motlon Of electrons iS frozen.
So far, the technique has been applied only to very
simple reactlons. For example, it IS possible tO watch the
ion pair Na+l¯ decompose in the gas phase intO separate
N a and I atoms. At the Start, the sodium 10n and iodide ion
are held together by the coulombic attraction 0f opposite
charges. The pair is then struck by a femtosecond pulse of
radiation from a laser. That pulse excites an electron from
the I- ion on to the Na ion, thereby creating an NaI mol-
ecule in which the tWO atoms are held together by a covalent
bond. The molecule has a lot of energy, and the bond length
vanes as the atoms swing and out. At this point, a second
femtosecond pulse is fired at the molecule. The radiation in
the second pulse has a frequency that can be absorbed by
the molecule only when the atoms have a particular separa-
tion. If the pulse is absorbed, we know that the atoms of the
vibrating molecule have that special internuclear separation.
The illustratlon shows a typical result. Th e absorption
reaches a maximum whenever the N a—l bond length returns
to the length to which the second pulse is tuned. The peaks
show that the sodium atom moves away from the iodine
atom (corresponding t0 the dips in the curve), only to be

that some N a atoms escape from their I atom partners on

N a atom can be sure Of escaping. When sodium bromide

Concentration and Time
We often want tO know hOW the concentration Of a reactant or product varies with
time. For example, how long will it take fo r a pollutant to decay? How much of
the alternative fuel methanol can be produced in an hour from coal in an industrial
process? How much of a sample of penicillin will be left after 6 months? These
questions can be answered by using formulas derived from the experimental rate
law fO r the reactlons. An integrated rate la 、 gives the concentration Of reactants
or products at any time after the start Of the reaction. Finding the integrated rate
law from a rate law is very much like calculating the distance that a car will have
traveled from its speed at each moment Of the j ourney.
The integrated rate law for a zero-order reactlon is easy tO find. Because th e rate
IS constant （ at k), th e difference concentration Of a reactant from its initial value,
[A] 0 ， is proportional tO the time for which th e reaction is in progress, and we can write

slope 一 the reaction comes to an end when = [A] 0 ， because then all the reac-
tant has been consumed （ [A] = 0 ） ·
ln the next tWO sections, concentrate on first- and second-order rate laws,
but the techniques can be used fO r Other reaction orders, tOO.

The half-life, 行 / 2 ， Of a substance is the time needed fO r its concentration tO fall to

Reaction Mechanisms
Knowing hOW a reaction takes place at the molecular level provides answers tO
many lmportant questions. For example, what controls the rate Of formation Of the
DNA double helix from its individual strands? What molecular events convert
ozone intO oxygen or turn a mixture Of fuel and air 1ntO carbon dioxide and water
when it ignites in an engine ？ ln the following sections we see hOW tO use the rate
law fO r a reaction as a window intO these changes.
15 ． 7 EIementary Reactions
We stressed in Section 15 · 3 that we cannot write a rate law from a chemical equa-
tion. The reason is that all but the simplest reactions are the outcome Of several, and
sometimes many, Steps called elementary reactions. Each elementary reaction
describes a distinct event, Often a collision Of particles. TO describe hOW a reaction
takes place, chemists propose a reaction mechanism, a sequence Of elementary reac-
tions or Steps that they believe take place as reactants are transformed intO products.
Although several different mechanisms might be proposed fo r a reaction, rate
measurements can be used tO eliminate some Of them. For example, in the decom-
position of ozone in reaction E (Section 15 · 3 ）， 2 03(g) 艹 3 02(g), we could imagine
the reaction taking place tWO different ways:
One-steP ec 方： TWO 03 molecules collide and rearrange intO three
02 molecules (FIG. 15 · 16 ）：
03 + 03 一 02 + 02 + 02
0 一 s p e 动 0 ： ln the first step, an 03 molecule is energized by solar
radiation and dissociates intO an O atom and an 02 molecule. ln the second
Step, the O atom attacks another 03 molecule tO produce tWO more 02
molecules (FIG. 15 · 17 ）：
Step 1 03 一 02 + O
Step 2 0 + 03 一 02 + 02
The free O atom in the second mechanism IS a reactlon intermediate, a species that
plays a role in a reaction but does not appear in the chemical equation for the overall
reaction; it is produced in one Step b ut is used up in a later Step · Th e tWO equations
for the elementary reactlons add together tO give the equation for th e overall reaction.

15 ． 8 The Rate Laws of EIementary Reactions
TO verify that a proposed reaction mechanism agrees with experimental data,
chemists construct the overall rate law implied by the mechanism and check tO see
whether it is consistent with the experimentally determined rate law. However,
although the constructed rate law and the experimental rate law may be the same,
the proposed mechanism may still be incorrect because some Other mechanism
may also lead tO the same rate law. Kinetic information can only support a pro-
posed mechanism; it can never prove that a mechanism IS correct. acceptance
Of a suggested mechanism IS more like the process Of proof in an ideal court Of law
than a proof in mathematics, with evidence being assembled tO give a convincing,
conSIStent p1Cture.
TO construct an overall rate law from a mechanism, write the rate law fO r
each Of the elementary reactions that have been proposed, then combine them intO
an overall rate law. One procedure is tO use the steady-state approximation, which
assumes that any intermediate formed remams at a constant, IOW concentration.
We begin by writing the rate law fo r each step of the mechanism, including any
reverse reactions that affect the rate. Because an elementary reaction shows hOW
that Step Of the reaction occurs, we can write 1tS rate law (but 0 the rate law fO r
the overall reaction) from its chemical equation, with each power Of concentration
（ [A] ， [A] ， etc. ） in the rate law being the same as the number of particles of a given
type participating in the step, as summarized in TABLE 15 · 3 ·

15 ． 9 Chain Reactions
ln a chain reactlon, a highly reactive intermediate reacts tO produce another highly
reactive intermediate, which reacts t0 produce another, and so on (FIG. 15 · 1 9 ） · ln
many cases, the reaction intermediate—which in this context is called a chain
carr1er—1S a radical, and the reaction iS called a radical chain reaction. ln a radical
chain reactlon, one radical reacts with a molecule tO produce another radical, that
radical goes on tO attack another molecule tO produce yet another radical, and SO
on. The ideas presented in the preceding sections apply tO chain reactions, tOO, but
they Often result in very complex rate laws, which we will not derive.
The formation of HBr in the reaction
H2(g) + Br2(g) 一 2 HBr(g)
takes place by a chain reaction. The chain carriers are hydrogen atoms (H') and
bromlne atoms (Br•). The first Step in any chain reactlon is imtiatlon, the formation
of chain carriers from a reactant. Often heat (denoted A) or light (denoted 方 is
used tO generate the chain carrlers:

elementary reactions fO r the propagatlon Of the chain are
Br• + H2 一 HBr + H•
H• + B r2 一 HBr + Br•
The chain carners—radicals here—produced in these reactions can go on tO attack
other reactant molecules （ H2 and Br2 ）， thereby allowing the chain t0 continue. The
elementary reaction that ends the chain, a process called t ermin ati on, takes place when
chain carners combine tO form products. TWO examples Of termmation reactlons are
Br• + Br• 一 Br2
H• + Br · 一 HBr
ln some cases, a chain propagates explosively. Explosions can be expected
When chain branching occurs—that iS, When more than one chain carner iS formed
in a propagation Step. Reactions that are explosively fast are Often chain reactions.
The characteristic pop that occurs when a mixture Of hydrogen and oxygen is

15 ． 12 CoIIision Theory
We are now ready to build a model of how chemical reactions take place at the
molecular level. Specifically, our model must account for the temperature depen-
dence Of rate constants, as expressed by the Arrhenius equation; it should also
reveal the significance Of the Arrhenius parameters A and Ea. Reactions in the
gas phase are conceptually simpler than those in solution, and SO we begin with
them.
First, we assume that a reaction can take place only if reactants meet. ln a gas,
that meeting is a collision, and so the model that we are building is called the colli-
sion theory Of reactions. ln this model, we suppose that molecules behave like
defective billiard balls: they bounce apart if they collide at low speed, but they
might smash intO pieces when the impact is more energetic. If two molecules collide
with less than a certain kinetic energy, they simply bounce apart. If they meet with
more than that kinetic energy, reactant bonds can break and new bonds can form,
resulting in products (FIG. 15 · 25 ） · We denote the minimum kinetic energy needed
for reaction by 五
TO set up a quantitative theory based on this qualitative picture, we need tO
know the rate at which molecules collide and the fraction Of those collisions that
have at least the energy Em1n required fO r reaction tO occur. The co / 方 s / 0 frequency
(the number Of collisions per second) between A and B molecules in a gas at a tem-
perature T can be calculated from the kinetic model of a gas (Section 5 · 10 ）：
Collision frequency = 仃 vrelNA [A ] [B]
（ 15 ）

the area that a molecule presents as a target during a collision. The bigger the
collision cross section, the greater is the collision frequency, because big mole-
cules are easier targets than small molecules. The quantity Vre1 is the mean relative
speed, the mean speed at which the molecules approach each other in a gas. The
mean relative speed is calculated by multiplying each possible speed by the frac-
tion of molecules that have that speed and then adding all the products together.

and the collision frequency therefore increases as well, Eq. 16 shows that the mean
relative speed increases only as the square root Of the temperature. This depen-
dence is fa r tOO weak tO account fO r observations. If we used Eq. 16 tO predict the
temperature dependence Of reaction rates, would conclude that an increase lll
temperature of 10 OC at about room temperature (from 273 K to 283 K) increases
the collision frequency by a factor of only 1 · 02 ， whereas experiments show that
many reaction rates double over that range. Another factor must be affecting
the rate.
To find this factor, we need a measure of the fraction of molecules that collide
with a kinetic energy equal tO or greater than a certaln nummum energy

When molecules collide, old bonds give way to new ones
and atoms ln one molecule become part Of another. ls there

Molecular beams provide the answer. We first met

a stream Of molecules moving in the same directlon With
nearly the same speed. A beam may be directed at a gaseous
sample or 1ntO the path Of a second beam, consisting Of
molecules Of a second reactant. The molecules may react
when the beams collide; the experimenters can then detect
the products of the collision and the direction at which the
products emerge from the collision. They also use spectro-
scop1C techniques tO determine the vibrational and rota-
tional excitation Of the products.
By repeating the experiment with molecules having dif-
ferent speeds and different states Of rotational or vibrational
excltation, chemists can learn more about the collision itself.
For example, experimenters have found that, in the reactlon
between a CI atom and an HI molecule, the best direction of
attack is within a cone of half-angle 30 。 surrounding the H
atom (see Fig. 15 · 28 ） ·
ln a “ sticky" collision, the reactant molecules orbit
around each Other fO r one revolution or more. AS a result
the product molecules emerge in random directions because
any 'memory" Of the approach direction is lost. However,
a rotation takes time—about 1 PS. If the reaction IS over
before that, the product molecules will emerge in a specific
direction that depends on the direction Of the collision. ln
the collision of K and 12 ， fo r example, most of the products
are thrown Off in the forward direction. This observatlon
IS consistent with the "harpoon mechanism ” that had been
proposed for this reaction. ln this mechanism, an electron
flips across from the K atom to the 12 molecule when they
are quite far apart, and the resulting K+ ion extracts one Of
the atoms of the negatively charged 12 一 ion. We can think of
the electron as a harpoon, the electrostatic attractlon as the
line attached to the harpoon, and 12 as a whale. Because the
crucial "harpoomng' occurs at large distances and there iS
no actual collision, the products are thrown Off in approxi-
mately the same directlon as the reactants were traveling.
The reaction between a K atom and a CH31 molecule
takes place by a different mechanism. A collision leads to
reaction only if the tWO reactants approach each Other very
closely. ln this mechanism, the K atom effectively bumps
into a brick wall, and the KI product bounces out in the
backward direction.

15 ． 13 Transition State Theory
Although collision theory applies tO gas-phase reactions, we can extend some Of its
concepts tO explain why the Arrhenius equation alSO applies tO reactions ln solu-
tion. There, molecules do not speed through space and collide, but jostle through
the solvent and Stay in one another's vicinity fO r relatively long periods. The more
general theory that accounts bOth for this behavior and fO r reactions in gases IS
called transitlon state theory (which is also known as 忉把 d complex 乃 eor 回 ·
This theory improves on collision theory by suggesting a way 0f calculating the
rate constant even When SteriC reqmrements are significant.
ln transition state theory we lmagme tWO molecules approaching each Other
and being distorted as they come close enough to affect each other. ln the gas
phase, that meeting and distortion are equivalent tO the "collision ” Of collision
theory. ln solution, the approach is a jostling zigzag walk among solvent mole-
cules, and the distortion might not take place until after the tw O reactant mole-
cules have met and received a particularly vigorous kick from the solvent molecules
around them (FIG. 15 · 29 ） · ln either case, the collision or the kick does not imme-
diately tear the molecules apart. lnstead, the encounter results in the formation Of
an activated complex, an arrangement Of the tWO molecules that can either go on
tO form products or fall apart again intO the unchanged reactants. An activated
complex is also commonly called a transitlon state.

Of reaction rates, it is supposed that the potential energy (the energy due tO position) increases
as the reactant molecules approach each Other and reaches a maximum as they form a n activated
complex. lt then decreases as the atoms rearrange intO the bonding pattern characteristic Of
the products, and these products separate. Only molecules with enough energy can cross the
activation barrier and rea ct tO form products.
ln the activated complex, the original bonds have lengthened and weakened,
and the new bonds are only partly formed. For example, in the proton transfer
reaction between the weak acid HCN and water, the activated complex can be
pictured as consisting Of an HCN molecule with its hydrogen atom in the process
of forming a hydrogen bond to the oxygen atom of a water molecule and poised
midway between the tw 0 molecules. At this point, the hydrogen atom could re-
form HCN or leave as the product H30+
ln transition state theory, the activatlon energy IS a measure Of the energy Of
the activated complex relative tO that Of the reactants. The reaction profile in
FIG. 15 · 30 shows how the energy 0f the reaction mixture changes as the reactants
meet, form the activated complex, and then go on tO form products. A reaction
profile shows the potential energy 0f the reactants and products, their total energy
arising from their relative location, not their relative speed. NOW consider what
happens when reactants approach each other with a certain kinetic energy. As the
reactants approach, they lose kinetic energy as they “ climb ” up the left side of the
barrier (that is, as their potential energles increase due tO the repulsion resulting
from their closer approach and the distortions of their bonds). If the initial kinetic
energy Of the reactants is less than Ea, they cannot climb tO the top Of the potential
barrier, and they "roll ” back down on the left and separate again. If their initial
kinetic energy is at least Ea, they can form the activated complex, pass over the top
of the barrier, and roll down the other side, where they separate as products.
A potential energy surface can help us visualize the energy changes in the course
Of a reaction as a functlon Of the locations Of the atoms. ln this three-dimensional
plOt, the z-axis is a measure Of the tOtal potential energy Of the reactants and prod-
uctS and the 无一 and y-axes represent interatomic distances. For example, the plOt in
shows the potential energy changes that occur in the attack Of a bromine

The low-energy locations corresponding tO the reactants and products are sepa-
rated by a barrier over which there is a path Of minimum potential energy and
which the kinetic energy 0f the approaching molecules must overcome. The actual
path Of the encounter depends on the tOtal energies Of the particles, but we can
gain insight intO the reactlon process by examining potential energy changes alone.
For example, SLIPP0se the H—H bond remained the same length as the Br atom
approached. That would take the system t0 point A, a state of very high potential
energy. ln fact, at normal temperatures, the colliding species might not have
enough kinetic energy t0 reach this point. The path with the lowest potential
energy is the one up the foot of the valley, over the "saddle point" (the saddle-
shaped region) at the top of the pass, and down the foot of the valley on the other
side of the pass. Only the lowest-energy path is available: the H—H bond must
lengthen as the new H—Br bond begins to form ·
As in collision theory, the rate Of the reaction depends on the rate at which
reactants can climb tO the top Of the barrier and form the activated complex. The
resulting expression for the rate constant is very similar tO the one glven in Eq. 15 ，
and SO this more general theory also accounts for the form Of the Arrhenius equa-

We have seen that the rates Of many reactlons lncrease if the concentratlon Of reac-

15 ． 14 Catalysis
One way tO increase the rate Of a reaction is tO use a catalyst, a substance that
increases the rate without being consumed in the reaction (FIG. 15 · 33 ） · The name
comes from the Greek words meaning "breaking down by coming together." ln
many cases, only a small amount Of catalyst iS necessary, because it acts over and
over again. This is why small amounts Of chlorofluorocarbons can have such a
devastating effect on the ozone layer in the stratosphere—they break down intO
radicals that catalyze the destruction 0f ozone (BOX 15 · 3 ） ·
A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway—a differ-
ent reactlon mechanism—between reactants and products. This new pathway has
a lower activation energy than the original pathway (FIG. 1 5 · 34 ） · At the same tem-
perature, a greater fraction Of reactant molecules can cross the lower barrier Of the
catalyzed path and turn into products than when no catalyst is present. Although
the reaction takes place more quickly, a catalyst has no effect on the equilibrium
composition. BOth forward and reverse reactions are accelerated on the catalyzed
path, leaving the equilibrium constant unchanged.
ln some cases the original reaction With a SIOW rate-determining Step may con-
tinue in parallel with the catalyzed reaction. However, the rate is determined by the
faster path, which governs the overall rate of formation 0f products. A very slow

A heterogeneous catalyst is a catalyst present in a phase different from that Of
the reactants. The most common heterogeneous catalysts are finely divided or
porous solids used in gas-phase or liquid-phase reactions. They are finely divided
or porous SO that they will provide a large surface area fO r the elementary reactions
that provide the catalytic pathway. One example is the iron catalyst used in the
Haber process fo r ammonia. Another is finely divided nickel, which is used in the
hydrogenation of ethene:
H2C =CH2(g) + H2(g) 一 H3C—CH3(g)
The reactant is adsorbed on the catalyst's surface. As a reactant molecule attaches
tO the surface Of the catalyst, its bonds are weakened and the reactlon can proceed
more quickly because the bonds are more easily broken (FIG. 15 · 36 ） · One impor-
tant Step in the reaction mechanism Of the Haber process fO r the synthesis Of
ammonia is the adsorption Of N2 molecules on the iron catalyst and the weakening
of the strong N=N triple bond.

which hydrogen molecules have already adsorbed. When they adsorb, they dissociate and stick to
the surface as hydrogen atoms. Next, after the ethene molecule also sticks tO the surface, it meets
a hydrogen atom and forms a bond. At this stage, the •CH2CH3 radical is attached to the surface by
O n e Of its carbon atoms until it meets another hydrogen atom; then ethane is formed and escapes

15 ． 15 lndustrial CataIysts
The catalytic converters Of automobiles use catalysts tO bring about the complete
and rapid combustion of unburned fuel (FIG. 15 · 37 ） · The mixture of gases leaving
an engine includes not only carbon dioxide and water, but alSO carbon monoxide,
unburned hydrocarbons, and the nitrogen oxides collectively referred to as NO ·
Air pollution is decreased if the carbon compounds are oxidized tO carbon diox-
ide and the NOx reduced, by another catalyst, to nitrogen. The challenge is to find
a catalyst—or a mixture Of catalysts—that will accelerate bOth the oxidation and
the reduction reactions and be active when the car is first started and the engine
IS COOI.
Microporous catalysts are heterogeneous catalysts used in catalytic converters
and fO r many Other specialized applications, because Of their very large surface
areas and reaction specificity. Zeolites, fO r example, are microporous aluminosili-
cates (see Section 7 · 7 ） with three-dimensional structures riddled with hexagonal
channels connected by tunnels (FIG. 15 · 38 ） · The enclosed nature 0f the active sites
ln zeolites gives them a special advantage over Other heterogeneous catalysts,
because an intermediate can be held in place inside the channels until the products
form · Moreover, the channels allow products tO grow only tO a particular size.
One successful application of zeolites is the catalyst ZSM-5, which is used to
convert methanol tO gasoline. The pores Of the zeolite are just large enough tO
allow product hydrocarbons consisting Of about eight carbon atoms tO escape, SO
the chains dO not grow tOO long and equilibrium IS never reached.
Zeolite catalysts that adsorb harmful pollutants preferentially have been devel-
oped fO r use in industry and in catalytic converters fO r vehicles. ln catalytic con-
verters, they trap nitrogen oxides SO that they can be reduced tO harmless nitrogen
gas. Catalysts with a different formulation trap incompletely burned hydrocarbons
and oxidize them tO carbon dioxide.
Catalysts can be poisoned, or inactivated. A common cause Of such poisoning
is the adsorption of a molecule so tightly to the catalyst that it seals the surface of
the catalyst against further reaction. Some heavy metals, especially lead, are very
potent poisons fO r heterogeneous catalysts, which is why lead-free gasoline must be
used in engines fitted with catalytic converters. The elimination Of lead has the
further benefit Of decreasing the amount Of poisonous lead in the environment.

FIGURE 15 · 39 The lysozyme molecule is a typical enzyme molecule. Lysozyme is present in a
number Of places in the bOdy, including tea rs and the mucus in the nose. One Of its functions is
t0 attack the cell walls 0f bacteria and destroy them. This "ribbon" representation shows only the
general arrangement Of the atoms, tO emphasize the overall shape Of the molecule; the ribbon

with a slotlike active site, where reaction takes place (FIG. 15 · 39 ） · The substrate,
the molecule on which the enzyme actS, fits intO the slOt as a key fits intO a lock
(FIG. 1 5 · 40 ） · However, unlike an ordinary lock, a protein molecule distorts slightly
as the substrate molecule approaches, and its ability tO undergo the correct distor-
tion also determines whether the “ key" will fit. This refinement of the original
lock-and-key model is known as the induced-fit mechanism of enzyme action.
Once in the active site, the substrate undergoes reaction. The product is then
released fO r use in the next Stage, which is controlled by another enzyme, and the
original enzyme molecule iS free tO receive the next substrate molecule. One exam-
ple of an enzyme is the amylase present in your mouth. The amylase in saliva helps
to break down starches in food into the more easily digested glucose. If you chew
a cracker long enough, you can notice the increased syveetness.

MAJOR TECHNIQUE 5 Computation
omputers have had an enormous lmpact on the prac-
tice Of chemistry, in which they are used tO control
apparatus, record and manipulate data, and explore
the structures and properties Of atoms and molecules. Com-
puter modeling is applied to solids as well as to individual
molecules and is useful for predicting the behavior of a
material, for example, for indicating which crystal structure
of a compound is energetically most favorable, and fo r pre-
dicting phase changes. Here we concentrate on the use Of
computers in the exploratlon Of molecular structure. ln this
context, they are used bOth tO explore practical problems
such as predicting the pharmacological activity of com-
pounds and to achieve a deep understanding of the changes
that take place during chemical reactions.
ln se 在 e p / e 0 s ， complicated integrals are set
equal tO parameters that provide the best fit tO experimental
data, such as enthalpies Of formation. Semi-empirical meth-
Ods are applicable tO a wide range Of molecules with a virtu-
ally limitless number of atoms, and are widely popular. The
quality Of results is very dependent on usmg a reasonable set
Of experimental parameters that have the same values across
structures, and SO this kind Of calculation has been very suc-
cessful in organic chemistry, where there are just a few dif-
ferent elements and molecular geometries.
ln the more fundamental ab / / 0 e 乃 0 s ， an attempt
is made tO calculate structures from first principles, usmg
only the atomic numbers Of the atoms present and their
general arrangement in space. Such an approach iS intrmsl-
cally more reliable than a seml-empirical procedure but it is
much more demanding computationally.
A currently popular alternative tO the ab / / 0 method
is e ” 0 ” c 0 ” eor in which the energy is expressed
in terms Of the electron density rather than the wavefunc-
tion itself. The advantage of this approach is that it is less
demanding computationally, requires less computer time,
and in some cases—particularly for d-metal complexes—
gives better agreement with experimental values than Other
procedures.
The raw output Of a molecular structure calculation IS a
list of the coefficients of the atomic orbitals in each LCAO
(linear combination Of atomic orbitals) molecular orbital
and the energles of the orbitals. The software commonly
calculates dipole moments too. Various graphical represen-
tations are used tO simplify the interpretation Of the coeffi-
cients. Thus, a typical graphical representatlon Of a molecu-
lar orbital uses stylized shapes (spheres for s-orbitals, for
instance) tO represent the basis set and then scales their S1ze
to indicate the value of the coefficient in the LCAO. D iffer-
ent S1gns 0f the wavefunctions are typically represented by
different colors. The total electron density at any point (the
sum Of the squares Of the occupied wavefunctlons evaluated
at that point) is commonly represented by an isodensity
surface, a surface Of constant tOtal electron density.
An important aspect Of a molecule, in addition tO its
geometric shape and the energies Of its orbitals, is the distri-
bution Of charge over its surface, because the charge distri-
bution can strongly influence hOW one molecule (such as a
potential drug) can attach to another (and dock into the
active Site Of an enzyme, for instance) · A common procedure
begins with a calculation Of the electrical potential at each
point on an isodensity surface. The net potential is deter-
mined by subtracting the potential due tO the electron den-
sity at that point from the potential due to the nuclei. Th e
result is an electrostatic po / s 7 俨 ce ()n "elpot sur-
face " ） in which net positive potential is shown in one color
and net negative potential is shown ln another, with interme-
diate gradations Of color. The software can also depict a
solvent-accessible s 7 ' 厂 ce ， which represents the shape Of the
molecule by imaglmng a sphere representing a solvent mol-
ecule rolling across the surface and plotting the locations Of
1tS center.
Some graphical representations of fluoroethene, CHFCHF: (a) the
isodensity su rface showing the general shape of the molecule;
(b) the electrostatic potential surface showing the relatively
negatively charged region (denoted in red) close to the fluorine
atom; (c) the highest-energy occupied molecular orbital showing
the TT-bond between the tWO carbon atoms and the partial
involvement of a fluorine orbital; @） the lowest-energy unoccupied
orbital, which is the antibonding counterpart of the n-orbital.
Procedures are now available that allow fO r the pres-
ence Of several solvent molecules around a solute molecule.
This approach takes intO account the effect Of molecular
lnteractlons with the solvent on propertles such as the
enthalpy of formation and the shape adopted by a nonrigid
molecule, such as a protein or a region of DNA. These stud-
les are important fO r investigating the structures and reac-
tions Of biological molecules in their natural envlronment.

THE ELEMENTS:
THE MAIN-GROUP ELEMENTS
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? Knowledge of the family relationships
of the elements will help you t0 comprehend the nature of matter and may allow you
tO design new materials. The elements in the fi rst four main groups include carbon,
the central element Of life; silicon and germanium, which a re used tO create artificial
intelligence; calcium, which is responsible fo r the rigidity 0f 0 u r bones and teeth; the
space-age metals aluminum and beryllium; the alkali metals; and hydrogen, the fuel of
the sta rs—a nd perhaps O u r future energy source O n Earth. The elements in the last four
groups Of the periodic table include S O m e that are vital to life, such as the nitrogen Of
proteins, the oxygen of the air, and the phosphorus of o u r bones, and so a familiarity
with their properties will help you t0 understand living systems.
What Are the Key ldeas? The structures Of atoms determine their properties;
consequently, the behavior Of elements is related tO their locations in the periodic table.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? The information in this chapter is organized
around the principles of atomic structure and specifically the periodic table (Chapter 2 ） ·
However, the chapter draws O n all the preceding chapters, because it uses those
principles tO account fO r the properties of the elements.
his chapter and the next survey the properties Of the elements and their com-
pounds in relation tO their locations in the periodic table. The chemistry Of
the elements and their compounds is very much the heart Of chemistry, where
you bring t0 bear all the principles you have encountered in the earlier chapters and
see how they apply to the structures of compounds and the reactions they undergo.
TO prepare fo r this j ourney through the periodic table and the extraordinary
variety Of the properties Of the elements, their chemical "personalities," we first
revlew the trends in properties discussed in earlier chapters, then start with the
unique element hydrogen and move on tO the elements Of the main groups, work-
ing from left to right across the table. The same principles apply to the elements of
the d- and f-blocks, but those elements have some unique characteristics (mainly
their wide variety Of oxidation states and their ability tO act as Lewis acids), and SO
they are treated separately in Chapter 17 ·
Although periodic trends are the main focus of this chapter, we shall encounter
details such as where specific elements are found in nature and hOW they are puri-
fied. ln part, the usefulness and availability of an element reflects its abundance on
Earth and specifically in the Earth's crust, which may be quite different from its

Periodic Trends
We saw in Chapter 2 that the members of each group have analogous valence-shell
electron configuratlons, which give them similar properties. However, the element
at the head Of a group Often has features that distinguish it from its congeners, the
Other members Of the group. ln these introductory sectlons, we revlew atom1C
properties that correlate with the position Of an element in the periodic table. Then
we lnvestigate periodic trends in bonding by comparing examples Of tw O impor-
tant tYP e s 0f compounds—hydrides and oxides.
16 ． 1 Atomic Properties
th e elements in a given main group have ln common a characteristic valence
electron configuration. Th e electron configuration controls the number Of bonds that
an atom Of th e element can form and affects its chemical and physical properties.
Five atomic properties are pnncipally responsible for the characteristic properties Of
each element: atom1C radius, lomzatlon energy, electron affinity, electronegativity,
and polarizability. AII five properties are related to trends in the effective nuclear
charge expenenced by the valence electrons and their distance from the nucleus.
Valence electrons experience lncreasing effective nuclear charge on golng
across a period from left to right （ Chapter 2 and Fig. 2 · 19 ） · The attraction of a
valence electron tO the nucleus weakens sharply when electrons enter a new shell
because valence electrons belong tO shells that are successively farther from the
nucleus and surround electron-rich cores. valence electrons Of elements at the
upper right Of the periodic table, near fluorine, experience the greatest attraction tO
their nuclei and those Of elements at the lower left, near cesmm, experience the
least. As a result:
Atomic radii typically decrease from left tO right across a periOd and increase
down a group (FIG. 16 · 2 ； see also Figs. 2 · 20 and 2 · 21 ） ·
As the effective nuclear charge experienced by the valence electrons increases
across a period, the electrons are pulled closer tO the nucleus, thereby decreasmg
the atomic radius. D own a group the valence electrons are progressively farther
from the nucleus because they occupy shells with higher principal quantum number
and surround increasingly electron-rich cores, which increases the atomic radius.
lonic radii follow similar periodic trends (see Fig. 2 · 22 ） ·
First ionization energies typically increase from left tO right across a periOd and
decrease down a group (FIG. 16 · 3 ； see also Figs. 2 · 24 and 2 · 25 ） ·

669
increase in first ionization energies from left tO right across a periOd iS due
tO the increasing effective nuclear charge, which grips the electrons more tightly.
decrease ln lonization energy down a group shows that it iS easier tO remove
valence electrons from shells that are farther from the nucleus and hence shielded
by a greater number Of core electrons.
The highest electron affinities are found at the t0P right of the periodic table
(see Fig. 2 · 28 ； the trends are too ill defined to depict simply).
The electron affinity Of an element is a measure Of the energy released when an
amon is formed. Except fO r the noble gases, elements near fluorine have the highest
electron affinities, and SO are present as amons ln compounds With metallic ele-
ments. The increasing effective nuclear charge accounts fO r the trends in electron
affinity: more energy is released when electrons attach tO atoms with high effective
nuclear charge. However, the attachment Of a second or third electron ()s in the
formation of 02- or N 一） typically requires an input 0f energy, not a release, as
there is a strong repulsion from the negative charge already present.
． Electronegativities typically increase from left tO right across a periOd and
decrease down a group (FIG. 1 6 · 4 ； see also Fig. 3 · 12 ） ·
The greater the effective nuclear charge and the closer the electrons are tO the
nucleus, the stronger is the pull on the electrons in a bond. The electronegativity Of
an element—a measure Of the tendency Of an atom tO attract electrons tO itself
when it is part of a compound—is a useful guide to the typ e of bond that the ele-
ment is likely tO form · When there is a large difference in electronegativity between
tW O elements, their atoms form 10nic bonds with each other; when the difference IS
small, the bonds are covalent.
． PoIarizabilities typically decrease from left to right along a period and increase
down a group (FIG. 16 · 5 ） ·
Polarizability measures the ease with which an electron cloud can be distorted by
charges on neighboring speues and is greatest for the electron-rich, heavier atoms Of
a group and fo r negatively charged ions. On th e other hand, high polarizing power—
the ability tO distort the electron cloud Of a neighboring atom or ion—is commonly
associated with small size and high positive charge. We saw in Section 3 · 13 that a
highly polarizable atom or ion （ such as iodine or the iodide ion) in combination
with an atom or ion of high polarizing power （ such as beryllium) is likely to have
considerable covalent character in its bonds.
