18 ． 3 The Pattern of NucIear Stability
The nuclei Of some elements are stable, but others decay the moment they are
formed. lt would be useful tO know if there is a pattern tO the stabilities and insta-
bilities Of nuclei, because such a pattern would allow us tO make predictions about
the modes Of nuclear decay. One clue is that elements with even atomic numbers
are conslstently more abundant than neighboring elements with Odd atom1C num-
bers. This difference can be seen in FIG. 18 · 11 which is a plot of the cosmic abun-
dance Of the elements against atom1C number. The same pattern occurs on Earth.
Of the eight elements present as 1 ％ or more of the mass of the Earth, only one,
aluminum, has an Odd atomic number.
Nuclei with even numbers Of bOth protons and neutrons are more stable than
those with a ny Other combination. Conversely, nuclei with Odd numbers Of bOth
protons and neutrons are the least stable (FIG. 18 · 1 2 ） · Nuclei are more likely to be
stable if they are built from certain numbers of either kind of nucleons. These
numbers—namely, 2 ， 8 ， 20 ， 50 ， 82 ， 114 ， 126 ， and 184—are called magic numbers.
For example, there are ten stable isotopes of tin (Z = 50L the most of any element,
but only tw o stable isotopes of its neighbor, antimony (Z = 51 ） · The 仪 particle
itself is a "doubly maglc" nucleus, with tW O protons and tWO neutrons. We show
later that a number of actinoids decay through a series of steps until they reach Pb
another doubly magic nuclide, with 126 neutrons and 82 protons. This pattern of
nuclear stability is similar tO the pattern Of electron stability in atoms: the noble gas
atoms have 2 ， 10 ， 18 ， 36 ， 54 ， and 86 electrons.
FIGURE 18 · 13 is a plot 0f mass number against atomic number fo r known
nuclides. Stable nuclei are found in a band of stability surrounded by a sea 0f insta-
bility, the region of unstable nuclides that decay with the emission of radiation. For
atomic numbers up t0 about 20 ， the stable nuclides have approximately equal
numbers Of neutrons and protons, and SO A is close tO 2Z. For higher atomic num-
bers, all known nuclides—both stable and unstable—have more neutrons than
protons, and so A > 2Z.
increase in the ratiO Of neutrons tO protons With increasmg atomic number
can be explained by considering the role Of the neutrons in helping tO overcome the
electrical repulsions between protons. The strong force that holds the protons and
neutrons together in a nucleus IS powerful enough tO overcome the electrostatlc
repulsion between the protons, but it can act over only a very short distance—about
the diameter 0f a nucleus (FIG. 18 · 1 4 ） · Because neutrons are uncharged, they can
contribute tO the strong force without adding tO the electrostatic repulsion. A lOt Of
neutrons are needed tO overcome the mutual repulsion Of the protons ln a nucleus
of high atomic number, which explains why the band of stability curves upward.

18 ． 5 NucIeosynthesis
TO study some nuclear processes, scientists may need tO create certain nuclides that
might not exist naturally. For example, 3Li is an unstable nuclide that has SO many
neutrons that the strong force allows its nucleus tO expand about 10 times, tO nearly
th e size Of a radium nucleus. Such a nuclide can provide valuable information for
nuclear theorists, b ut it must be synthesized, because it does not occur naturally. Th e
process Of forming elements is nucleosynthesis. This process occurs naturally. Hydro-
gen and helium were produced in the Big Bang; all other naturally occurring elements
are descended from these tWO, as a result Of nuclear reactions taking place either in
stars or in space. Some elements—among them technetium and promethium—are
found in only trace amounts on Earth. Although these elements were made in Stars,
their short lifetimes did not allow them tO survive long enough tO contribute tO the
formation Of our planet. However, nuclides that are tOO unstable tO be found on Earth
can be made by artificial techniques, and scientists have added about 2700 different
nuclides to the approximately 270 that occur naturally.
TO overcome the energy barriers tO nuclear synthesis, particles must collide
vigorously with one another (FIG. 18 · 17 ）， as they d0 in the h0t interiors 0f stars.

Nuclear Radiation
Nuclear radiation IS sometimes called ion1ZIng radiation, because it IS energetic
enough tO eject electrons from atoms. Hospitals use nuclear radiation tO kill
unwanted tissue, such as cancerous cells (see Box 18 · 1 ） · Yet the same powerful
effects that help to diagnose and cure illness can also damage healthy tissue. The
damage depends on the strength of the source, the type of radiation, and the length
0f exposure. The three principal types 0f nuclear radiation have different abilities
t0 penetrate matter (TABLE 18 · 3 ） ·
18 ． 6 The BioIogicaI Effects of Radiation
Relatively massive, highly charged 仪 particles interact so strongly with matter that
they slow down, capture electrons from surrounding matter, and change intO bulky
helium atoms before traveling very far. They penetrate only the first layer of skin
and can be stopped by glass, by clothing, even by a sheet of paper. Most 仪 radiation
is absorbed by the surface layer of dead skin, where it can do little harm. However,
仪 particles can be extremely dangerous if inhaled or ingested. The energy 0f their
impact can knock atoms out Of molecules, which can lead tO serious illness and
death. For example, plutonium, considered tO be one Of the most toxic radioactive
materials, is an 仪 emitter and can be handled safely with minimal shielding. How-
ever, it is easily oxidized tO Pu + ， which has chemical properties similar tO those Of
Fe3+. PIutonium can take the place of iron in the body and become absorbed into
bone, where it destroys the body's ability to produce red blood cells. The result is
radiation sickness, cancer, and death.
Next in penetrating power is 阝 radiation. These fast electrons can penetrate
about 1 cm intO flesh before their electrostatic interactions with the electrons and
nuclei of molecules bring them to a standstill.
Most penetrating of all is radiation. The high-energy PY-ray photons can pass
right through buildings and bodies and can cause damage by ionizing the molecules
in their path. Protein molecules and DNA that have been damaged in this way can
no longer functlon, and the result can be radiation sickness and cancer. lntense
sources of A)'-rays must be surrounded by shields built from lead bricks or thick
concrete tO absorb this penetrating radiation.
The absorbed dose of radiation is the energy deposited in a sample ()n particu-
lar, the human body) when it is exposed to radiation. The SI unit of absorbed dose
is the gray, Gy, which corresponds to an energy deposit of 1 J•kg-l. The original unit
used for reporting dose was the radiation absorbed dose (rad), the amount Of radia-
tion that deposits 10 一 J of energy per kilogram of tissue, and so 1 rad = 10 一 2 Gy.

A dose of 1 rad corresponds to a 65-kg person absorbing a total of 0 · 65 J, which is
not very much energy: it is enough t0 boil only 0 · 2 mg 0f water. However, the
energy of a particle of nuclear radiation is highly localized, like the impact of a
subatomic bullet. As a result, the incoming particles can break individual bonds as
they collide with molecules in their path.
The extent of radiation damage t0 living tissue depends on the type of radia-
tion and the type Of tissue. We must therefore include the relative biological effec-
tivenes s, Q, when assessing the damage that a given dose Of each type Of radiation
may cause. For 阝 and radiation, Q is set arbitrarily at about 1 ； however, fO r 仪
radiation, Q is close to 20 · A dose of 1 Gy of radiation causes about the same
amount of damage as 1 Gy of 阝 radiation, but 1 Gy of 仪 particles is about 20 times
as damaging （ even though these particles are the least penetrating). The precise
figures depend on the tOtal dose, the rate at which the dose accumulates, and the
type Of tissue, but these values are typical.
The dose equivalent is the actual dose modified tO take intO account the differ-
ent destructive powers Of the vanous types Of radiation ln combination with vari-
ous tYP e s of tissue. lt is obtained by multiplying the actual dose ()n gray) by the
value of Q fo r the radiation type · The result is expressed in the SI unit called a
sievert (Sv):
Dose equivalent (Sv) = Q × absorbed dose (Gy)
The former (non-Sl) unit Of dose equivalent was the roentgen equivalent m an
(rem), which was defined in the same way as the sievert but with the absorbed dose
in rad; thus, 1 rem = 10 一 2 Sv.
A dose of 0 · 3 Gy （ 30 rad) of radiation corresponds to a dose equivalent of
0 · 3 Sv （ 30 rem) ， enough to cause a reduction in the number of white blood cells (the
cells that fight infection) ， but 0 · 3 Gy of 仪 radiation corresponds to 6 Sv （ 600 rem) ，
which is enough tO cause death if an 仪 emitter is ingested or inhaled. A typical
average annual dose equivalent that we each receive from natural sources, called
background radiation, is about 2 mSv•a¯ (where a, fO r annum, is the Sl abbreviation
for year), but this figure varies, depending on our life style and where we live · About
20 ％ of background radiation comes from our own bodies. About 30 ％ comes from
cosmic rays (a mix 0f PY-rays and high-energy subatomic particles from outer space)
that continuously bombard the Earth, and 40 ％ comes from radon seeping out of the
ground. Th e remaining 10 ％ is a result largely of medical diagnoses (a typical chest
x-ray gwes a dose equivalent of about 0 · 07 mSv). Emiss10ns from nuclear power
plants and Other nuclear facilities contribute about 0 · 19 in countries where they are
widely used.

The equation fo r the decay 0f a nucleus (parent nucleus 艹 daughter nucleus +
radiation) has exactly the same form as a unimolecular elementary reaction (Sec-

type Of decay is expected for a process that does not depend on any external factors
but only on the instability of the nucleus. The rate of nuclear decay depends only
on the identity Of the isotope, not on its chemical form or temperature.

Half-lives span a very wide range (Table 18 · 5 ） · Consider strontium-90, for
which the half-life is 28 · 1 a · This nuclide is present in nuclear fallout, the fine dust
that settles from clouds Of airborne particles after the explosion Of a nuclear bomb,
and may also be present in the accidental release Of radioactive materials intO the
air. Because it is chemically very similar tO calcium, strontium may accompany that
element through the envlronment and become lncorporated intO bones; once there,
it continues tO emit radiation for many years. About 10 half-lives (for strontium-90,
281 a) must pass before the activity of a sample has fallen to 1 / 1000 of its initial
value. lodine-131 is a radioisotope that was released in the accidental fire at the
1986 Chernobyl nuclear power plant and in the explosion at the Fukushima Daiichi
nuclear plant after the tsunami in Japan in 2011 · lt has a half-life of only 8 · 05 d,
but it accumulates in the thyroid gland. Supplemental iodine pills were issued to
people near these disasters so that their thyroids would already be saturated with
iodine, thus reducing the amount Of radioactive iodine that could be absorbed.
Despite these precautions, several cases Of thyroid cancer were linked tO iodine-131
exposure from th e Chernobyl accident. Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24 ka
（ 24 000 years) · Consequently, very-long-term storage facilities are required fo r
plutonium waste, and land contaminated with plutonium cannot be inhabited again
fO r thousands Of years without expensive remediation efforts.
The constant half-life of a nuclide is used to determine the ages of archaeo-
logical artifacts. ln isotopic dating, we measure the activity Of the radioactive iSO-
topes that they contain. lsotopes used fo r dating 0bj ects include uranium-23 8
potassium-40, and tritium. However, the most important example is radiocarbon
dating, which uses the 阝 decay of carbon-14, for which the half-life is 5730 a ·
Carbon-12 is the principal isotope of carbon, but a small proportion of
carbon-14 is present in all living organisms. lts nuclei are produced when nitrogen
nuclei in the atmosphere are bombarded by neutrons formed in the collisions Of
cosmic rays With Other nuclei:
7N + on 一 12C + IP
Carbon-14 atoms are produced in the atmosphere at an almost constant rate and,
as a result, the proportion Of carbon-14 tO carbon-12 atoms in the atmosphere
tends tO be constant over tlme. Carbon-14 atoms enter living organisms as 1 C02
through photosynthesis and digestion. They leave the organisms by the normal
processes Of excretlon and respiration and also because the nuclei decay at a steady
rate. As a result, all living organisms have a fixed ratio ()f about 1 to 1012 ） of
carbon-14 atoms to carbon-12 atoms, and 1 · 0 g of naturally occurring carbon has
an activity Of 15 disintegrations per minute.
When an organism dies, it no longer exchanges carbon With itS surroundings.
However, carbon- 14 nuclei already inside the organism continue tO decay with a con-
stant half-life, and so the ratio of carbon- 14 to carbon- 12 decreases. The ratio observed
a sample Of dead tissue can therefore be used tO estimate the time since death.

18 ． 8 Uses of Radioisotopes
Radioisotopes are radioactive isotopes. They are used not only tO cure disease (as
described in Box 18 · l), but also tO preserve fOOd, tO trace mechanisms Of reactions,
and tO power eqtupment in spacecraft.
Radioactive tracers are isotopes that are used tO track hOW substances change
and move. For example, a sample of sugar can be labeled with carbon-14; that is,
some carbon-12 atoms in sugar molecules are replaced by carbon-14 atoms, which
can be detected by radiation counters. ln this way, the progress through the body
Of even a tiny amount Of sugar molecules, tOO small an amount tO be detected by
Other means, can be monltored. Fertilizers labeled with radioactive nitrogen, phos-
phorus, or potassium are used to follow the mechanism of plant growth and the
passage Of these elements through the environment. Chemists and biochemists use
tracers tO help determine the mechanisms Of reactions. For example, if water con-
taining oxygen- 18 is used in photosynthesis, the oxygen produced is oxygen-18 ：
6 C02(g) + 6 H2180(l) 一 C6H1206(), glucose) + 6 1802 （ g ）
This result shows that the oxygen produced in photosynthesis comes from the
water molecules, not the carbon dioxide molecules.
Radioisotopes have lmportant commercial applications. For example,
amer1Cium-241 iS used in smoke detectors. ltS role iS tO iomze any smoke particles,
which then allow a current tO flow and set Off the alarm. Exposure tO radiation is
also used tO sterilize fOOd and inhibit the sprouting Of potatoes. Radioisotopes that
give Off a lOt Of energy as heat are used tO provide power remote locations, where
refueling Of generators is not possible. The instruments in unmanned spacecraft,
such as VO g 2 ， are powered by radiation from isotopes with long half-lives,
such as plutonium.
THINKING POINT Why a re some people opposed to the irradiation of food?
lsotopes are also used tO study the environment. Just as carbon-14 is used tO date
organic materials, geologists can determine the age Of very Old substances such as
rocks by measuring the abundance in rocks of radioisotopes with longer half-lives.
Uranium-238 / 2 = 4 · 5 Ga, 1 Ga = 109 years) and potassium-40 / 2 = 1 · 26 Ga ） are
used to date very old rocks. For example, potassium-40 decays by electron capture t0
form argon-40. The rock is placed under vacuum and crushed, and a mass spectrom-
eter is used tO measure the amount Of argon gas that escapes. This technique was used
to determine the age of rocks collected on the surface of the Moon; they were found
to be 3 · 5 · 0 billion years old, about the same age as the oldest rocks on Earth.

Nuclear Energy
Nuclear reactlons can release huge amounts Of energy, and nuclear reactors are
widely used to provide power. The benefits of nuclear power include the large
quantity 0f energy that can be obtained from a small mass of fuel and the absence
of chemical pollution of the kind associated with fossil fuels. However, like other
powerful resources, nuclear energy presents us with great technical challenges and
hazards. The following sections outline some of the principles.
18 ． 9 Mass—Energy Conversion
The energy released when the nucleons a nucleus adopt a more stable arrange-

nuclear products. Einstein's theory Of relativity tells us that the mass Of an Obj ect

its energy. Specifically, the total energy, ， and the mass, ， are related by Einstein's

The mass loss that always accompanies the loss 0f energy is normally fa r t00

The nuclear binding energy, Ebind, is the energy / e 然 e when protons and

reported as the energy per nucleon, and another way to think of binding energy is
as the average energy that must be supplied tO separate a nucleon from a nucleus.

Spontaneous nuclear fission takes place when the natural oscillations Of a
heavy nucleus cause it t0 break int0 tw 0 nuclei of similar mass (FIG. 1 8 · 21 ） · We can
think of the nucleus as distorting into a dumbbell shape and then breaking into two
smaller nuclei. An example is the spontaneous disintegration Of amencium-244
into iodine and molybdenum:
244
95Am 一 1 I + 42Mo + 3 on
107
Fission does not occur in precisely the same way ln every lnstance. For example, more
than 200 isotopes of 35 different elements have been identified among the fission prod-
ucts of uranium-235, with most products having mass numbers close to 90 or 130
(FIG. 18 · 22 ） ·
lnduced nuclear fission is fission caused by bombarding a heavy nucleus with
neutrons (FIG. 18 · 23 ） · The nucleus breaks into two fragments when struck by a
projectile. Nuclei that can undergo induced fission are called fissionable. For most
nuclei, fission takes place only if the impmging neutrons travel so rapidly that they
can smash intO the nucleus and drive it apart with the shock Of impact; uranium-23 8
undergoes fission in this way. Fissile nuclei, however, are nuclei that can be nudged
into breaking apart even by slow neutrons. They include uranium-235, uranium-233 ，
and plutonium-239—the fuels of nuclear power plants.
Once nuclear fission has been induced, it can continue, even if the supply Of
neutrons from outside is discontinued, provided that the fission produces more
neutrons. Such self-sustaining fission takes place in uranium-235, which undergoes
numerous fission processes, including

Neutrons produced in a chain reaction are moving very fast, and most escape
intO the surroundings without colliding with another fissionable nucleus. However,
if a large enough number Of uramum nuclei are present in the sample, enough neu-
trons can be captured tO sustain the chain reaction. ln that case, there is a critical
mass, a mass Of fissionable material above which SO few neutrons escape from the
sample that the fission chain reaction is sustained. If a sample is supercritical, with
a mass ln excess Of the critical value, then the reaction IS not only self-sustaimng
but difficult tO control and may result in an explosion. The critical mass fO r a solid
sphere of pure plutonium of normal density is about 15 kg, about the size of a
grapefruit. The critical mass is smaller if the metal is compressed by detonating a
conventional explosive that surrounds it. Then the nuclei are pressed closer together
and become more effective at blocking the escape Of neutrons. The critical mass can
be as low as 5 kg fo r highly compressed plutonium. A sample that has less than the
critical mass fO r its density is said tO be subcritical.
ln a nuclear weapon, the fissile material is initially subcritical. The challenge is
tO produce a supercritical mass SO rapidly that the chain reaction takes place UIII-
formly throughout the metal. Supercriticality can be achieved by shooting two sub-
critical blocks toward each other ()s was done in the bomb that fell on Hiroshima)
or by implosion of a single subcritical mass (the technique used in the bomb that
destroyed Nagasaki). A strong neutron emitter, typically polonium, helps t0 initiate
the chain reaction.
Explosive fission cannot occur ln a nuclear reactor, because the fuel iS not
dense enough. lnstead, reactors sustam a much slower, controlled chain reaction by
making efficient use Of a limited supply Of neutrons and slowing the neutrons
down · The fuel is shaped intO long rods and inserted intO a moderator, a material
that slows down the neutrons as they pass between fuel rods; the slower neutrons
have a greater probability of collision with a nucleus (FIG. 18 · 25 ） · Slow neutrons
have three significant roles: they dO not induce the fission Of fissionable ()s distinct
from fissile) material; they are most effectively absorbed by the fissile uranium-235 ·
and they are more easily controlled. The first moderator used was graphite. Heavy
water, D20, is also an effective neutron moderator, but light-water reactors （ LWR s ）
use ordinary water as a moderator. They are the most common type Of nuclear
reactor in the United States (FIG. 18 · 26 ） ·
If the rate Of the chain reaction exceeds a certain level, the reactor will become
tOO hOt and begin tO melt. Control rods—rods made from neutron-absorbing ele-
ments, such as boron or cadmium, and inserted between the fuel rods—help tO
control the number Of available neutrons and the rate Of nuclear reaction.
One of the many problems of nuclear power is the availability of fuel:
uranium-235 reserves are only about 0 · 7 ％ of those of the nonfissile uranium-238
and the separation of the isotopes is costly (Section 18 · 12 ） · One solution is t0 syn-
thesize fissile nuclides from Other elements. ln a breeder reactor, a reactor that is used
tO create nuclear fuel, the neutrons are not moderated. Their high speeds result in the
formation of not only uranium-235 but also some fissile plutonium-239, which can
be used as fuel ()r for warheads) · However, breeder reactors are more hazardous tO
operate than nuclear power plants. They run very hOt, and the fast reactions reqmre
more careful control than reactors used for nuclear poyver generation.

From the plOt in Fig. 18 · 20 ， we can see that there is a large increase ln nuclear
binding energy upon going from light elements such as deuterium to heavier ele-
ments. Consequently, energy is released when deuterium nuclei fuse together tO
form nuclei Of those elements. Unfortunately, the strong electrical repulsion between
protons makes it difficult fo r them to approach each other closely enough to fuse
together. The nuclei of the heavier isotopes of hydrogen fuse together more readily,
because the additional neutrons contribute tO the strong force and help tO capture
the approaching protons. To achieve the high kinetic energies needed fo r successful
collisions, fusion reactors need tO operate at temperatures above 108 K.
One fusion scheme uses deuterium (), H) and tritium (), H) in the following
sequence Of nuclear reactlons:
D + D 一 He + n
D + D 一 T + p
D + T 一 4He + n
D + 3He 一 4He + p
Overall reaction: 6 D 一 2 He + 2 p + 2 n
The overall reaction releases 3 × 108 kJ for each gram Of deuterium consumed.
That energy corresponds tO the energy generated when the Hoover Dam operates
at full capacity fo r about an hour. Additional tritium is supplied to facilitate the
process. Because tritium has a very IOW natural abundance and iS radioactive, it iS
generated by bombarding lithium-6 with neutrons in the immediate surroundings
Of the reaction zone:
6
Li + n 一 T + He
Nuclear fusion is very difficult tO achieve because the charged nuclei must be
hurled at each Other with enormous kinetic energies. One way Of accelerating
nuclei to sufficiently high speeds is to heat them with a fission explosion; this
method is used tO produce a thermonuclear explosion, an explosion due tO nuclear
fusion. ln "hydrogen bombs," a fission bomb (using uramum or plutonium) ignites
a lithium-6 fusion bomb. Fusion bombs can be Of varying destructive capacities,
because there iS no critical mass tO mamtain. Typical fusion bombs have a destruc-
tive capacity greater than 200 times that of the fission bombs that were dropped on
Hiroshima and Nagasaki in World War II.

18 ． 12 The Chemistry of NucIear Power
Chemistry is the key tO the safe use Of nuclear power. lt is used in the preparation
of the fuel itself, the recovery of important fission products, and the safe disposal
or utilization Of nuclear waste.
Uranium is the fuel Of nuclear reactors. The most important Of its minerals is
pitchblende, U02 (FIG. 1 8 · 28 ）， much of which is obtained from strip mines in New
Mexico and Wyoming. Uranium is refined tO reduce the ore tO the metal and tO
enrich it, that is, tO increase the abundance Of a specific isotope—in this case,
uranium-235. The natural abundance of uranium-235 is about 0 · 7 ％； fo r use in a
nuclear reactor, this fraction must be increased tO about 3 9 么 ·
The enrichment procedure uses the small mass difference between the hexa-
fluorides of uranium-235 and uranium-238 to separate them. The first proce-
dure tO be developed converts the uramum intO uranium hexafluoride, UF6,
which can be vaporized readily. The different effusion rates of the two isotopic
fluorides are then used tO separate them. From Graham's law Of effusion (rate Of

Spent nuclear fuel remams radioactive and conSISts Of a mixture Of uramum

The processing Of nuclear waste is complex. Any remaimng uramum-235
must be recovered, any plutonium produced must be extracted, and the largely
useless but radioactive fission products must be stored safely (FIG. 18 · 29 ） · The
highly radioactive fission (HRF) products from used nuclear fuel rods must be
stored until their level of radioactivity is no longer dangerous (about 10 half-
lives). Generally they are buried underground, but even burial of radioactive
wastes is not without problems. Metal storage drums can corrode and allow
liquid radioactive waste t0 seep into aquifers that supply drinking water (FIG.
18 · 30 ） · Leakage can be mimmized by incorporating the HRF products into a
glass—a solid, complex network Of silicon and oxygen atoms—ln a process
called c 0 Most Of the fission products are oxides Of the type that form
one of the components 0f glass: they are network formers (see Section 7 · 10 ）， that
is, they promote the formation of a relatively disorderly Si—O network rather
than inducing crystallization mto an orderly array Of atoms. Crystallization IS
dangerous because crystalline regions easily fracture, exposing the incorporated
radioactive materials tO moisture. Water could dissolve them and carry them
from the storage area. An alternative iS tO incorporate radioactive waste
intO hard ceramic materials (Section 7 · 11 ） · An example is Synroc, a fracture-
reslstant titanate-based ceramic that can accept radioactive waste products lnto
its lattice.

THE HYDROCARBONS
Why Do Yo u Need to Know This Material? AII life o n Earth is based o n carbon;
SO is the fuel we burn, O u r fOOd, and the clothes we wear. Therefore, tO understand a
major part of the everyday world, it is important to be familiar with the chemistry of this
extraordinary element. Compounds of carbon and hydrogen a re the foundation of the
petrochemical industry; petroleum products a re used tO generate electricity and tO heat
o u r homes. They a re also used to make the flexible, strong polymeric and composite
materials that make modern communication and transportation possible.
What Are the Key ldeas? La rge numbers of different hydrocarbons arise from the
ability Of carbon atoms tO form long chains and rings with O n e another; the types Of
carbon—carbon bonds present give hydrocarbons their characteristic properties.
What Do Yo u Need to Know Already? This chapter draws o n the introduction
tO organic formulas and nomenclature in Fundamentals, Sections C and D, the
structure of molecules (Chapters 3 and 4 ）， intermolecular forces (Sections 6 · 3 一 6 · 5),
reaction enthalpy (Section 8 · 1 3 ）， reaction mechanisms (Sections 15 · 7 一 1 5 · 9 ）， and
isomers (Section 17 · 7 ） ·
wo elements, carbon and hydrogen, are the basis 0f nearly all our fuels
including not only petroleum products but their alternatives. Carbon, the
focus Of this chapter and the next, is also the basis Of many materials that
are essential tO modern technology and even tO life itself. Understanding the com-
pounds that carbon forms and their reactions is therefore important not only tO
our technological and medical advances but also tO our very survival. Carbon
forms such a huge variety Of compounds that an entire field Of chemistry, organic
chemistry, is devoted tO its study. Carbon atoms are SO adaptable because they can
string together tO form chains and rings Of endless variety. This versatility allows
the element tO form thousands Of complicated biomolecules that contribute tO the
structure and function Of every organism on Earth. Synthetic carbon-based materi-
als also have a wide range Of properties, from the softness Of fabrics and artificial
skin tO the tough composite materials used in experimental aircraft.
THINKING POINT Why is carbon so special in its ability to form complex chains
and rings?
This chapter deals with hydrocarbons, compounds built from only carbon and
hydrogen. There are two broad classes of hydrocarbons: an aromatic hydrocarbon has
a benzene ring as a part Of its molecular structure; an aliphatic hydrocarbon does not.

CONCEPTUAL BASIS
Because the types Of carbon—carbon bonds present in the
molecule tend tO dominate its propertles, an aliphatic hydro-
carbon is first classified as an alkane, alkene, or alkyne. Then
the longest chain Of carbon atoms is used tO form the "root ”
of the name. Other hydrocarbon groups attached to the
longest chain are named as Side chains.

19 ． 3 Properties of Alkanes
The electronegativities of carbon and hydrogen （ 2 · 55 and 2 · 20 ， respectively) are so
similar and rotation about bonds SO free that hydrocarbon molecules are best
regarded as nonpolar. The dominant interaction between alkane molecules is there-
fore the London force (Section 6 · 4 ） · Because the strength Of this interaction
mcreases with the number Of electrons in the molecule, we can expect the alkanes
ln petroleum, their maJ or source, tO become less volatile With increasmg molar mass
and therefore to be separable by fractional distillation, as described in Section 10 · 19
(FIG. 19 · 4 ） · The lightest members, methane through butane, are gases at room tem-
perature. Pentane is a volatile liquid, and hexane through undecane （ C11H24 ） are
moderately volatile liquids that are present in gasoline, which is discussed further in
Section 19 · 9 · All alkanes are insoluble in water. Because their densities are lower than
that Of water, they float on th e surface Of water. Even a small Oil spill at sea can form
an organic layer on the surface Of the ocean and spread over a huge area.
THINKING POINT How could you estimate the area that 1 L of gasoline might
spread over on water?
Alkanes with long, unbranched chains tend to have higher melting points, boil-
lng points, and enthalpies Of vaporization than those Of their branched isomers.
The difference arises because, compared with unbranched molecules, the atoms Of
neighboring branched molecules cannot get as close together (FIG. 19 · 5 ） · As a
result, molecules with branched chains have weaker intermolecular forces than
their unbranched isomers.

The alkanes were once called the p 伊 ” s ， from Latin words meaning “ little
affinity." As this name suggests, they are not very reactive. They are unaffected by
concentrated sulfuric acid, by boiling nitric acid, by strong oxidizing agents such as
potassium permanganate, and by boiling aqueous sodium hydroxide. One reason
for their resistance to chemical onslaught is thermodynamic: the C—C and C—H
bonds are strong (their mean bond enthalpies are 348 kJ•mol-l and 412 kJ•mol
respectively), and SO there is little energy advantage in replacing them with most Other
bonds. Th e most notable exceptions are C=O （ 743 kJ•mol- ), C— O （ 360 kJ•mol- ），
and C—F （ 484 kJ•mol-l) bonds.
ln addition tO the catalyzed reactions used in the refining Of petroleum (see
Sections 19 · 5 and 19 · 9), alkanes undergo tWO common reactions: oxidation and
substitution (Section 19 · 4 ） · The alkanes are commonly used as fuels, because their
combustion to carbon dioxide and water is highly exothermic (Section 8 · 21 ）：

ln this reaction, the strong carbon—hydrogen bonds are replaced by the even stronger
O—H bonds （ 463 kJ•mol-l), and the oxygen—oxygen bond （ 496 kJ•mol- ） is replaced
by tw 0 very strong C==O bonds. Th e excess energy is given off as heat.

reactive compounds. Starting with alkanes obtained from the refining Of
petroleum, organic chemists introduce reactive groups Of atoms 1ntO the
molecules in the process called functionalization. Th e functionalization Of
alkanes can be achieved by a substitutlon reactlon, a reaction in which an
atom or group Of atoms replaces an atom ()n alkanes, a hydrogen atom)
in the original molecule (FIG. 19 · 6 ） · An example 0f a substitutlon reaction
is that between methane and chlorine. A mixture Of these tWO gases sur-

more than 300 OC, the gases react explosively:

high concentrations Of chlorine.

19 ． 5 Properties of AIkenes
carbon—carbon double bond in alkenes IS more reactive than carbon—carbon
single bonds and gives alkenes their characteristic properties. As we saw in Section
4 · 4 ， a double bond consists of a o-bond and a fi-bond. Each carbon atom in a
double bond is sp hybridized and uses the three hybrid orbitals to form three
c-bonds. The unhybridized p-orbitals on each carbon atom overlap each other and
form a q-bond. As we also saw in Section 4 · 7 ， although a double carbon—carbon
bond is stronger than a single carbon—carbon bond, the carbon—carbon fi-bond is
relatively weak because the overlap responsible fo r the formation of the q-bond is
less extensive than that responsible fO r the formation Of the ff-bond, and the
enhanced electron density does not lie directly between the tw O nuclei. A conse-
quence Of this weakness is the reaction most characteristic Of alkenes, the replace-
ment of the fi-bond by tw o new c-bonds, which is discussed in Section 19 · 6 ·
The C==C group and all four atoms attached to it lie in the same plane and are
locked into that arrangement by the resistance t0 twisting 0f the fi-bond (FIG. 1 9 · 7 ） ·

The addition of hydrogen chloride to give chloroethane is an example of a hydro-
halogenatlon reaction:
CH2== CH2 + HCI 一 CH3—CH2Cl
The model that organic chemists have built of the mechanism of alkene addition
reactions is quite different from that Of alkane substitution reactlons. Th e crucial
difference between the tw 0 types of molecules arises from the high density of elec-
trons in the region of the double bond (FIG. 1 9 · 1 0 ） · Because electrons are negatively
charged, this reglon represents an accumulation Of negative charge that can attract
a positively charged reactant. A reactant that is attracted tO a region Of high electron
density is called an electrophile. The mechanism of alkene addition is by electro-
philic attack on the carbon atoms that make up the double bond. An electrophile
may be a positively charged species or it may be a species that has a partial posltive
charge or can acqulre one in the course Of the reaction.
An example is the bromination of ethene. When ethene ()r a ny other alkene) is
bubbled through a solution of bromine, the solution is decolorized as the bromine
reacts tO form dibromoethane (this reaction is illustrated in Fig. 3 · 9 ） · Bromine mol-
ecules are polarizable; and, as a Br2 molecule approaches the high electron density
of an alkene double bond, a partial positive charge is induced on the Br atom closer
to the double bond (FIG. 19 · 1 1 ） · This separation of charges means that a Br2 mol-
ecule can act as an electrophile. As it moves in for the attack, the partially positively
charged Br atom becomes more and more like Br and itS partner becomes more
like Br-. The bond between the tw o Br atoms snaps, and the Br ion forms a bridge
between the tWO carbon atoms Of the alkene, g1V1ng a cyclic "bromonlum 10n
Almost immediately, a Br¯ ion swoops in fO r the attack, attracted by the positive
charge Of the bromomum ion. lt forms a bond tO one carbon atom, and the bond
from that carbon atom tO the bromine atom already present breaks as the bromine
atom moves onto the second carbon atom, g1Ving l,2-dibromoethane:
With the use of a solid-state catalyst, hydrogen can be added to carbon—carbon
double bonds in a hydrogenatlon reaction:
catalyst
This reaction is used in the fOOd industry tO convert vegetable Oils intO shortening
(FIG. 19 · 1 2 ） · Oil and solid fa t molecules both have long hydrocarbon chains, but
oils have more double bonds. Because double bonds resist twisting, oil molecules
do not pack together well, and so the oil is liquid at ordinary temperatures. When
some of the double bonds are replaced by single bonds, the chains become much
more flexible, and so the molecules pack together better and form a solid.

Aromatic Compounds
Aromatic hydrocarbons, which originally got their name from the distinctive odors
many Of them have, are called arenes. They all contain an aromatic ring, usually
the six-membered ring of benzene, which was introduced in Sections 3 · 7 ， 4 · 7 ， and
4 · 12 · An abundant source Of arenes IS coal, which is a very complex mixture Of
compounds, many Of which consist Of extenslve networks contalning aromatic
rings (Section 19 · 10 ） ·
19 ． 7 Nomenclature of Arenes
The parent compound of aromatic hydrocarbons is benzene, C6H6 （ 30 ） · 、 When
the benzene ring is named as a substituent, it is called the p 乃 e ， / group, as ln
2-phenylbutane, CH3CH(C6H5)CH2CH3. ln general, aromatic hydrocarbon groups
are called 0 / groups. Aromatic compounds also include the fused-ring analogs of
benzene, such as naphthalene, C10H8 （ 31L and anthracene, C14H10 （ 32 ）， obtained

19 ． 8 EIectrophiIic Substitution
Arenes are unsaturated but, unlike the alkenes, they are not very reactive. Whereas
alkenes commonly take part in addition reactions, arenes undergo predominantly
s b 豆 0 reactions, with the q-bonds Of the ring left intact. For example, bro-
mine immediately adds to a double bond of an alkene but reacts with benzene only
in the presence of a catalyst—typically, iron(lll) bromide—and it does not affect
the bonding in the ring. lnstead, one of the bromine atoms replaces a hydrogen
atom tO give bromobenzene, C6H5Br:
FeBr3
C6H6 + Br2 一 C6H5Br + HBr
The mechanism Of substitution on an electron-rich benzene ring is electrophilic sub-
s titutl on, electrophilic attack on an atom and the replacement Of one atom by another
or by a gr O up Of atoms. The fact that substitution occurs rather than addition tO the
double bonds can be traced to the stability of the delocalized fi-electrons in the ring ·
Delocalization give s th e electrons such low energy—that is, they are bound so tightly—
that they are unavailable for forming new o-bonds (see Sections 3 · 7 and 4 · 12 ） ·
The bromination Of benzene illustrates the difference between electrophilic
addition tO alkenes and electrophilic substitution Of arenes. First, tO achieve the
bromination Of benzene it is necessary tO use a catalyst, such as iron(lll) bromide.
The catalyst acts as a Lewis acid, binding to the bromine molecule (a Lewis base)
and ensuring that the outer bromme atom has a pronounced partial positive charge:

atoms. ） The outer bromme atom Of the complex is now primed tO act as a strong
electrophile (FIG. 19 · 1 3 ） ·

Certain groups attached tO an aromat1C ring can donate electrons intO its delO-
calized molecular orbitals. Each Of these electron-donating substituents has an elec-
tronegative atom with at least one lone pair Of electrons attached directly tO the
aromatic ring. Examples include —NH2 and —OH. EIectrophilic substitution of
benzene IS much faster When an electron-donating substituent iS present. For exam-
ple, the nitration of phenol, C6H50H, proceeds so quickly that it requires no cata-
lyst. Moreover, when the products are analyzed, the only products are found to be
2-nitrophenol (ortho-nitrophenol, 38 ） and 4-nitrophenol (para-nitrophenol, 39 ） ·
Why is th e meta position such an unattractive location for substitution, and why
does phenol react much faster than benzene ？ An electrophile is attracted tO regions Of
high electron density. Therefore, tO account for the fast reaction Of phenol, the electron
density must be greater in the ring when the electron-donating ¯OH substituent is
present. TO account for the dominance Of the O rth O and para products, electron den-
sity must be relatively high at the ortho and para positions. A molecular orbital calcu-
lation, such as those described in Maj or Technique 5 ， shows that there is indeed a
higher concentration Of electrons in the ring in phenol, especially at the O rth O and para
posltlons, than in benzene, largely because the O atom has lone pairs Of electrons that
can participate in q-bonding with th e carbon atoms (FIG. 19 · 14 ） ·

19 ． 10 CoaI
As reserves Of petroleum decline worldwide, interest in making better use Of coal
is growing. The thought Of an automobile that runs on coal is strange, but the use
0f gasoline substitutes derived from coal is a real possibility. Unfortunately, the
lncreased usage Of coal raises envlronmental concerns. Coal contams a much lower
ratio of hydrogen t0 carbon than petroleum and is harder to purify, to work, and
tO transport. Although bOth coal and petroleum contribute tO the greenhouse
effect, the use of coal is potentially more damaging. When it burns, coal also
releases a large amount Of pollution in the form Of particulate matter (primarily
ash) and sulfur and nitrogen oxides. Much Of the research on coal is aimed at
converting lt mtO more useful fuels.
Coal contains many aromatic rings (FIG. 19 · 1 6 ） · Coal is the end product of the
decay Of swamp vegetation in e 了 Ob / C conditions (With a very IOW concentration
of oxygen) · Oxygen and hydrogen are gradually lost through the 乙 0 ca 0 ” pro-
cess. As coalification proceeds, hydrogen is released and the aromatic structures
lncrease.
When coal is destructively distilled—heated in the absence 0f oxygen so that it
decomposes and vaporizes—its sheetlike molecules break up ， and the fragments
include aromatic hydrocarbons and their derivatives. CO / gas, which is given Off
first, contams carbon monoxide, hydrogen, methane, and small amounts Of other
gases. The complex liquid mixture that remams is called co A large number
Of pharmaceuticals, dyes, and fertilizers come from coal tar. Benzene is the raw
material fO r many plastics, detergents, and pesticides. Naphthalene is used tO make
synthetic indigo (the dye in blue jeans), ammonia is used as fertilizer, and pitch,
which contains the heaviest tars, IS used for waterproofing and rustproofing.

carbon monoxide and hydrogen in coal gas can be used as is, but that nuxture IS

MAJOR TECHNIQUE 6 Mass Spectrometry
n spectroscopy, a diffraction gratmg or prism is used tO
separate photons of light by their wavelengths. ln 然 s
spectrometry, a magnetic field is used tO separate ions by
their masses. This technique IS one Of our most powerful
analytical methods because it provides bOth quantitative and
qualitative informatlon about the substance being analyzed,
it requires only tiny samples, and it can be conducted in the
field, by using lightweight, portable units · Mass spectrometry
is used tO determine isotopic abundance （尸 e / s ， Sec-
tion B), to study the composition of bone and other body
tlssues, tO analyze the blood Of newborns for congenital dis-
eases, tO detect vanishingly small concentrations Of drugs in
urlne, and tO determine the structure Of the human genome.
The Technique
We met a classic type Of mass spectrometer in 尹 e / s ，
Section B. Another common type Of mass spectrometer is
the / ge 一 g ” s “ 0 (Fig. 1 ） · ln each case, the
spectrometer uses the degree tO which charged particles are
deflected by a magnetic field tO determine the relative masses
Of the particles. ln a mass spectrometer, the sample is first
vaporized and then ionized. resulting ions are acceler-
ated by an electric field intO a narrow beam that, as it passes
between a set Of magnets, is deflected toward a detector. The
heavier the particle, the less it is deflected, and the degree of
deflection allows the relative masses Of the particles tO be
determined. The results are displayed as a senes 0f peaks,
with the height of each peak being proportional to the rela-
tive number Of particles with a given mass.
The entire spectrometer must first be evacuated (have all
the air pumped out) tO ensure that no gas molecules can COI-
lide with the ions produced from the sample and deflect them
in unpredictable ways. Then the sample is introduced in the
form of a vapor into the sample inlet chamber and through
a pinhole intO the iomzation chamber. ln this chamber, rap-
idly moving electrons collide violently with the molecules of

the vapor. When one Of the accelerated electrons collides with
a molecule, the colliding electron knocks another electron
out Of the molecule, leaving a molecular cation. Th e molecu-
lar ion may split apart intO tw O or more charged fragments.
Th e positive ions—the onginal （ "parent" ） molecular ions
and their fragments—are accelerated out of the chamber by
a strong electric field applied across a series of metal grids.
Th e speeds reached by the ions depend on their masses: light
IOIIS reach higher speeds than heavier ones.
The rapidly moving lons pass between the poles of an
electromagnet. Th e magnetic field bends the paths of th e ions
tO an extent that depends on their speeds and on the strength
of the field. ln the large-magnet mass spectrometer, the mag-
netic field is kept constant but the strength of the electric field
iS varied, and SO the molecular ions are accelerated tO differ-
ent speeds. At a gwen electric field strength, ions of only one
particular mass reach the detector. Any ions with different
masses collide with the walls of the chamber. The strength of
th e electric field is varied and the result is a mass spectrum—a
plot of the detector signal against the strength of the electric
field. The positions of the peaks in the mass spectrum give th e
mass-to-charge ratios Of the ions. If all the ions have charges
of + 1 ， then the peaks give the mass ratios and their relative
heights give th e proportions Of ions Of various masses.
Analyzing a Mass Spectrum
If the sample consists Of atoms Of one element, the mass
spectrum gives the isotopic distribution Of the sample, as in
Fig. B.6 of 尹 ” e ” / s · The relative molar masses of the
1S0topes can be determined by comparison with atoms Of
carbon-12. If the sample is a compound, the formula and
structure of the compound can be determined by studying
the fragments. For example, the + 1 ions that CH4 could
produce are CH4 ， CH3+, CH2+, CH+, C+, and H+. Some of
the particles that strike the detector are those that result
when the molecule simply loses an electron (for example, t0
produce CH4+ from methane) ：
Molecule + e 一一 molecule + + 2 e
The mass Of this molecular ion, the p e / 0 is called the
p 了 e mass. The parent ion has essentially the same molar
mass as the compound itself. However, if the electron beam
moving at a very high speed, only fragments of the mole-
cule may survive. Some fragments are almost always pro-
duced, and other information must be used to help with the
lnterpretation. For example, a sample Of a known com-
pound can be analyzed and its spectrum compared tO that Of
an unknown sample to look for similar fragments. Th e
sample can also be passed through a gas chromatograph first
(see MaJ or Technique 4 ） · The chromatogram allows com-
panson with a large number of possible compounds, and the
mass spectrum verifies the identification.
The identification Of a molecular structure from a mass
spectrum reqmres good chemical detective work. Let's see
how that is done by trying t0 identify a simple compound, the
one that produced the mass spectrum summarized in the table.

Why Do Yo u Need to Know This MateriaI? Organic chemistry is the foundation
Of the pharmaceutical industry and, consequently, Of medicine. Organic chemistry
is also the basis of biochemistry and molecular biology; through those disciplines, it
provides a n understanding of life. The great diversity 0f organic molecules found in
li\/ing systems results fro m the presence Of groups Of atoms with characteristic functions.
Once you understand the properties of these groups, you will be able t0 predict the
properties Of Other organic molecules, even those Of the giant biomolecules Of proteins,
carbohydrates, and genetic material, and the synthetic polymeric materials that have
revolutionized O u r lives.
What Are the Key ldeas? The properties and reactions of many organic compounds
a re due tO the presence Of characteristic groups Of atoms known as functional groups.
What Do Yo u Need to Know AIready? This chapter builds o n Chapter 1 9 and
requires the sa m e preparation, as well as the concepts Of acid—base and redox reactions
(FundamentaIs, Sections J and K) · lt also makes use of the concepts of molecular
polarity (Section 4 · 3 ） and solubility (Section 10 · 9 ） ·
O solve some Of the most difficult problems related tO materials, scientists
must lOOk tO organic chemistry. For example, soldiers and law enforcement
officers sometimes did not wear bOdy armor because its bulk interfered with
their movement, leading t0 tragic loss of life. Today, body armor made from organic
compounds is lightweight and flexible and so is saving lives. The whole of the life-
saving pharmaceutical industry is an application Of organic chemistry. Molecular
biology, the understanding of the processes of life, is another. This broad array of
applications shows the immense variety Of orgamc compounds, a variety that can
be intimidating at first sight. Fortunately, organic compounds can be understood in
terms of a relatively small number of functional groups, which are small groups of
atoms with characteristic properties. Whereas the hydrocarbons are built only from
carbon and hydrogen, functional groups may include atoms of other elements.
Because functional groups have characteristic chemical properties, it iS not neces-
sary t0 learn all the properties 0f each different compound—once the functional
groups that are present have been identified, you will have gone a long way toward
understanding and predicting the likely chemical properties of the compound.
This chapter has three parts. ln the first part, we lOOk at the structures and
properties Of some Of the common functional groups and describe some Of the
characteristlc mechanisms by which the groups react. Then we examine hOW func-
tional groups are used tO create modern polymers. AS in SO many spheres, nature
has preceded chemists' explorations. ln the final part Of the chapter, we meet some
examples Of hOW functional groups in nature sustaln LIS, feed us, and reproduce LIS.

Common Functional Groups
Functional groups are either attached tO the carbon backbone Of a molecule or form
part of that chain. Examples are the chlorine atom in chloroethane, CH3CH2CI, and
the —OH group in ethanol, CH3CH20H. Carbon—carbon multiple bonds, such
as the double bond in 2-butene, CH3CH=CHCH3, are also often considered func-
tional groups. TABLE 20 · 1 lists the most common functional groups. Double and
triple carbon—carbon bonds were considered in Chapter 19 · ln the following eight

The haloalkanes (also called alkyl halides) are alkanes in which at least one hydro-
gen atom has been replaced by a halogen atom. Although they have important
uses, many haloalkanes are highly toxic and a threat to the envlronment. The halo-
alkane 1,2-dichlorofluoroethane, CHClFCH2Cl, is an example of a hydrochloro-
fluorocarbon (HCFC), one of the compounds held responsible fo r the depletion of
th e ozone layer (see Box 15 · 3 ） · Many pesticides are aromatic compounds with several
halogen atoms.
Carbon—halogen bonds are polar （ 1 ） · The carbon atom to which the halogen
atom is attached is partially positive, making it susceptible tO nucleophilic sub-
stltution, in which a nucleophile replaces the halogen atom. A nucleophile is a
reactant that seeks out centers Of positive charge in a molecule. TWO examples
are the hydroxide ion, OH-, and the water molecule, H20. ln each case a lone
palr on the oxygen atom is attracted tO regions Of partial positive charge; the
hydroxide ion is the stronger nucleophile because Of its negative charge. Water
actS as a nucleophile in a hydrolysis reaction, a reaction with water in which a
carbon—element bond is replaced by a carbon—oxygen bond. For example, bro-
momethane undergoes hydrolysis by hydroxide ions in aqueous ethanol to
methanol and bromide ions:

Ethers are more volatile than alcohols of the same molar mass because their mol-
ecules do not form hydrogen bonds to one another (FIG. 20 · 2 ） · They can form
hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but they are less soluble in water than alco-
hOls because they can only accept protons, not donate them, and as a result they
cannot form as many hydrogen bonds tO water molecules as alcohols dO. Because
ethers are not very reactive and not very polar, they are useful solvents fO r Other
organic compounds. However, ethers are dangerously flammable; diethyl ether is
easily ignited and must be used with great care.
Cyclic ethers (ethers in the form of a ring) with alternating —CH2CH2—O—
units are called cr own ethers, owmg t0 the crownlike shape of the molecules （ 3 ） ·
Crown ethers bind very strongly tO certain metal cations; fO r example, a crown
ether effectively encases K+ in a shell with the O atoms pointing inward toward
the K+ ion and the hydrocarbon chain wrapped around the outside. Thus, crown
ether molecules act as a sort Of "Trojan horse ” fO r the K+ ions, which in this form
are soluble in nonpolar solvents. Potassium permanganate, KMn04, fO r example,
dissolves readily in benzene when a crown ether with six O atoms is added tO it.
resulting solution can be used tO carry out oxidation reactlons ln orgamc
solvents.

20 ． 9 Addition PoIymerization
Alkenes can react with themselves tO form long chains in a process called addition
polymerizatlon. For example, an ethene molecule may form a bond tO another
ethene molecule; another ethene molecule may add tO that, and SO on, forming a
long hydrocarbon chain. The original alkene, such as ethene, is a small molecule
called the monomer. Each monomer becomes one repeatlng unit, the structure that
repeats over and over t0 produce the polymer chain. The product, the chain of
covalently linked repeating units, is the polymer. The simplest addition polymer is
polyethylene, 一（ CH2CH2)n—, which is made by polymerizing ethene and so con-
sists of long chains of thousands of repeating —CH2CH2— units. Many addition
polymer molecules also have a number of branches, which are generated as new
chains sprout from intermediate points along the "backbone ” chain.
Th e plastics industry has developed polymers from a number of monomers with
the formula CHX=CH2, where X is a single atom （ such as the CI in vinyl chloride,
CHCl==CH2 ） or a group of atoms （ such as the CH3 in propene ） · These substituted
ethenes are used to make polymers of formula 一（ CHXCH2 )n—, including p 0 lyvinyl
chloride (PVC), 一（ CHC ℃ (2)n—, and polypropylene, —(CH(CH3)CH2)n— (TABLE
20 · 2 ） · They differ in appearance, rigidity, transparency, and resistance t0 weathering.

20 ． 11 Copolymers
Copolymers are polymers made up of more than one type 0f repeating unit
(FIG. 20 · 14 ） · One example is nylon-66, in which the repeating units are formed
from 1,6-diaminohexane, H2N （ CH2 ） 6NH2, and adipic acid, HOOC(CH2)4COOH.
They form an alternating copolymer, in which acid and amine monomers alternate.
ln a block copolymer, a long segment made from one monomer is followed by
a segment formed from the other monomer. One example is the block copolymer
formed from styrene and butadiene. Pure polystyrene is a transparent, brittle ma-
terial that is easily broken; polybutadiene IS a synthetic rubber that is very resilient,
but soft and opaque. A block copolymer of the two monomers produces g 乃巧 p
p00S0 了 e e ， a material that is a durable, strong, yet transparent plastic. A different
formulation of the tw o polymers produces sty ” e 一 b d 讵 ” e rubber (SBR), which
IS used mainly fO r automobile tires and running shoes, but also in chewing gum.
ln a random copolymer, different monomers are linked in no particular order.
A graft copolymer consists Of long chains Of one monomer with shorter chains Of
the Other monomer attached as side groups. For example, the polymer used tO
make hard contact lenses is a nonpolar hydrocarbon that repels water. The polymer
used tO make soft contact lenses is a graft copolymer that has a backbone Of non-
polar monomers but side groups Of a different water-absorbing monomer. SO much
water is absorbed by the side chains that 50 ％ of the volume of the contact lens is
water, which makes it pliable, soft, and more comfortable tO wear than a hard con-
tact lens. Composite materials (Section 7 · 17 ） differ from copolymers in that the
tw O materials making up the composite retain their identities in the material and
the separate regions can be large.

20 ． 12 Physical Properties of PoIymers
A polymer can be designed to have the desired properties fo r an application. The
first consideration is chain length. Because synthetic polymers consist Of mole-
cules with different lengths, they do not have definite molar masses. We can speak
only of the average molar mass and the average chain length of a polymer. Because
of the variability in chain length, polymers do not have definite melting points;
rather, they soften gradually as the temperature is raised. The viscosity 0f a poly-
mer, its ability to flow when molten (Section 6 · 7), depends on its chain length. The
longer the chains, the more tangled together they may be, and hence the slower
their flow.
The mechanical strength Of a polymer lncreases as the strength Of the interac-
tions between chains lncreases. Therefore, the longer the chains, the greater is the
strength of the polymer. For chains of the same length, stronger intermolecular
forces result in greater mechanical strength. The nature Of the groups Of atoms
attached to or that form a part of the backbone of a polymer affects the strength of
intermolecular forces and contributes tO the mechanical strength Of the polymer.
For example, nylon is a polyamide and so has a series of repeating —NH— and
—(CO)— groups that are hydrophilic and can take part in hydrogen bonding.
Consequently, nylon is a strong polymer. lt is also 乃， g 了 0 釔 0 庳 c (absorbs water),
because the water molecules are attracted tO these polar groups. ln contrast, poly-
ethylene is a hydrocarbon that contains only C—C and C—H bonds, which are
hydrophobic. As a result, whereas polyethylene repels water, water can penetrate
through thin nylon fabrics because H20 molecules can migrate by forming and
breaking hydrogen bonds to the polymer molecules.
The chain-packing arrangements that maxlnuze mtermolecular contact result
in greater strength as well as greater density. Long, unbranched chains can line up
next tO one another like uncooked spaghetti and form crystalline regions that result
in strong, dense materials. Branched polymer chains cannot fit together as closely
and form weaker, less dense materials (FIG. 20 · 1 5 ） · A soft, lightweight body armor
has been developed by creating arrays of long polyethylene chains that are closely
aligned in the same direction, g1V1ng rise tO very strong intermolecular forces. This
bOdy armor is reported tO be 15 times stronger than steel, yet it has such a IOW
density that it floats on water. lt is also soft and flexible, SO it is comfortable tO wear
(FIG. 20 · 16 ） ·
The elasticity Of a polymer is its ability tO return tO its original shape after
being stretched. Natural rubber has long hydrocarbon chains with low elasticity
and is easily softened by heating. However, the "vulcanization ” Of rubber increases

The secondary structure of a protein is the shape adopted by the polypeptide
chain—ln particular, hOW it coils or forms sheets. The order Of the amino acids in
the chain controls the secondary structure, because their intermolecular forces hOld
the chains together at specific points. The most common secondary structure in am-
mal proteins is th e 仪 helix, a helical conformation of a polypeptide chain held in
place by hydrogen bonds between residues (FIG. 20 · 20 ） · One alternative secondary
structure is the 阝 sheet, which is characteristic Of the protein that we know as silk. ln
silk, protein molecules lie side by side to form nearly flat sheets. Th e molecules of
many other proteins consist 0f alternating a-helical and ß-sheet regions (FIG. 20 · 21 ） ·
Th e tertiary S tru cture Of a protein is the shape intO which its secondary structure
is folded as a result Of interactions between residues. The globular form Of each chain
in hemoglobin is an example. One important typ e 0f link responsible for tertiary
structure is the covalent disulfide link, —S—S—, between residues containing sulfur.
Other links are formed by the various typ e S Of intermolecular forces. ln most cases, a
glven protein will fOld intO a precise three-dimensional conformation determined by
the locations of the hydrophobic and hydrophilic groups on the chain (FIG. 20 · 22 ） ·
Sometimes, however, the proteins do not fold properly. When this incorrect folding
happens in the body, it can lead to illnesses such as Alzheimer's disease. ln Alzheimer's
disease, brain function is constricted by deposits Of proteins that have misfolded and
can no longer perform their functions · Th e so-called diseases," such as variant
Creutzfeld 刁 akob disease （ "mad cow disease" ）， are also due to protein misfolding. If
scientists can solve the puzzle Of why proteins misfold and discover hOW tO correct
that, then diseases now considered untreatable can be cured.

20 ． 14 Carbohydrates
The carbohydrates are so called because many have the empirical formula CH20
which suggests a hydrate of carbon. They include starches, cellulose, and sugars
such as glucose, C6H1206 （ 18L which contains an aldehyde group, and fructose
(fruit sugar), a structural isomer of glucose that is a ketone （ 19 ） · Carbohydrates
have many —OH groups, and so they may also be regarded as alcohols. The pres-
ence of these —OH groups allows them to form numerous hydrogen bonds with
one another and with water.
The polysaccharides are polymers of glucose. They include starch, which we
can digest, and cellulose, which we cannot. Starch is made up Of tWO components:

The nucleus of every living cell contains at least one deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)

(FIG. 20 · 28 ） · The ribonucleic acid （ RNA ） molecule is closely related to DNA. One
Of its functions is tO carry informatlon stored by DNA tO a reglon Of the cell where
that information can be used in protein synthesis.

cle 了 g ” 记 so ” ” “ (NMR) is the principal

The Technique
Many atonuc nuclei behave like small bar magnets, with
energies that depend on their orientation in a magnetic field.
An NM R spectrometer detects transltlons between these
energy levels. The nucleus most widely used for NMR is the
proton, and we shall concentrate on it. Two Other very com-
mon nuclei, those of carbon-12 and oxygen- 16 ， are nonmag-
netic, SO they are invisible in NMR.
Like an electron, a proton possesses the property Of
spm, which fo r elementary purposes can be thought 0f as an
actual spinnmg motlon. Because a proton has an electric
charge and because a moving charge generates a magnetic
field, a proton actS as a tiny bar magnet that can have either
of two orientations, which are denoted 忄（ or and ()r 阝） ·
ln the presence Of a magnetic field these tWO orientatlons
have different energies.
If the sample is exposed tO electromagnetic radiation,
the nuclei are flipped from one onentatlon tO another when
the energy of the incommg photons (which is 乃 " ， where " is
the frequency of the radiation) matches the energy separa-
tlon Of the tWO SPIII orientations. The strong coupling
between nuclei and radiation that occurs when this condi-
tlon iS satisfied iS called 了 eso C 巳 At resonance, the radia-
tlon is strongly absorbed and a sharp peak appears in the
detector output. Superconducting magnets are used tO gen-
erate very high magnetic fields, and resonance requires
radio-frequency radiation at about 500 MHz.
Each proton ln a compound comes intO resonance at a
frequency related tO its location in the molecule. Figure 1 ，
fO r instance, shows the NMR spectrum Of ethanol, and we
see that there are three groups Of peaks and a characteristic
pattern of splitting within the groups. Because all com-
pounds that contain hydrogen gwe a charactenstic NMR
fingerprint, or pattern 0f peaks, many can be recognized by
comparing the observed pattern with a library Of patterns
from kn own substances or by calculating the expected pattern
of lines.
The ChemicaI Shift
The separation Of the absorption 1ntO groups Of lines is due
tO the different proton envlronments within the molecule.
Thus, in ethanol, CH3CH20H, three protons are present
the methyl group (CH3), two are present in the e 到 e ” e
group (CH2), and one is present in the hydroxyl group (OH).
The applied magnetic field acts on the electrons in these
three groups and causes them tO circulate throughout the
nuclear framework. These circulating charged particles give
rise tO an additional magnetic field, and SO the protons
each of the three groups experience a local magnetic field
that is not the same as the applied magnetic field. Because

Let's imagine that we are a proton in the methyl group

Magnetic Resonance lmaging
N/1agnet1C resonance lmagmg IS a nomnvaslve structural
technique f0 r complex systems of molecules, such as people.
ln its simplest form, MRl portrays the concentration Of pro-
tons in a sample. If the sample—which may be a living
human body—is exposed tO a uniform magnetic field in an
NMR spectrometer and if we work at a resolution that does
not show a ny chemical shifts or fine structure, then the pro-
tons g1Ve rlse tO a single resonance line. However, if the
magnetic field varies linearly across the sample, the protons
will resonate at different frequenues according tO their loca-
tlon in the field. Moreover, the intensity Of the resonance at
a given field will be proportional to the number of protons
at the spatial location corresponding tO that particular field
value. If the field gradient is rotated intO different orienta-
tlons, another portrayal Of the concentratlon Of protons
through the sample is obtained. After several such measure-
ments Of the absorption intensity, the data can be analyzed
on a computer, which constructs a two-dimensional image

molecules, are interactmg with the central O atom through hydrogen
bonds. Thus, more than one orientation is possible in th e crystal and
entropy will not be zero at T = 0 ·

13 · 85 To use qualitative analyses, the sample must first be
dissolved. This can be accomplished by digesting the sample with
concentrated HN03 and then diluting the resulting solution. Once
the sample is dissolved and diluted, an aqueous solution containing

solution is acidic. The remaining solution can then be treated with
H2S. ln acidic solution, Bi2S3 will precipitate but NiS will not. Once
the Bi2S3 has been precipitated, the pH of the solution can be raised by
addition of base. Once this is done, Ni S should precipitate.

reverse Of that Of the more IOnic halides, because the ions are not easily
hydrated, which makes them less soluble.

19 · 81 C8H10 will have an absorption maxlmum at a longer
wavelength. Molecular orbital theory predicts that electrons in
conjugated hydrocarbons (molecules that contam a chain Of carbon
atoms with alternating single and double bonds) become delocalized
and are free tO move up and down the chain Of carbon atoms. Such
electrons may be described using the one-dimensional "particle in
a box ” model introduced in Chapter 1 · According to this model, as
the bOX tO which electrons are confined lengthens, the quantized
energy states available tO th e electrons get closer together. As a result,
the energy needed tO excite an electron from uppermost filled state
tO the next higher state is lower fO r electrons confined tO longer
boxes. Therefore, lower-energy photons, i.e., photons with longer
wavelengths, will be absorbed by the C8H10 molecule because it
provides a longer ' ' box ” than C6H8.

because there is no fixed point at which the chain-lengthening process
